title: refactor(email): invert ingestion↔gateway layering, converge post-sync pipeline, unify upserts (2/2)
body:
Part 2 of the email debt-paydown stack. Fixes the layering inversion between `email_ingestion` and `gateway`, then uses the resulting seam to converge three divergent sync pipelines into one.

> **Stack:** #73 → #74 (part 1) → **this PR**.
> Review #74 first. Retargets automatically as the stack merges.

---

## C2 — invert the `email_ingestion` → `gateway` layering

The ingestion scheduler lazy-imported `gateway.routes.email` to run its post-sync jobs (rules / categorize / classify / auto-archive / digest / follow-up / subscription). The **lower** layer reached **up** into the higher one, so neither package could be built or tested independently.

Direction is now correct:

- **`email_ingestion/post_sync.py`** — a hook registry (7 optional callbacks).
- **`gateway/routes/email/scheduler_hooks.py`** — registers the gateway callbacks. `auto_run_rules_for_account` absorbs the settings-gating that had leaked into the scheduler (it's gateway-domain logic).
- **`main.py`** lifespan calls `register_email_post_sync_hooks()` before sync starts.
- **`scheduler.py` now has ZERO gateway imports** — it invokes hooks via `run_hook()`, preserving the exact same new-mail gating, ordering, `try`/`except` and log messages.

Behaviour-preserving: same jobs, same order. An unregistered hook is a no-op, so `email_ingestion` runs standalone (tests, gateway-less processes).

## H1 — converge the post-sync pipeline

One shared `process_new_mail(account_id)` — auto-run rules → categorize senders → classify threads (Reply Zero) → auto-archive, **each step failure-isolated** — now runs from **all** sync paths via the `on_new_mail` hook:

| Path | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| Scheduler loop | 4 separate steps | one `hooks.on_new_mail` call |
| Manual sync (`trigger_sync`) | re-classified inline only — **mail showed up unlabeled until the next 20s poll** | enqueues `process_new_mail` as a FastAPI `BackgroundTask`; Sync stays fast *and* rules/labels/archive actually apply |
| Graph webhook (`_webhook_sync`) | rules + classify only | full pipeline |

Digest / follow-up / subscription stay every-cycle scheduler-only (time-gated). Registry simplified from 4 granular new-mail hooks to 1 `on_new_mail` orchestrator.

## C1 — collapse 5 message-upsert copies into one helper

The `email_messages` upsert SQL was copy-pasted across four received-message ingest paths — manual sync, the background scheduler, the on-demand history backfill, and the inbound SMTP/webhook handler. **The copies had drifted:**

- `unsubscribe_link` was bound in only two of them
- scheduler/webhook stored bodies **untruncated**
- the backfill **clobbered `snippet`** with an empty re-send

Unified behind **`email_ingestion.persist.upsert_message`** — which lives in the *lower* layer, so the gateway calls **down** into it (consistent with C2 above). One `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT` with a conflict-mode switch (`update` for sync/scheduler/backfill, `nothing` for inbound), consistent body truncation, and `COALESCE`-preserve for body/snippet/`unsubscribe_link` so a headers-only re-sync never clobbers a hydrated body or an already-parsed unsubscribe link. **Net −334 LOC.**

The parity guard is rewritten from *"keep the copies in sync"* to *"there is one helper and no ingest path re-grows its own INSERT"*, plus a DB-free unit test for conflict modes, truncation, unsubscribe binding and attachment persistence.

## Frontend — "processing" sync state

H1 made `/email/sync` return as soon as new mail is persisted, running the pipeline in the background. The old `triggerSync` fetched once — too early to see the labels/categories/auto-archive applied a moment later, so they only appeared on the 20s poll.

`triggerSync` now flips to a **`processing`** state after the response: it shows what's already persisted immediately, then runs two catch-up refetches (`softRefresh` + `fetchFolders` at 2.5s and 6s) so labels land and auto-archived mail drops out without a manual refresh — degrading gracefully into the 20s poll if the pipeline runs long. Catch-up timers are module-scoped and cancelled on re-sync, so they survive unmounts and account switches.

The sync controls (top-bar button, `MailboxActions`, `EmailList` pull-to-refresh) treat `processing` as busy so the spinner keeps turning, and `MailboxActions` shows a "Processing new mail…" hint.

---

title: docs(impeccable): add flex-1 nav anti-pattern to the layout checklist
body:
Adds one entry to the `impeccable` skill's layout anti-pattern checklist, capturing a lesson learned from the mobile-nav work.

**The anti-pattern:** a row of equal siblings that must *all* stay visible (bottom-nav tabs, a segmented toolbar) built with a hard `min-w-[Npx]` per item plus padding inside `justify-around`. It overflows the moment the summed minimum exceeds the smallest target viewport (320px).

What makes it worth writing down is that it's a **latent** regression — correct at 3 items, clipped when someone later adds a 4th or 5th. The fix is `flex-1 min-w-0` so siblings distribute the row and can never overflow; fixed min-widths + horizontal scroll are reserved for lists whose item count is genuinely unbounded.

### Notes for review

- **Docs only** — one line, in [`.github/skills/impeccable/SKILL.md`](.github/skills/impeccable/SKILL.md). `pr-check.yml` has `paths-ignore: "**.md"`, so no CI will run here; that's expected.
- **Not clobbered by the skills sync.** `skills-upstream-sync.yml` only mirrors into `skills/upstream/`, so this edit under `.github/skills/` is safe.
- **No code change needed.** I grepped `min-w-[Npx]` across `workbench/control_plane/src` — the remaining hits are popovers, badges, tables and already-`flex-1` toolbars. No nav currently exhibits the anti-pattern, so this is purely preventive.

### Why it was orphaned

This commit sat on top of `chore/impeccable-nav-antipattern`, whose other 10 commits were the agent blob-store / memory-scopes work that already shipped in #60, plus an email attachment-thumbnails commit that also reached `main`. This one line was the only thing left behind — cherry-picked onto a clean branch off `main`.

title: docs(workflows): visual workflow editor — analysis, architecture RFC + interactive mockup
body:
Lands the design work for a **Visual Workflow Editor** — a no-code, node-based builder that composes automated workflows from CommandCenter's existing agents, tools and integrations, triggered on command, by schedule, by webhook, or by an inbound event.

**This PR is documentation only. There is no implementation and nothing here executes.** It is merged to capture the analysis so it stops living on an orphan branch.

### What's in it

- [`docs/workflow-editor/README.md`](docs/workflow-editor/README.md) — RFC: analysis of Copilot Studio (the UX model), [Sim](https://github.com/simstudioai/sim) and [open-agent-builder](https://github.com/firecrawl/open-agent-builder) (the implementation patterns), plus a proposed architecture and phased plan.
- [`docs/workflow-editor/mockup.html`](docs/workflow-editor/mockup.html) — a standalone interactive mockup of the three-pane editor (palette · canvas · inspector).

### The core recommendation

Build a "Workflows" surface in the control plane that **reuses the existing runtime** rather than adding a second one — `call_agent`, the integrations registry, the ingestion/webhook pipeline, AG-UI SSE streaming.

The load-bearing architectural rule, validated by both reference implementations: **separate the edit-model from the run-model.** Persist an editable graph; compile it to a flat, versioned execution DAG at run time. Never execute your database rows directly.

| Concern | Proposed |
|---|---|
| Canvas | React Flow (`@xyflow/react`) |
| Persistence | New Postgres tables + a migration (no workflow tables exist today) |
| Execution | Compile the visual graph to a MAF `WorkflowBuilder` of executors + edges |
| Triggers | Extend the existing ingestion pipeline + `webhook_routes` with a binding table |
| Streaming | Reuse AG-UI SSE + the Redis stream-relay |

### Reviewer notes

- **Version claims verified.** The RFC leans on `agent-framework-core >=1.8.0` for `WorkflowBuilder`; the repo currently resolves **1.8.1**, and `WorkflowBuilder` graphs do build on it today. So the recommended engine is available now, not blocked.
- **One caveat the RFC doesn't call out:** the separate MAF *orchestrations* package (Sequential / Concurrent / GroupChat / Magentic) requires core **≥1.9**, so those patterns are not reachable until we upgrade. `HandoffBuilder` also rejects Copilot-SDK agents, while Sequential/Concurrent/GroupChat/Magentic do not. Worth folding into the doc if we act on it.
- Scope is honest about being **mostly green-field on the graph/UI side** while heavily reusing the runtime — this is a multi-phase epic, not a next-sprint item.

### Why it was orphaned

The work sat on `claude/visual-workflow-editor-aaqqof` and never got a PR. Cherry-picked onto a clean branch off `main`; no other content on that branch.

title: feat(email): Email Cleaner covers the whole mailbox, uncapped; folder-scoped inbox filters
body:
The cleaner could not show its own categories and could not finish its own work. Three separate caps were involved, only one of which was defensible.

## Scope

Rename **Inbox Cleaner → Email Cleaner** and scope `/senders` to the whole mailbox (excluding trash/junk/drafts) instead of the inbox.

The inbox scope made the Marketing and Cold Email chips **structurally unfillable**: those preset rules label *and archive* on Gmail, so the mail had already left the inbox by the time the cleaner looked. Those chips were advertising categories the view was incapable of showing.

## Caps

The caps were never a database limit — one set-based `UPDATE` costs the same at 50 rows or 50,000. They existed because the **provider** was walked one HTTP call per message. The constraint was applied at the wrong layer.

- **`bulk_action`: no row cap.** The old `_BULK_MAX = 1000` silently truncated — "archive everything from this sender" stopped at 1000 and reported success. Now one set-based `UPDATE ... RETURNING`. Uncapping makes an *unfiltered* request mean "trash my entire mailbox", so that is refused explicitly — the right guard, since a cap truncates the legitimate case just as hard as the dangerous one.
- **Provider batching.** New `BaseEmailProvider.bulk_apply`, overridden by Gmail with `batchModify` (1000 ids per request). Archiving a 40k backlog is 40 calls, not 40,000. Trash stays on its own endpoint rather than assuming `batchModify` accepts the `TRASH` system label on a destructive path. Per-item failures are isolated so one 404 cannot strand the rest.
- **Outlook re-keys persisted.** `/move` returns a *new* message id; the old reconciler discarded it, leaving every bulk-archived Outlook message pointing at a dead id until a full re-sync.
- **Sweep runs to completion.** Pages until the mailbox runs dry instead of stopping at 2000, and reports `exhausted` so it never implies "done" when it means "stopped". The offset advances by exactly the rows that stayed uncategorized — categorized rows drop out of the query, no-evidence rows never do. Evidence is read **once** and held: refreshing per page would let the sweep's own projections become evidence for further projections.
- **Sender list paging.** `limit` is a payload bound, not a scope bound — `offset` paging plus "Load more" so the quiet tail is reachable, not merely counted.
- **`restore_provider_labels`:** one statement per distinct label-set instead of one per message (~20 round-trips instead of 40,000, on a synchronous route).

## Inbox filters

- **New `GET /email/messages/facets`** — per-label counts plus `unread`/`uncategorized` for a folder. The chip row now shows only filters with mail behind them: the fixed list offered "Cold Email" in Sent and "Needs reply" in Drafts, and an empty result from a chip cannot be distinguished from a broken one. An *active* chip stays visible at zero, so filtering never strands you with no way back.
- **New `uncategorized` filter** (chip, filter menu, `is:uncategorized`). The label vocabulary moves from `automation/senders.py` to `core.py` so the inbox chip and the Email Cleaner's Uncategorized tab resolve to the **same mail** — two definitions across two views of one mailbox is the drift this package keeps paying down. It means "carries none of the RULE labels", not "has no labels at all".

## Fixes

- The sender pill showed **"Blocked"** for auto-archived senders with no unsubscribe link. That discriminated on a property of the *sender*, not of how the decision was reached — so a deliberate auto-archive rendered as a status the user never picked, implying a fourth state that doesn't exist. The provider filter it meant to convey already has its own "Filtered" pill. Now always **"Auto-archive"**; "Kept" → **"Keep"**.
- Picking a **search scope** now navigates the sidebar there, so the list, the bar and the sidebar name the same place.

## Verification

428 unit tests pass (27 new), `tsc --noEmit` clean, `next build` clean, blocking ruff gate clean.

New tests cover: sweep paging/termination and offset correctness, Gmail batch chunking and its per-message fallback, provider id re-keys, per-item failure isolation, the unfiltered-bulk guard, and one shared definition of "uncategorized".

**Not verified against the live mailbox** — no DB access from this session. The Gmail-specific paths (`batchModify`, label restore) are reasoned + unit-tested only.

title: fix(email): stop the sweep blanket-labelling internal mail; honest restore on non-Gmail
body:
Found by inspecting the **live production mailbox**, which turned out to be Microsoft/Outlook — not Gmail. Three problems, one of them a regression introduced by #78 widening the sweep from the inbox to the whole mailbox.

## 1. Domain consensus fired on the user's own company domain

The sweep falls back to a per-domain consensus for senders with no history of their own. It excluded shared free-mail hosts (`gmail.com` etc.) but **not the user's employer domain** — which is a shared domain in exactly the same way: every colleague sends from it, so "same domain" implies nothing about the sender.

Live numbers from production:

| | |
|---|---|
| `@fracktal.in` labelled Notification | 12 |
| other categories on that domain | 2 |
| dominance | **0.857** |
| `_DOMAIN_MIN_DOMINANCE` | 0.9 |
| margin | **0.043** — six more Notification-labelled internal mails |

Had it crossed, the sweep would have stamped **Notification onto 3,307 uncategorized internal colleague emails**, each also writing the label upstream to Outlook.

`_decide` now refuses a domain consensus for the account's own domain plus any configured org domains — the same set `sender_scope` treats as internal. Sender-level evidence still applies to a *specific* internal address; only the blanket is refused.

## 2. The sweep scanned Sent

Cleanup categories describe *inbound bulk mail* — a message you wrote is never a Newsletter. Widening the scope pulled 434 sent/self-addressed messages in. Now excluded by folder **and** by from-address, since self-addressed mail can sit outside Sent.

## 3. `restore-labels` lied on providers that can't read labels back

Only Gmail implements `fetch_label_assignments`; the base returns `{}`. That empty result is indistinguishable from *"your mailbox has no labels"* — so the UI told an Outlook user with **1,909 labelled messages** that they had none, the exact opposite of the truth the repair path exists to restore.

Added an explicit `SUPPORTS_LABEL_READBACK` capability flag, checked *before* authenticating, with a UI message that explains the provider limitation instead.

## Verification

433 unit tests pass (5 new), `tsc` clean, `next build` clean, blocking ruff gate clean.

Blast radius confirmed against the live database: sweep scope drops 3,931 → 3,497 with the Sent exclusion, and the domain guard protects the 3,307 internal messages above.

title: feat(email): backfills don't draft by default; rename Assistant → AI Settings in code
body:
## Drafting is opt-in on "Process past emails"

The backfill ran **every** matched rule action, including `REPLY` / `DRAFT_EMAIL` / `FORWARD`. Each spends a call on the drafting model — on conversations that, being months old, have usually ended. Pointing the date picker at 90 days silently generated (and billed for) a pile of drafts to delete by hand.

`draft_replies` now defaults to **false**. Labels, folders, archiving and mark-read still apply: **filing** old mail is the point of a backfill; **answering** it is a separate, deliberate choice.

- Dialog gains a `Categorize only / Also draft replies` toggle, off by default, with copy that states the cost *before* it's switched on rather than after the drafts appear.
- The job reports `drafts_skipped`, so a run that suppressed drafting can't read as one where the rules ran in full.
- **Live runs are unaffected** and still draft — that's the feature working as intended on a conversation that's actually live. Pinned by a test.
- `_without_drafting` returns a **copy**: the rule dict comes from the shared rule cache, so mutating it would disable drafting for every later message in the run *and* for the live runner.

This also removes the sharpest edge of the open **H5** gap (process-past skips the thread-status re-determination that stops a resolved thread auto-drafting). H5 itself is still open — the label-stacking and missing thread status remain.

## Naming

The UI has said "AI Settings" for a while; the code still said `Assistant`. Reading the code and describing it produced a name the user couldn't find on screen — which is exactly what happened.

Renamed **the scene only**: `AssistantView` → `AISettingsView`, `components/automation/assistant/` → `ai-settings/`, feature key `"assistant"` → `"ai-settings"`.

Deliberately **not** renamed: the email assistant **agent** — the chat, `agent-email-assistant`, the message `role`, and `email_assistant_settings`. That genuinely is an assistant, and those settings genuinely configure it; renaming them would be the same confusion in reverse, plus a migration for a label change.

Also renamed internal `quickClean` → `archiveOldMail` to match the button that actually renders ("Archive old mail"). The old name existed only in source and got quoted at the user as if it were something they could look for.

## Verification

441 unit tests pass (8 new), `tsc --noEmit` clean, `next build` clean, blocking ruff gate clean. The rename was verified by `tsc`, which caught the one site the scripted pass missed.

title: fix(email): H5 — thread status parity across both rule paths, and let the classifier reach old mail
body:
Measured against the live mailbox **first**, which reshaped the fix — my original H5 description was partly wrong.

## What was actually wrong

| symptom | reality |
|---|---|
| auto-drafting into dead threads | **already fixed** in #80 — backfills don't draft |
| label stacking | **1 message**, 68 threads. Real, but minor |
| **Reply Zero coverage** | **295 of 3,487 threads — 8.5%.** This was the real damage |

`_maybe_classify_threads` selected *"the newest 200 threads from the last 30 days"* and then skipped the already-classified ones — which, on a real mailbox, is all of them. It spun without reaching anything older, and **mail past a month could never acquire a status at all**.

It also wrote the status row but never called `_reconcile_thread_labels`, so superseded labels stayed on older messages — 68 threads carrying Reply AND Awaiting AND Done. The status row and the labels are two views of **one** decision; only the second was written. `_process_past_emails_job` did neither.

## Fixes

**Coverage.** The classifier now selects threads that *need work* in SQL (`LEFT JOIN email_thread_status`, no date window), so each cycle makes real progress. **Inbox threads ordered first** — filed threads outnumber live ones ~10:1, and ordering by date alone put 2,622 already-handled threads ahead of the 273 that might still need a reply.

**Cost.** Inbound-last threads the user already **filed** resolve to FYI deterministically — filing it *is* the answer. No model call: these are the bulk of an old mailbox, and re-litigating them would be thousands of calls on mail already put away. `preserve_done` keeps an explicit Done intact.

Net: ~273 model calls to drain the backlog instead of ~3,191.

**Parity.** Both paths now record status *and* collapse labels. The backfill does it **after** the loop, per thread, from each thread's newest in-range message — it cannot do it inline, because the live runner reads newest-first and takes the first message per thread while the backfill reads **oldest-first by design**. Inline projection would let a thread's oldest message decide its status, which is exactly what the live runner's ordering exists to prevent. Threads with newer mail outside the range are skipped rather than moved backwards.

**Tidying.** `_reconcile_thread_labels` handles `provider=None` explicitly instead of relying on `None.set_labels` raising into the best-effort handler.

## Verification

451 unit tests pass (10 new), `tsc` clean, blocking ruff gate clean.

The new parity suite asserts both paths do both writes, that the two jobs iterate in opposite directions, that projection happens after the loop, and that the backfill projection spends no model calls — the drift-guard whose absence caused this.

Query plans for the new selection were checked against the production database: it returns 200 inbox-first rows that genuinely need work, where the old query found 79.

title: fix(email): run Reply Zero classification every sync cycle, not only on new mail
body:
Follow-up to #81, found by **watching the deploy on the live account**: thread-status coverage climbed 303 → 321 and then stopped dead.

`_maybe_classify_threads` is reached through the `on_new_mail` hook, which the scheduler fires only `if new_mail`. So the classifier — whose entire job is working through a **backlog** — could only run when fresh mail happened to arrive.

On a mailbox with 3,167 unclassified threads, processing 25 per cycle, gated on inbound deliveries, it would never catch up. #81 made the backlog *reachable*; this makes it actually get *reached*.

Registered as its own `classify_threads` post-sync hook, called unconditionally alongside the digest and follow-up hooks. Cheap when idle — the selection query is indexed, returns no rows, and the hook does nothing.

Kept inside the `post_sync` registry rather than importing the gateway from the scheduler, so the C2 layering inversion stays fixed. `test_email_layering` asserts the new hook is registered.

451 tests pass, blocking ruff gate clean.

title: fix(email): repair the follow-up reminder scan, dead in production since it shipped
body:
`_maybe_send_follow_up_reminders` raised on **every** sync cycle:

```
asyncpg.AmbiguousParameterError: could not determine data type of parameter $2
[SQL: SELECT ts.thread_id, ts.status, ts.l…
```

A bare `:param IS NOT NULL` gives asyncpg no type to infer from. The exception was swallowed by a best-effort handler that logged a warning nobody reads — so the feature looked present in the UI and **did nothing at all, for its entire life**.

Reproduced and fixed against the production database: `PREPARE` on the old shape errors, on the new shape it succeeds.

## The fix

The NULL guards were **redundant**: `last_message_at < NULL` is NULL, not TRUE, so an unconfigured window already excludes its own branch. Verified live — passing the NEEDS_REPLY cutoff as NULL returns AWAITING rows only. Removed them, and cast both cutoffs explicitly so the types are unambiguous by construction rather than by inference.

## Staleness ceiling (`_FOLLOW_UP_MAX_AGE_DAYS = 30`)

Repairing a long-dead job releases everything it never processed:

| | |
|---|---|
| AWAITING threads due, no ceiling | **67**, oldest from Oct 2025 |
| ...with `auto_draft` on | one AI nudge **each** |
| AWAITING threads due, 30-day ceiling | **35**, all within the last month |

A reminder about last week is useful; one about last autumn is noise, and those threads are only queued because this job was broken long enough for them to pile up.

Stale threads are **excluded by the query, not stamped as reminded** — `_upsert_thread_status` re-arms `follow_up_reminded_at` when a thread changes hands, so one that comes back to life becomes eligible again on its own merits.

Also ordered newest-first, since the per-cycle `LIMIT` means order decides what gets attention while a backlog exists.

## Landing

Coordinated with the account owner: `follow_up_auto_draft` was switched **off** before this deploys, so the accumulated backlog gets **labelled only** and no drafts are written. Drafting is re-enabled from AI Settings when wanted.

458 tests pass (7 new), blocking ruff gate clean. The regex guard strips comments before checking — a guard that trips on its own explanation just gets the explanation deleted.

title: fix(email): sign above the quoted thread, and stop the drafter quoting it back
body:
Reported from production — an AI-drafted reply went out like this:

```
Hi Suresh,

Noted. Hope the appointment goes well.

On 2026-07-19T14:47:23+00:00, Fracktal Finance wrote:
> Hi,
> Please consider my half day leave by tomorrow 20th July...

Vijay          <- the signature, below the whole quoted thread
```

Two independent defects produced it.

## 1. The signature was appended below the quote — on every signed reply

`build_signed_bodies` appended the signature to the END of `body_text`. The composer sends **one** body — new text + `\n\n` + quote (`ComposePanel.combinedBody()`) — so the signature landed under the entire quoted conversation. This was never specific to AI drafting: it happened on every reply sent from Command Center with a signature configured.

It now splits at the quote boundary and inserts the signature above it, in the text part and the HTML part alike. (No composer currently sends HTML, so the HTML part was derived from the same combined text and had the identical bug.)

## 2. The reply drafter was allowed to quote the thread

`_llm_draft_reply` had rules against sign-offs, placeholders, narration and subject lines — but nothing about quoting. Its sibling `_llm_compose_assist` already said *"no quoted prior conversation"*. Because the report came from an empty-body reply, `/compose-assist` routed to the full reply drafter and inherited the gap.

The ISO-8601 timestamp in that quote header is the tell: it is our own `_fetch_thread_context` formatting (`From: {sender} · {received_at.isoformat()}`) echoed back by the model.

Fixed with the prompt rule, plus a strip in `_clean_draft_body` — a prompt is an instruction, not a guarantee, and the client reattaches the real quote itself, so a model-authored one is always a duplicate.

## Quote detection

New `gateway/routes/email/quoting.py`, the Python counterpart of the frontend's `email/lib/quoting.ts`, using the same markers so client and server agree on where a quote starts.

It diverges in one place, which a test caught: the scan starts at line 0, so a body that is **entirely** a quote (a bare forward) is returned whole rather than cut between two quoted lines. Both splitters return the input untouched whenever they cannot split confidently — a misplaced signature is a far smaller problem than a truncated message.

## Verification

- 18 new tests in `tests/unit/test_email_signature_placement.py`, including the exact reported body
- 475 email unit tests pass; blocking ruff gate clean

title: fix(email): the client quote splitter must scan from line 0 too
body:
Follow-up to #85. Porting `splitQuotedText` to Python surfaced a latent bug in the TypeScript original — #85 fixed it only on the Python side, so the two splitters disagreed.

## The bug

`splitQuotedText` scanned from line **1**, which skips the "is the whole body a quote?" check. A bare forward — a body that is nothing but quoted mail — was therefore cut at its **second** line, making the first quoted line look like new content:

```
> just the quote      <- became "main" (new content)
> and more            <- became "quoted"
```

Three call sites were affected:

- **ComposePanel** and **ConversationView** hand `main` to the AI drafter as the user's own text — so the model was told a stray `> …` line was the draft to improve.
- **MessageContent** leaves `main` uncollapsed in the viewer — so one orphaned quote line showed above the `•••` toggle.

The `idx < 1` guard already handles this correctly once the scan starts at 0: a boundary found at line 0 returns the body whole.

## Parity guards

`quoting.py` and `quoting.ts` must agree on where a quote starts — the client splits the compose box, the server splits at send time, and a disagreement puts the signature relative to a boundary the user never saw. This divergence is exactly that failure mode, caught only because the Python port had a test.

There is no JS test runner in CI (`pr-check.yml` is Python lint + tests only), so the two new guards read the TypeScript source directly: one asserts the scan start, one asserts both sides carry the same six boundary markers.

## Verification

- 20 tests in `tests/unit/test_email_signature_placement.py` (2 new), 477 email unit tests pass
- Blocking ruff gate clean
- `tsc --noEmit` clean — run locally, since CI does not type-check the frontend

title: fix(email): auto-drafting defaults OFF, including at the column level
body:
> "When processing rules on old emails, do not do auto drafting. Otherwise you will burn tokens. Autodrafting off by default if not already the case."

## Process past emails — already correct, verified

`RuleProcessPastRequest.draft_replies` defaults `False` and `_without_drafting` strips `REPLY` / `DRAFT_EMAIL` / `FORWARD` from every match (#80, pinned by `test_email_process_past_drafting.py`). No change needed.

Both columns were created `NOT NULL DEFAULT true` (migrations 26 and 29). **The column default beats any API-side default on an INSERT that omits the column**, and one such INSERT exists: `derive_writing_style` writes `(account_id, writing_style, updated_at)` only. So an account could acquire auto-drafting from a background writing-style capture, having never opened AI Settings.

| switch | what it does |
|---|---|
| `draft_replies` | adds `DRAFT_EMAIL` to the Reply rule → every Reply-classified email costs a drafting-model call |
| `follow_up_auto_draft` | drafts a nudge on awaiting threads |

`follow_up_auto_draft` has the sharper edge: the follow-up scan was dead from the day it shipped until #84, so its first working run releases a whole window's backlog at once. On by default, that backlog arrives as AI drafts.

All three layers now start OFF — the Pydantic model, the GET fallback the UI renders the toggle from, and the column default (migration 81).

## Existing rows are not rewritten

A stored value may be a deliberate choice. Changing what new accounts inherit is the fix; silently flipping a switch a user set is not. Pinned by a test that fails if migration 81 ever grows an `UPDATE`.

title: fix(email): live reply-drafting defaults back ON; only backfills stay opt-in
body:
Corrects #87, which was too broad.

> "so basically, any new rules, any new emails that come in, the drafting will be on. It's just that when I'm processing previous emails using the process past emails feature in ai setting, the drafting should be off by default unless turned on via the checkbox. The regular rules apply as is for new mails that come in."

The rule is about the **age of the thread**, not the act of drafting. A draft on mail that just arrived is the feature — it is waiting when you open the message. A draft on a months-old thread is spend on a conversation that already ended, and a backfill can produce hundreds in one run.

That distinction is enforced where it belongs: `RuleProcessPastRequest.draft_replies` defaults `False` and `_without_drafting` strips `REPLY` / `DRAFT_EMAIL` / `FORWARD` from every backfill match (#80).

## Where each switch lands

| switch | default | why |
|---|---|---|
| `RuleProcessPastRequest.draft_replies` (backfill) | **OFF** | opt-in per run via the "Also draft replies" checkbox |
| `email_assistant_settings.draft_replies` (live) | **ON** | restored — new mail still gets a draft |
| `email_assistant_settings.follow_up_auto_draft` | **OFF** | stays off, see below |

`follow_up_auto_draft` nudges threads **by age** — the hundreds-at-once case, not the just-arrived one. Its scan was also dead from the day it shipped until #84, so the first working run on a long-configured account releases a whole window at once.

`draft_replies` is restored in all three places: the API model, the GET fallback the toggle renders from, and the column default (migration 82).

## Test change worth noting

The column-default assertions no longer check one migration file. They replay every migration in order and assert the value each column **ends up** with — so a later flip cannot leave an earlier assertion passing and wrong. That is precisely the failure mode this PR is correcting.

Existing rows are still never rewritten, now pinned across both migrations.

## Verification

484 email unit tests pass; blocking ruff gate clean.

title: feat(email): process past emails skips mail the rules already ran over
body:
> "when processing past emails, if emails in a particular time frame are already processed, there is no need for you to reprocess them. Only process emails that are unprocessed."

## The problem

The date picker is a **range**, not a cursor. Re-running "last 7 days", or nudging it out to 30, re-covered everything the previous run already did — one classification call per message, to rewrite labels those messages already carry. The job's own docstring admitted it: *"Reprocesses regardless of `rules_processed_at`"*.

The watermark that makes it idempotent already existed, and this job was already **stamping** it. Nothing was reading it.

## The change

`_date_range_clause` gains `unprocessed_only`, and `RuleProcessPastRequest.skip_processed` defaults `True`.

Reprocessing stays reachable — it's how you re-apply after editing a rule — as an explicit **Reprocess everything** toggle, with the cost stated next to it rather than discovered afterwards.

The watermark is only earned by a run that actually applied (live, with a working provider), so a dry-run preview or an auth failure still leaves mail eligible instead of silently consuming it. Pinned by a test that checks the stamp stays inside its guard.

## Reporting: "Processed 0 emails" is now distinguishable from failure

That is the **correct** outcome of a repeat run, and it reads exactly like the feature finding nothing. So the endpoint and the job tracker carry `already_processed`, and the banner says:

> Nothing new to process — 412 emails were already done.

It is counted separately from `skipped`, which means "processed this run, matched no rule" — merging them would report thousands of skips on a run that did nothing at all. The job re-measures the figure after the provider download, since the endpoint's count predates any mail that arrives during it.

## Verification

- 10 new tests in `tests/unit/test_email_process_past_idempotent.py`; 494 email unit tests pass
- Two existing assertions updated for the two new response fields (real contract change)
- Blocking ruff gate clean; `tsc --noEmit` clean

title: feat(email): rename the "Personal" sender category to "Conversation"
body:
> "in the inbox cleaner, I see a pill called 'personal'. Where is this coming from? I do not know."

Fair question — it was findable nowhere else. No message carries it, no rule produces it, it never syncs to the provider. It's a **sender-level** rollup, but the Email Cleaner rendered it identically to the rule categories, under a tooltip claiming it came *"from your rules — same categorization as the rest of the app."* Both halves of that were false for this one chip.

## Why not "Personal"

Wrong twice over:

1. **It implied private-life mail.** All 19 senders it matched on the live account are work colleagues and clients (`suresh@fracktal.in`, `geo@fracktal.in`, …).
2. **It collided with Cold Email** — which is *also* one human writing to another, one-to-one. What separates them is not that a person is involved; it's that a reply came back.

"Conversation" names the actual signal, and matches the labels it's derived from (Reply / Awaiting Reply / FYI / Done).

## The rename had a trap in it

The value is produced in `senders.py` and consumed in `messages.py`, which scores it **+15** in "important emails". Different modules, inlined string literals — a rename reaching only one side would have silently dropped the boost for those senders rather than failing.

Both sides now read `CONVERSATION_SENDER_CATEGORY` / `HUMAN_SENDER_CATEGORIES_LOWER` from `core`, and the ranking query binds the list rather than inlining `'personal'`. Pinned by a test.

## Migration 83 rewrites rows — deliberately, unlike 81/82

Those two changed only defaults, because a stored setting is a choice someone made. This value is a derived rollup the categorize job recomputes on its own schedule. Leaving the old string would strand those 19 senders under a name no code produces any more — invisible to the ranking boost, which matches on the category text.

## Also

- The chip gets an honest tooltip: *"You exchange mail with this sender. Derived from reply activity — not a label on any email, and not synced to your mailbox."*

title: feat(email): deterministic bulk signals + stop counting colleagues as backlog
body:
Phase 1 of making the Email Cleaner work without model calls.

## 1. A fourth `_decide` step: the message's own shape

A `List-Unsubscribe` header (RFC 8058 — transactional mail doesn't carry one), or an unattended local part (`noreply@`, `alerts@`, `billing@`).

The first three steps — learned pattern, sender consensus, domain consensus — **all require the sender to have been labelled before**, so none of them can touch a sender seen for the first time. Measured live, they could reach 265 of the backlog.

Three signals of exactly this kind already existed in `engine.py`, wired only as **negative gates**: allowed to say "not a Reply", never allowed to say "this is a Notification". This promotes them.

Design points:
- **Added last**, so no verdict the user or the rules produced changes. It only reaches mail that was previously getting nothing.
- **Ambiguous role addresses are never classified** (`info@`, `support@`, `team@`). A human answers those, and the Cleaner offers archive on top of whatever gets stamped. Live: `support@fracktal.in` is the user's own helpdesk, 231 messages.
- **Long run-together locals matched by substring** (`customernotification@`, `hdfcbanksmartstatement@`) — but only tokens ≥ 8 chars. Substring matching is how a classifier starts labelling people called Newsom, so the bar is enforced by a test.

## 2. `_CLEANUP_SCOPE` — one definition, shared by the sweep and the badge

It excludes the user's own organisation, because that mail **is not miscategorized** — its correct cleanup category is *none*, and no classifier will ever make a colleague a newsletter.

Measured live: **2,799 of 3,434 "uncategorized" messages were internal human mail.** The badge could never reach zero, and the sweep re-read them every five minutes to conclude nothing.

Carve-out: internal mail carrying a `List-Unsubscribe` stays in scope (an all-staff ESP campaign is worth cleaning). An internal `noreply@` without one is given up to the rules run, which has no scope limit — that's the one thing this trades away, stated in the code.

The badge also previously ran its **own, wider** query — no Sent exclusion, no self exclusion — so it counted mail the sweep could never act on.

## A regression the existing suite caught

The shape step overrode a learned **exclude** pattern. `deals@shop.com` reads as Marketing, but the user had taught via Fix that it isn't. Step 1 honours an exclude by skipping the rule; the shape step has no rule to skip, so `_taught_otherwise` asks separately.

A guess must always yield to an instruction. Now pinned by two tests — including one that a Receipt-exclude must *not* suppress a Notification verdict, since blanket suppression would let one Fix silently mute the whole step.

## Verified against the live account

130 in-scope senders, 635 messages:

```
newly classified : 106 (16%)  — Notification 81, Receipt 19, Marketing 4, Newsletter 2
false positives  : 0
left for a human : 529        — overwhelmingly real external people
```

528 email unit tests pass; blocking ruff gate clean. The scope SQL was `PREPARE`d against production Postgres before shipping.

title: fix(email): the per-cycle sweep budget must bound writes, not reads
body:
> "it says 65 uncategorized emails match patterns you've already taught the assistant... I have already done it and it's showing up again."

## The button was fine; the background sweep was stuck

Verified first: the sweep **is** applying and the labels **do** stick — 121 labels written in two hours, 121/121 still present, zero provider write failures.

The problem is the automatic sweep. It capped the **scan** at 100 rows per cycle, the query is ordered newest-first, and every cycle restarts at offset 0. A block of no-evidence mail at the top was therefore re-read every five minutes and nothing behind it was ever reached:

```
16:17  scanned: 100, applied: 0, no_evidence: 100
16:22  scanned: 100, applied: 0, no_evidence: 100
```

…with 575 older messages waiting behind the wall. The number kept coming back because the backlog genuinely wasn't moving.

## The fix

Reading a page is one indexed query. Writing a label is a provider round-trip. They are not comparable costs and must not share a budget.

- `sweep_uncategorized` gains `max_apply` — bounds labels written
- the scheduler passes a 5000-row scan budget with `max_apply=100`
- the summary reports `apply_capped` separately from `exhausted`, so "stopped early" is never rendered as "the mailbox is clean"
- `max_apply` defaults to `None`, so the manual **Categorize** button still covers the whole mailbox

## The spacing

The preview line was assembled from JSX text nodes split across source lines around `{expressions}`, so the spacing between `email` / `s` / `match` depended on JSX whitespace collapsing — hard to verify by reading and invisible in review. It's now built from explicit strings that read as the sentence they render.

Bonus: the singular case now says *"1 uncategorized email **matches**"* instead of *"match"*.

## Verification

533 email unit tests pass; blocking ruff gate clean; `tsc --noEmit` clean. Five new tests pin the write-vs-read distinction, including one that the cap is checked *before* fetching another page.

title: feat(email): Clean older mail — fetch history, then categorize it with no AI
body:
> "how come my email cleaner still has only 564 emails when my mailbox shows over 43,000?"

Because it had never seen them.

## The cause

`_sync_account` fetches `INITIAL_SYNC_DAYS = 365` on an account's **first** sync, and every sync after that is incremental. Even the *Full re-sync* button is pinned to the same one-year window — so there was **no path in the product** to mail older than a year.

Measured on the live account: **6,803 messages held**, and almost every folder starting within days of `2025-06-30` — exactly one year before the account was connected on `2026-06-20`.

## The feature

The deterministic counterpart of *Process past emails*, placed in the Cleaner where the problem is visible. One action, two phases behind one progress line:

| phase | what happens |
|---|---|
| `downloading` | deep provider sync from a chosen floor — 2y / 3y / 5y / **Everything** |
| `cleaning` | the ordinary sweep over everything now present |

The sweep spends **nothing** on models, so this phase doesn't get more expensive as the backlog grows. It actually gets *better* with history: sender and domain consensus finally have enough labelled mail to fire.

## The load-bearing detail

`_mark_history_rules_processed`.

The scheduled rule run selects `folder = 'inbox' AND rules_processed_at IS NULL`, 50 per cycle, **and classifies each one with a model**. Backfilled mail all arrives with that column NULL — so downloading 36,000 messages would have silently queued 36,000 model calls. Precisely the cost this feature exists to avoid.

Three details make it safe, each pinned by a test:

- **Stamped before the sweep starts.** The rule run fires on its own schedule; every cycle the stamp is late is a cycle it can bill for.
- **The floor is the oldest message held *before* the sync.** Mail arriving during the backfill is newer than that, so it stays eligible for the rules — stamping it would silently stop new mail being classified.
- **The sweep doesn't consult the watermark.** Held-back mail is still fully cleanable, just not by the model.

## Notes

- Storage is not a constraint: 4 KB/message measured → ~178 MB for a full 43,000-message mailbox, against 23 GB free.
- A second run is refused while one is in flight, rather than racing the provider and the shared progress row.
- Progress is reported per phase because downloading years of mail takes minutes, and a job that reports nothing until it finishes reads as stuck.

## Verification

11 new tests; 544 email unit tests pass; blocking ruff gate clean; `tsc --noEmit` clean.

title: fix(email): history hold-back was inert, and it hid mail from AI categorization
body:
## The defect

`_backfill_and_clean_job` used `MIN(received_at)` over the whole account as the floor for "this is downloaded history, keep it away from the model". On the live account that value is **2019-06-28** — a single message in Trash. A full backfill would have stamped roughly zero rows, and the scheduled rule run would then have classified every backfilled inbox message at one model call each.

The test asserted the floor was *passed correctly*. It never asserted the floor was *meaningful*.

The floor is now the job itself: `created_at >= started` identifies exactly the rows this backfill inserted (`created_at` is never in the upsert's `DO UPDATE SET`, so a re-sync preserves it), and `received_at < started` keeps mail that arrives mid-backfill eligible.

## Held back ≠ processed

The hold-back wrote `rules_processed_at`. That is the one column meaning "the rules have decided about this", and **Process past emails skips it**. So once the floor worked, backfilled history would have been permanently invisible to AI categorization — and the UI would have reported it as *already processed*.

> Ensure this does not interfere with AI categorization of past emails.

Migration 84 gives the second state its own column:

| | automatic per-cycle run | Process past emails | deterministic sweep |
|---|---|---|---|
| `rules_processed_at` | skips | skips | ignores |
| `rules_held_back_at` | skips | **reaches** | ignores |

Plus a partial index matching the live run's predicate — without it a full backfill leaves ~36,000 held-back rows inside `idx_email_messages_unprocessed` for every 5-minute cycle to scan through to find 50 candidates.

## Cost guard

The dialog had a free date picker and a Process button with nothing between them.

- **`GET /rules/process-past/estimate`** — `will_process` is `eligible` clamped to the row limit. The job reads `LIMIT :limit` and the tracker reports *that* as the total, so a 4,000-email range read as "processed everything" when it processed the oldest 1,000.
- **366-day cap, enforced in the API** — a bound that lives only in the client is not a bound. Checked before any DB work, so the refusal is cheap. An open-ended range is refused too: now that a whole mailbox can be synced, no start date means every message ever received.
- **The dialog** shows the count on the button, warns above 500, names the truncation, and says how much of the range is freshly-fetched history.

> limit processing to a few months up to a year

## Verification

- 558 email unit tests pass; blocking ruff gate clean; `tsc --noEmit` clean
- 13 new tests, incl. the regression itself (`test_the_floor_is_the_job_not_the_oldest_message_held`) and both halves of the split (`test_the_live_rule_run_skips_held_back_mail`, `test_process_past_still_reaches_held_back_mail`)
- Live figures in this PR were measured against production

title: feat(email): learned patterns need approval before the cleaner projects them
body:
> Stacked on #94. `pr-check` only runs against `main`, so this gets **no CI** until #94 merges — verified locally instead (574 email tests, blocking ruff gate, `tsc --noEmit`, all clean).

## What I found reviewing the learning patterns

**45 patterns on the live account. Every single one `source='AI'`.** Zero from Fix, zero from a label changed in the mail client, zero typed by hand.

So every pattern in the system was inferred by the machine from its own output. `_sender_consistent_for_rule` requires three matches to one rule and no other rule ever — which measures *consistency*, not *correctness*. If the classifier was wrong three times, the gate entrenches the error rather than catching it.

And a pattern is not a small thing: it short-circuits the classifier completely, and it is the **first and strongest** evidence `_decide` uses in the cleaner, which then offers archive / unsubscribe / delete on top. Top reach measured: 46 messages from one pattern.

**The review screen couldn't support review.** Settings → Learned patterns → Manage showed a sender, a rule, a source badge and a delete button. "Is this pattern right?" is unanswerable from that, which is why 45 of them accumulated untouched.

## The gate

Migration 85 adds `approved_at` / `rejected_at`. Two asymmetries, both deliberate:

**Includes vs excludes.** An include *asserts* a category; an exclude only ever *prevents* one. There is nothing to approve about "this sender is not Marketing" — gating it would make the cleaner label mail the user explicitly said it shouldn't. Only includes are gated.

**Cleaner vs classifier.** The classifier keeps using unreviewed patterns — its alternative is an LLM call, so a pattern there *saves* money and a mistake is one message the user can Fix. The cleaner's alternative is leaving mail uncategorized, and it applies one pattern across every matching message in the mailbox. Different blast radius, different bar.

Patterns the user authored (`FIX`/`USER`/`LABEL_ADDED`/`LABEL_REMOVED`) are approved on creation — that act *is* the confirmation.

## Rejection has to stick

Rejecting **keeps the row**. Deleting it would let the auto-learner re-infer the same pattern from the same sender within the hour, so rejection would be a gesture rather than a decision. `_upsert_rule_pattern` refuses to resurrect a rejected pattern — unless the *user* overturns it via Fix or a label change.

Resetting the rules now carries review state across the reseed. Without that, one reset silently un-approves everything.

## The screens

- **Learned patterns** — each row shows its reach ("about 46 emails"), with Approve / Reject per row and "Approve all N". Pending ones are visually separated; `SUBJECT` patterns no longer mislabel themselves as "From".
- **Email Cleaner** — "N patterns the assistant taught itself are waiting for your approval · would categorize about M more emails". A gate with no number and no route to the decision reads as the cleaner having got worse.

## Sequencing

This closes the loop the request describes: **AI-categorize a bounded window** (now cost-capped by #94) → **patterns populate** → **you approve them** → **the cleaner projects them across the whole mailbox for free**.

One honest note: on this account all 45 patterns are includes, so **all 45 go dark until reviewed**. That is the requested behaviour, and the Cleaner says so — but it is a real, visible change on first deploy.

title: fix(email): the auto-learn gate enforced neither of the two bars it claimed
body:
You asked me to verify the learned patterns are actually working. They were not. **24 of the 45 patterns on your account — 53% — would not be learned under this commit.**

## What the gate claimed vs what it did

`_sender_consistent_for_rule` documented "at least 3 consistent matches, and no other rule ever matched this sender". It enforced neither.

**1. Dry runs taught.** The filter excluded `SKIPPED`/`REJECTED` but not `PENDING` — which is exactly what a *preview* logs.

```
arvind@exinous.com → Calendar
  7 log rows · 1 distinct message · 5 of them PENDING previews
```

Pressing "Test" on one email three times wrote a permanent pattern. A dry run is documented as changing nothing.

**2. It counted log rows, not messages.** `COUNT(*)` over a table that gets a row per rule per run.

```
donotreply@gst.gov.in       10 rows → 1 message
ar.zstoreind@zohocorp.com    9 rows → 1 message
almashines@mails.org.in     10 rows → 1 message
```

Re-running a backfill over the same mail manufactured its own evidence. Now `COUNT(DISTINCT message_id)`, and the 616 live rows with a NULL `message_id` no longer count — nothing can corroborate them.

**3. The "no other rule" invariant was unenforceable.** `multi_rule_execution` is **ON** for your account, so one message legitimately matches several rules — and `_apply_and_log_match` is called once per match *in a loop*, so the first rule's check reads a log that doesn't yet contain its own siblings.

```
Info@yourstory.com → pinned to Marketing
  but every message matches  Marketing + Newsletter
                          or Marketing + Cold Email
```

The pattern then short-circuits the classifier down to the single pinned rule, silently discarding the other half of a multi-rule outcome. Fixed with `sole_match`: an ambiguous classification teaches nothing, because pinning a sender only means something when the answer was unambiguous.

**4. People were pinned to cleanup categories.** The existing guard refuses to pin a sender to a conversation-status *rule*, but nothing stopped pinning a *human* to Receipt or Calendar.

```
midhun.vm@link-innovations.com → Calendar   (has Awaiting Reply, Done)
debesh@metafora.sg             → Receipt    (has Awaiting Reply)
```

Both send documents *and* ask questions. Pinned, their next real request is filed as a receipt. `_sender_is_a_correspondent` uses the conversation-status labels as evidence — they're assigned per-thread from the whole conversation, so their presence proves a real exchange — and **fails closed** on error.

## Replaying the fixed gate over all 45

| verdict | n | why |
|---|---|---|
| ok | 21 | would be learned again |
| AMBIGUOUS | 8 | sender routinely matches 2+ rules |
| THIN | 11 | 1–2 distinct messages, not 3 |
| CORRESPONDENT | 5 | a person you actually converse with |

## Also fixed

Pattern **reach** in the review screen no longer counts Trash/Junk. `news-noreply@news.pitchbook.com` showed "about 46 emails" — all 46 sitting in Trash, 0 labelled. That number argued *for* approving a pattern using your own deletion of its mail as supporting evidence.

## Verified clean, not changed

The deterministic sweep logs `rule_id = NULL` and the gate requires `rule_id IS NOT NULL`, so the Email Cleaner's own output does **not** feed back into learning. I checked because a closed loop there would be self-reinforcing with no new information; it isn't one.

586 email unit tests (12 new, one per defect with the live evidence in the docstring); blocking ruff gate clean.

title: feat(email): rebuild Analytics around what the user can act on
body:
## The range selector was decorative

`Analytics` read **"Inbox activity for the last 30 days"** above figures with no date predicate at all. On the live account that day:

| card said | actual 30-day figure |
|---|---|
| Total **6,803** | 1,431 |
| Unread **4,517** | 739 |

6,803 reaches back to a stray 2019 message in Trash. Only the volume chart and the rule counters moved when the selector moved.

Beyond the lie, the panels were inert — read-rate, starred count and per-folder totals answer *"what is in my mailbox?"*, which the sidebar already answers, and nothing follows from the answer. Top senders ranked by raw volume, which on an internal-heavy mailbox just lists colleagues.

**The rule applied: a metric ships only if the user can act on it, and every list ends in a button.**

## What replaced it

- **Responsiveness, per thread** — median + p90 time to first reply, and what share of arriving conversations got answered. Threads enter by *arrival*, so the rate can't be gamed by a quiet week clearing old debt. The unreplied count is shown next to the median rather than folded into it.
- **Reply backlog, both directions, bucketed by age** — deliberately *not* windowed, and labelled "right now" so it never inherits the range caption. Carries **Reply Zero coverage**: "3 need a reply" means nothing if only a twelfth of threads were ever classified — a state this mailbox has genuinely been in (295 of 3,487).
- **Senders you have never once replied to** — ranked by unread, annualised (`~2,725/yr`), wired to the Email Cleaner.
- **Category mix vs the previous period** — doubles as a classifier-coverage read-out.
- **Automation *trust*, not just throughput** — how often you overruled it, how many actions failed at the provider, how many learned patterns sit unreviewed.

## What this immediately found on the live account

- **192 failed actions in 30 days.** Rows logged `APPLIED` whose Graph call returned 404 (146 `LABEL`, 137 `MOVE_FOLDER`) — the mailbox was never actually changed, and nothing surfaced it. Also 5 × `'asyncpg.pgproto.pgproto.UUID' object has no attribute 'strip'` in `DRAFT_EMAIL`, a real bug.
- **21 learned patterns unreviewed**, so the Email Cleaner is projecting none of them.
- **142 uncategorized arrivals** in 30 days vs 159 in the 30 before — classification is not keeping up.

Each is a separate follow-up, not fixed here.

## Verification

Rendered and screenshotted at 1440 / 860 / 390 px against live-shaped data. That caught a bug static review did not: the volume chart drew **nothing**, because `items-end` makes each column shrink to content height, so the bars' percentage heights resolved against `auto`. Zero horizontal overflow at all three widths.

Backend SQL was run against the production database before the UI was written.

**20 new tests** (606 email tests green). The load-bearing one runs the real endpoint and asserts every statement it issues carries `:days` unless it is one of three levels exempt by design — per-helper assertions would have missed the regression, since two helpers receive their window as an argument.

title: fix(email): rules that changed nothing no longer report that they did
body:
Follow-up to #99, which found this on its first run.

## What was happening

**138 rule applications in 30 days returned 404 from Graph.** Every one logged `status='APPLIED'` with `actions_taken='[]'`. The rule matched, the mailbox was never touched, and no surface said so.

### Cause 1 — we invalidated our own message id

Outlook re-keys a message when it moves: `/move` returns a new id and the old one 404s. Inside a single rule, `_apply_rule_actions` already threads the new id forward. But the per-match loop calls it **once per matched rule from a row fetched before the loop**, so with `multi_rule_execution` on (it is) the second rule called Graph with the id the first rule's `MOVE_FOLDER` had just invalidated.

Traced end to end on one message:

| 03:57:43 | Cold Email | `MOVE_FOLDER` → succeeds, message re-keyed |
| 03:57:43 | Marketing | `LABEL` + `MOVE_FOLDER` → **404 on the stale id** |

46 of the 138 had a sibling rule that moved the message in the same run.

Fixed by re-reading the current `provider_message_id` before acting. `_apply_rule_actions` already persists it, so no signature threading is needed, and it also catches a re-key done by anything else.

### Cause 2 — the provider racing us (not fixable here)

The other ~92 are Outlook's own junk/delete filtering re-keying or removing a message between our sync and our call; 92 of the 138 ended in `trash`. Not preventable from this side — which is exactly why the status has to be honest about it.

### And `APPLIED` was load-bearing

- `_sender_consistent_for_rule` counts `APPLIED` rows as evidence → **three failed runs were three votes for pinning a sender to a rule forever**, off a mailbox that was never modified. This is a **fourth** defect in the gate audited in #97 (after dry runs counting, log rows counting as messages, and multi-rule ambiguity).
- Analytics counts `APPLIED` as "handled for you", overstating the assistant on the screen built to measure it.

## Changes

- `FAILED` when every action errored; `APPLIED` when any succeeded (errors ride along in `action_errors`); `PENDING` unchanged. Auto-learn is now gated on the computed status, not on `apply`.
- **Migration 86** backfills the 184 rows written under the old rule. The predicate is exact, not heuristic: nothing taken **and** at least one error. `actions_taken='[]'` with no errors is a rule with an empty action list — a no-op by configuration — and is left alone.
- History **shows** `FAILED` rows instead of filtering them out, in rose with "didn't apply" — distinct from the green of a real apply and from the red of "no match", because a rule that correctly decided to do nothing is not the same as one the mail server refused.

## Effect on the patterns awaiting review

Replaying the corrected gate over the 21: **one drops below the bar** — `anil.pradhan@haigcapital.com → Cold Email` had three votes, one of which was a run that failed entirely. The other 20 are unaffected.

11 new tests; 617 email tests green.

Reported from the Notification tab: expanding a colleague listed their **Awaiting Reply, Done and FYI** mail alongside the notifications, so the drill-down silently contradicted the filter that produced it.

**The grouping itself is correct and unchanged.** A sender already appears under *every* cleanup category their mail carries — in the report's screenshot, Mirza Faizaan showing both `Calendar` and `Notification` is exactly that working. Ayush Sarkar shows one chip because his other labels (Awaiting Reply, FYI, Done, Follow-up) are **per-thread conversation states**, not things the Cleaner can act on, so they are deliberately not facets.

What did not follow the filter:

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| **Drill-down** | sender's 25 most recent, any category — 14 of Ayush's 69 aren't Notification and all were listed | scoped to the open tab, with a caption saying so |
| **Row count** | sender's whole volume — Ayush read as **69 notifications** | **55 of 69** |
| **Chips** | top 2 by volume, so filtering to a sender's 3rd-busiest category showed no chip for it | active category pulled to the front |

New `category_counts` per sender comes from the label tally that was already being computed, so this is one extra field, not an extra query.

This is the same class of defect as the Analytics range selector fixed in #99: **a number displayed under a filter it does not respect.**

## Also: the tag filter was case-sensitive

`labels=` matched with an exact `= ANY(categories)`, but the rule engine stores a rule's label **verbatim**. The Cleaner's own tally already had to fix this exact trap — an uppercase or space-padded rule name silently matched nothing. Left as-is, the drill-down would report "no Notification messages" for a sender the row says has 55.

Live data is fully canonical today, so this is **prevention, not a live fix**. Three existing tests asserted the literal SQL shape and were updated to the new contract; their behavioural intent (pills AND together, tag matches label *or* category) is unchanged and now covered explicitly.

## Verification

Screenshotted the Cleaner with the Notification tab open: counts read `55 of 69`, the drill-down lists only Notification mail, and a sender with three categories leads with the active one. Zero horizontal overflow at 1440px and 390px.

title: fix(email): repair refused rule runs; stop calling classified mail uncategorized
body:
Three defects, all found by checking the live account after #99 / #100.

## 1. Classification was **not** behind — the panel was wrong

Analytics reported **142 uncategorized arrivals in 30 days** and advised running a backfill. Checked against the mailbox:

| where | count | state |
|---|---|---|
| junk / trash / drafts | 681 | already excluded from the figure |
| **inbox** | **125** | **all `rules_processed_at IS NOT NULL`** |
| user-created folders | 18 | genuinely never processed |

Then the decisive query — of those 125, how many have a thread status?

```
DONE 68 · AWAITING 32 · FYI 15 · NEEDS_REPLY 10   →  125 of 125
```

**Not one was unclassified.** Conversation mail is classified per-*thread*; the per-message `categories` array stays empty by design. The panel was counting correctly-filed conversations as outstanding work and telling you to spend model calls redoing it.

Now a message with no categories falls back to its thread's status, so `(uncategorized)` means what it says. The status enum is mapped to its display name — unmapped, the chart grew `Done 41` directly above `DONE 69`. Live 30-day result after the fix: **eleven categories, no uncategorized bucket at all.**

The real gap it still surfaces: **18 messages in user-created folders**, which the inbox-only rule run never touches.

> This is the third time in this workstream a number was shown under a label that didn't match what it measured, and the second one I shipped myself.

## 2. The scheduler passed a UUID where every signature said `str`

`asyncpg` returns `row.id` as a UUID object, and `_account_sync_loop` handed it straight into the shared new-mail pipeline. Anything that merely put it in a SQL parameter worked fine — so it stayed invisible for months, until the reply drafter did string work with it:

```
'asyncpg.pgproto.pgproto.UUID' object has no attribute 'strip'
```

The `LABEL` action on the same rule succeeded, so the rule looked healthy and just never produced a draft.

## 3. Failed runs had no way back

184 rows were stranded, and the only repair was re-running the rules — which re-classifies (model calls) and re-enters drafting.

`retry_failed_executions` replays the rule **already chosen**:

- no matcher → no model calls, no chance of a different decision
- `REPLY` / `DRAFT_EMAIL` / `FORWARD` / `SEND_EMAIL` / `CALL_WEBHOOK` refused outright — a retry re-runs a decision made weeks ago, and a label is idempotent where a reply is not
- each row re-read for its **current** `provider_message_id` — the stale id is what stranded them
- a row that fails again **stays FAILED**: ~92 of the live failures are the provider racing us and those messages are gone; flipping them to APPLIED would hide them exactly as the original bug did

`POST /email/rules/history/retry-failed`, plus a button on the trust panel labelled **"Re-apply them (no drafts or sends)"** — "retry" on a mail assistant could plausibly mean re-sending something, and a button whose blast radius is ambiguous doesn't get pressed.

10 new tests; 634 email tests green.

title: fix(email): a rule-run repair must never lift mail back out of the bin
body:
Caught while preparing to run the #102 repair against the live mailbox — before running it, not after.

The retry selected **every** `FAILED` row for the account. But the commonest cause of these failures is the provider racing us, and the commonest form of that is the user **deleting or junking** the message: **92 of the 138 live failures ended in `trash`**.

Replaying such a row's `MOVE_FOLDER` would have moved the message *out* of Deleted Items and into its category folder — undoing a deletion, in bulk, with no prompt. Exactly the kind of unrecoverable surprise the action-skip list was written to prevent, missed on the selection side.

Disposed folders are now excluded from the selection. Those rows stay `FAILED` and visible rather than being silently 'fixed' into resurrection.

title: feat(email): auto-learn needs a second opinion, and only for bulk senders
body:
Counting agreements measures **consistency, not correctness**. A classifier confidently wrong about one sender is wrong the same way every time — and a streak of three was the *entire* bar for writing a permanent sender pin.

## We had copied half of upstream

Inbox Zero's [`analyze-sender-pattern`](reference/inbox-zero/apps/web/app/api/ai/analyze-sender-pattern/route.ts) uses its threshold as a **floor**, then runs a dedicated second LLM call over up to 10 of the sender's messages asking a *different question* — not "what is this email?" but **"will every future email from this address serve the same purpose?"**, at 90%+ confidence or nothing.

We had the floor and none of the judgment.

## Three changes

**Ported the second opinion.** `_ai_confirms_sender_pattern` judges the sender's 10 most recent messages, with upstream's guidance made explicit: no people, no generic domains unless plainly automated, no mixed content, any doubt is a no. **Fails closed at every step** — no model, too few samples, unparseable answer, exception → no pattern. Not learning is free; a wrong pin is silent, permanent, and short-circuits the classifier that would have caught it.

**Floor raised 3 → 5.** Three is short enough to reach by accident. No longer the only bar, but still a real one.

**Scope restricted to Newsletter / Marketing / Cold Email.** A FROM pattern asserts something about the sender's *identity* — that this address only ever sends one kind of thing. True of a list, a blast, an outreach account: the mail is defined by who sent it.

Not true of Receipt, Calendar or Notification, which describe what a message *is* and routinely arrive from people you also converse with. A colleague sends an invite Monday and a question Tuesday; pinned to Calendar, the question is filed as a calendar item. **Two of the patterns purged from the live account were exactly this** (`midhun.vm` → Calendar, `debesh@metafora.sg` → Receipt) and the correspondent check alone hadn't stopped them.

You can still pin any category by hand. This restricts only what the assistant may decide **unattended**.

Ordering is deliberate: cheap local checks gate the one that costs a model call, so the verdict is only asked about a sender that earned it.

10 new tests; 641 email tests green.

title: feat(email): a Fix now teaches the classifier instead of bypassing it
body:
You were right, and upstream agrees with you.

## The problem

A Fix could only produce a learned **pattern** — a hard sender→rule pin that short-circuits the model. So correcting a mistake never made the assistant better at anything: it removed *one* sender from the AI's reach and left the same misunderstanding in place for every other sender.

All 21 patterns on the live account are machine-inferred. **Not one encodes something you taught.**

> "Correcting a classification should enhance future AI classifications. I am not focusing on learned patterns."

**Inbox Zero has no Fix→pattern button at all.** Corrections go through the assistant's tools — `update-rule-conditions`, `update-personal-instructions`, `add-to-knowledge-base` — all of which change what the model *reads*. Patterns are a separate, conservative background analysis. We had copied only the pattern half.

## Guidance — the missing half

Free text attached to a rule, injected into the classification prompt. One correction about "vendor product digests are Newsletter, not Cold Email" now generalises to **every vendor** instead of exempting the one that was wrong. Migration 87.

Stored as rows rather than an LLM rewrite of `email_rules.instructions`:

- **Auditable** — you see exactly what was added and from which email. A rewrite destroys the sentence you wrote with nothing to compare against.
- **Revertible** — one row, one delete. Un-editing a paragraph is not.
- **Separable** — which is what makes the two-section screen possible.

## Pattern writes are now opt-in

`_teach` is the single choke point for both include and exclude writes in the Fix flow, gated on `pin_sender`, default **off**. The dialog surfaces it as *"Always file mail from this sender here"*, stating plainly that it skips the AI and therefore suits newsletters and bulk mail rather than people.

## Two sections, as you described

| | what it does | scope | cost |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Teaching the AI** | changes how it *reasons* | every sender | a model call |
| **Skipping the AI** | *replaces* it for a sender | one sender | free |

Each carries a one-line explanation of that trade-off, so you can tell which kind an entry is before deciding whether to keep it.

The prompt labels guidance as "correction from the user" rather than merging it into the rule's description — the model should weigh something you explicitly taught differently from the preset blurb shipped with the rule. Account-wide guidance (`rule_id NULL`) gets its own block. Guidance loads *after* the pattern short-circuit, since a pinned sender never reaches the LLM.

## Verification

- Migration + upsert exercised against the **live database**: two inserts differing only in case and whitespace collapse to one row, second updates the first. Test rows removed.
- Two-section screen screenshotted at 900px and 390px — zero horizontal overflow.

11 new tests; 648 email tests green.

Stacks on #104 (auto-learn gate).

title: fix(email): stop AI "Draft with AI" 502 by extending proxy timeout
body:
## What & why

Drafting a reply with the AI bar left blank ("What should this email say?" empty) returned a **502 gateway error** and produced no draft.

**Root cause:** the Next.js email proxy (`workbench/control_plane/src/app/api/email/[...path]/route.ts`) aborts every POST to the gateway after **30 seconds**, and on abort its `catch` returns `{ status: 502 }`. An empty reply body routes server-side to the heavy orchestrating drafter — memory retrieval + a routing LLM call + a specialist agent (capped at ~18s) + a `tier-powerful` generation of up to 3000 tokens — which routinely runs past 30s. (The lighter "improve existing text" path usually finishes in time, which is why only the blank case failed.) The GET handler in the same file already grants 120s for the same reason.

## Change

- Give the known LLM/agent-backed POST endpoints (`compose-assist`, `draft-reply`, `ai/chat`, `rules/generate`, `rules/run-message`, `messages/summaries`, …) the same 120s budget the GET handler uses for large downloads.
- Every other POST keeps the tight 30s abort so a genuinely hung upstream still fails fast.

One file, +33/−1. No infra change needed — the gateway is co-located at `127.0.0.1:8000`, so this proxy timeout was the sole source of the 502.

## Email-chain threading (reviewed, no change)

Also reviewed whether replies thread correctly instead of starting a new chain. They do, across all three providers: **Gmail** threads via `threadId` + matching `Re:` subject, **Outlook** uses Graph's native `/reply` + `/createReply`, and **IMAP** sets `In-Reply-To`/`References`. The send choke point resolves the thread id from the replied-to message and hands it to the provider. No fix required.

## Testing

- Verified the diff compiles as valid TypeScript (a `Set<string>` lookup keyed on the joined proxy path); the fresh clone has no installed toolchain to run `tsc`/build here.
- No tests reference the previous 30s email-proxy timeout value.

title: fix(email): the All folder is mail that arrived, not a log of everything
body:
## The bug

The sidebar's **All** excluded junk and trash but never **sent** or **drafts** — so 442 + 144 of the live account's messages were the user's own mail. Every conversation appeared twice and the list read as an activity log rather than an inbox.

```python
FOLDER_ALL_EXCLUDES = ("junk", "trash")   # sent and drafts were never here
```

The principle: **All is mail that arrived, and the user's own mail never did.** Sent doubles every conversation; a draft is unfinished text with no counterparty, which belongs in a composer rather than a reading list.

Excluding them costs nothing in reach: each has its own sidebar entry, and the thread view already ignores the folder filter, so opening a conversation still shows both sides of it.

## Search deliberately does not follow

That constant was shared with the search bar's "All folders" scope, under a comment saying `all` must never mean two things. I split it anyway:

| | answers | the user's own mail |
|---|---|---|
| Browsing All | "what came in?" | hidden |
| Searching All folders | "where is that message?" | **included** |

"What did I tell them?" is one of the commonest reasons to search. A scope labelled *All folders* that silently skipped your own replies would be a worse defect than the one this fixes — and half-written text is a poor thing to browse but a fine thing to go looking for. `folder_scope` grows an `include_sent` flag that only search passes.

## Two things that would have been easy to miss

**The frontend keeps its own copy of the set**, and it both filters the list *and* derives the sidebar's All count. Fixing only the server would have left the badge claiming mail the list beneath it could not account for. Both updated; the existing parity test guards them.

**No `"spam"` or `"draft"` entries**, though `"spam"` was in my first draft as "defensive for Gmail". `providers/base.py` canonicalises spam → junk and draft → drafts on ingestion for *every* provider, so both would have been dead weight that reads as coverage.

## Live effect

All goes **5,724 → 5,138**.

## Tests

- browsing All hides sent and drafts; searching All still finds both
- the two sets differ by exactly `{"sent", "drafts"}` — any other divergence means drift, not design
- the **facet chips** (third caller of `folder_scope`) count the same mail the list shows

657 email tests pass; `tsc --noEmit` clean.
