title: feat(notes): mobile recording resilience (wake lock + backgrounding safeguard) + meeting-bot docs
body:
Two commits.

## 1. Keep mobile recordings alive — screen wake lock + backgrounding safeguard
Best-effort resilience for long recordings on phones, within what the web platform allows.

**Screen Wake Lock:** request `navigator.wakeLock('screen')` while recording so the phone doesn't auto-lock mid-meeting (browsers suspend mic capture when the screen sleeps). Released on pause/stop; re-acquired on resume and whenever the page returns to the foreground (the OS drops the sentinel when hidden). Fully best-effort — silently no-ops where unsupported (older iOS, Firefox) or denied.

**Backgrounding safeguard:** watch `document` visibility. When the app is hidden (screen off / switched away) we force `MediaRecorder.requestData()` and flush the upload queue, so whatever was captured is uploaded *before* the OS freezes the tab — a truncated recording instead of a lost tail. Surfaced honestly in the UI: a standing "keep this app open" reminder during recording, and, if the app was ever backgrounded mid-recording, a warning that capture may have paused and the transcript could have a gap.

This does **not** make iOS record in the background (the platform forbids web mic capture when backgrounded) — it maximises reliability while the app stays open and is honest about the limits.

Files: `recorder.ts` (wake lock + visibility), `recordingStore.ts` (`hidden` / `wasBackgrounded` state), `session/[id]/page.tsx` (reminder + warning banners).

## 2. Docs: meeting-bot capture (§3.13 + decision D10)
Records the design for remote-call capture (join a Meet/Teams/Zoom call as a bot):
- **Phase 1 — on-demand "join by link"** (near-term): paste a meeting URL, a bot joins and feeds the existing transcription/diarization/summary pipeline.
- **Phase 2 — calendar auto-join** (deferred): per-meeting opt-in toggle + rules; documented for later, explicitly out of scope for now.

Captures the hard dependency (the gateway can't join a call itself — needs a pluggable `bot_provider` backend), provider trade-offs (Recall.ai managed vs self-hosted Vexa/Attendee) and why a managed API is the only fit for the single 4 GB VPS, the dock-based UX, and the consent posture.

## Verification
Frontend `next build`, `tsc --noEmit`, and `eslint` all green (no new lint errors). Docs-only for commit 2.

title: WhatsApp: sync native labels/lists from the number and mirror them in the inbox
body:
## What

Pulls the labels/lists you created **inside WhatsApp** ("Clients", "Suppliers", "Follow up", …) into the app and mirrors them **read-only** into the triage inbox — distinct from `wa_categories`, which are our own policy carriers.

## Why

Those labels are the founder's existing organisation of who's who. They live in WhatsApp's app-state, and the whatsmeow (personal-number) bridge can see them — but nothing surfaced them yet. This brings them across so the inbox reflects the same tags you set up on your phone, and lets you filter the queue by a label.

## How

**Bridge (Go)**
- Enable `EmitAppStateEventsOnFullSync` and force a **one-time full sync** of the `regular` app-state collection on connect (guarded by a per-account meta flag), so an already-paired number **backfills its existing labels** — not just live edits.
- Handle `LabelEdit` / `LabelAssociationChat`: drop WhatsApp's built-in system lists (Unread, Groups, Favourites, Archived, …) by type, map the colour index to a hex swatch, and POST labels + chat associations to the gateway.

**Gateway**
- Migration `113`: widen `wa_labels` (colour, list_type, sort, active/deleted) and add `wa_chat_labels`, keyed by JID so an association can land before the chat's messages sync. Upsert key becomes the WhatsApp label id.
- `POST /whatsapp/bridge/labels` upserts labels + associations; `GET /whatsapp/labels` serves them with per-label chat counts; `/whatsapp/chats` now returns each chat's labels and accepts a `label` filter.

**Frontend**
- Colour label chips on chat rows; a **Labels** section in the desktop spine and the mobile triage drawer that filters the queue to a WhatsApp label.

## Scope / notes

- **Read-only mirror** — viewing/filtering by your labels, not editing them back to WhatsApp.
- Existing labels populate on the bridge's **next reconnect** (the forced full-sync re-imports them); live edits flow automatically after.

## Testing

- Go bridge: `go build` + `go vet` clean.
- Gateway: 30 unit tests pass, incl. new label-parser + ingest-route tests (persist / unlabel / unknown-account / bad-secret).
- Frontend: `tsc --noEmit` clean, vitest green, production `next build` succeeds.
- The live WhatsApp→bridge app-state sync couldn't be exercised in the sandbox (no paired number); it's built against whatsmeow's documented app-state contract.

title: Artifacts: lint generated HTML, and add React artifacts (inline + full-page)
body:
Started as a review of our artifact system against Anthropic's `web-artifacts-builder` skill, and turned into closing the two gaps that review found: no feedback loop, and no React.

## 1. Lint generated artifact HTML (`a2f2e39`)

The sandbox (`SandboxedHtml`) is strict and **silent**. A CDN `<script src>` is CSP-blocked with no error, a typo'd `cc-` class renders unstyled, a `cc-bar` missing its `--v` draws an empty track. The agent wrote the file, the tool returned success, and the user opened a broken report.

`acb_skills/artifact_lint.py` parses the markup and reports what the sandbox swallows:

- **error** — CSP-blocked remote fetches (the artifact is genuinely broken)
- **warning** — unknown `cc-` class (with a nearest-match suggestion), kit blocks missing the custom property or child that makes them draw, missing `cc-report` wrapper, hard-coded colors, and the generic-AI design tells (purple gradients, explicit Inter, over-centering) named by the Anthropic skill

`write_artifact` returns `warnings` for `.html`; `emit_generative_ui` returns them for `html` nodes. Advisory only — never blocks a write, never raises, and a parse failure degrades to no findings. Clean input produces zero findings on a realistic kit-heavy report.

`CC_CLASSES` mirrors the sandbox stylesheet and a drift test parses `SandboxedHtml.tsx` and fails in **both** directions, so a `cc-` block can't be added to the CSS without being registered (or removed while agents are still told it's valid). That test immediately found a real doc bug: the sandbox CSS comment documented `cc-cell-stat` and `cc-row`, neither of which the stylesheet defines — any agent following it emitted silently-unstyled markup.

## 2. React artifacts (`78618dd`, `e381dff`)

Agents could emit HTML but not React, so anything stateful — a filterable table, a multi-step form, a calculator, a live dashboard — had to be hand-rolled as DOM scripting. Now they write an ordinary component and default-export it, on both existing surfaces: an inline chat card (`emit_generative_ui` `react` node) and a full-page side-panel artifact (`outputs/*.jsx`).

`SandboxedReact` hands the compiled bundle to `SandboxedHtml` rather than building its own frame, so the CSP, the `cc-*` design kit, and the `ccAction`/`ccSubmit` bridge stay in one place and React artifacts can't drift from HTML ones.

### Three decisions worth reviewing

**Preact under the alias.** The frame has no network and React 19 dropped UMD, so the runtime must be bundled with the component. Agents write standard `from "react"`; esbuild aliases it to `preact/compat`. Byte-identical source compiles to **19 KB instead of 194 KB** — and every inline card inlines its whole runtime into `srcDoc`, so ten cards would otherwise be ~2 MB. Since the sandbox has no network, agents can't pull third-party packages anyway, which is where real React's advantage would show up. `RUNTIME_ALIAS` is one table — point it back at react/react-dom to ship real React.

**The import allowlist is a security boundary, not ergonomics.** This bundles untrusted model output *server-side*. Unrestricted resolution would let an artifact `import x from "/etc/passwd"` and inline the bytes into output we hand back to the client. Only the React runtime resolves, so no caller-supplied path reaches the filesystem resolver. Tested against node builtins, absolute paths, relative escapes, sibling sources, and npm packages.

**`.jsx`/`.tsx` render as React only under `outputs/`.** Elsewhere they stay source code, so an agent opening `src/components/Foo.tsx` to read it never silently turns into building and running it.

### Two non-obvious things

- `esbuild` must be in `serverExternalPackages`. Without it `next build` **fails outright**, tracing the native binary and dying on its non-UTF8 bytes.
- vitest needs `pool: "forks"` — esbuild's stdio child process deadlocks in worker threads.

## 3. A pre-existing test-suite landmine (`0bb1ec8`)

Adding a test file that sorts early and calls `write_artifact` hung the entire suite with no output. Not the new file's fault: any test that populates `_WRITE_ARTIFACT_CONTEXT` without restoring it leaks a live `session_id`, and `executor.resolve_run_queue` keys on it, so the next test down that path blocks on a gateway call that never returns.

Reproduced at `HEAD~1` with no new code:

```
pytest tests/unit/test_write_artifact.py tests/unit/test_email_tool_consolidation.py   # hangs
```

A probe that only does `_WRITE_ARTIFACT_CONTEXT.update({"session_id": ...})` hangs it identically — no file writes, no asyncio. It stayed invisible because the tests that populate the global sort near the end of the run. Fixed by snapshotting/restoring the dict in `tests/conftest.py` rather than depending on filenames.

## Verification

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| Python unit tests | 2245 passed, 8 skipped |
| vitest | 43 passed |
| `tsc --noEmit` | clean |
| eslint (changed files) | clean |
| `next build` | passes, `/api/artifacts/compile` registered |
| Live POST against production build | compiles a component; refuses a disallowed import |
| Playwright e2e | 2 passed |

The e2e spec is the one that matters most: it runs the real compiled bundle under the **real CSP** in an opaque-origin frame and asserts hooks re-render, `cc-*` tokens apply, and `ccSubmit` works **from first mount**. That last one is subtle — `SandboxedHtml` appends its bridge *after* the body content, so a synchronous mount would run React before the bridge exists; the mount is deferred to `load`.

## Reviewer notes

- **CI won't run the e2e spec.** `pr-check.yml` runs `pytest tests/unit/`, typecheck, and vitest. `e2e/react-artifact.spec.ts` only runs under `npm run test:e2e` (which needs a build). Worth wiring in separately if you want it enforced.
- **Bare `pytest`** (no path arg) is broken on `main` already — `apps/skills/skill-clickup-sync/tests/` collides with the root `tests` package. Untouched here; CI runs `pytest tests/unit/` so it isn't biting.
- Compilation is cached per-source in the browser; a shared server-side cache would help if the same artifact is opened across sessions.
- Multi-file React artifacts aren't supported (single component). That's App Workshop Tier 2 territory, which has its own plan in `docs/app-workshop/README.md`.

title: email: contact card on a sender's name/avatar, and the contacts directory it builds
body:
Clicking a display name, avatar orb, or any To/Cc recipient in the mail app opens a people card — the Outlook affordance. Reading a card also files what it learned, so the mailbox accumulates a contacts directory as a side effect of being used.

## The card

`GET /email/contacts/card` (`transport/contacts.py`) → `ContactCard.tsx`:

- **Identity** — name, address, job title · company, each with a copy button
- **Actions** — *Email* (opens the composer to them), *All mail* (searches every folder for `from:`)
- **Contact details** — phones as `tel:` links, organisation, links; copy button on every field
- **Relationship** — `47 received · 31 sent · 2 unread · last 2d ago`, sender category, and an *Unsubscribed* / *Auto-archived* chip when the Cleaner is suppressing them
- **Recent mail** — last 3 messages as previews; clicking one opens it and closes the card

Wired into the reading pane's sender block, its To/Cc lines, and every message header in the conversation view. The popover portals to `<body>` so the scrolling pane can't clip it, flips above/left near a viewport edge, sizes to available room, and becomes a bottom sheet under 480px.

`ConversationView`'s message header changed from a `<button>` to a `div`: the trigger renders a real `<button>`, which a `<button>` row can't legally contain.

## Where the data comes from

There is no contacts table upstream and no directory to read from. Everything is derived from mail already in the caller's own accounts — every query goes through `core._account_scope`, and the caller's own drafts are excluded from "mail from them" (some providers echo the counterparty into `from_address`).

Phone / title / company are parsed from the sender's own signature block. That is the only place the card guesses, so it is deliberately conservative:

- cuts at the first quoted-reply banner, so a reply's "signature" is never the person being replied *to*
- requires a label or a country code before believing a digit run is a phone
- declines to guess a title without the display name to anchor on
- order numbers, invoice totals, dates and marketing plumbing yield nothing
- free-mail domains never become an organisation

## The directory (migration 119)

Each card open upserts into `email_contacts` — name, title, organisation, phones, links, with `source_message_id` + `parsed_at`. The card then renders the **merged** row, so a phone an older signature taught us survives today's one-line reply.

Invariants, each pinned by a test:

- **`manual_fields[]` is permanent** — names the columns a human edited; the parse skips them forever. Without it the next mail silently reverts a correction, which is the one failure that would make a contacts view untrustworthy.
- An empty parse never blanks a stored value.
- Derived facts (counts, first/last seen) are never stored — they are a live query and would be wrong the moment mail arrives.
- The domain→company guess is display-only, applied *after* the write, so the directory is never seeded with invented company names.
- The write is best-effort; a failure costs the caller the directory entry, never the card.

An optional `name` param means someone you only ever write *to* — no `from_address` to read a name from — is still filed under their name.

## Verification

- **16 new unit tests** pin the signature parser from both directions and the directory's write invariants; full suite `2271 passed, 8 skipped`
- **Live Postgres**, schema + migration 119 applied, real fixtures: case-insensitive address match, drafts excluded, To+Cc sent counts, another user's mailbox with the same correspondent never leaking in; parse → store → hand-edit a title → re-open → the edit survives and `source` flips to `user`
- **Migration 119 applied twice** — idempotent
- **Real browser** (dark, light, mobile): avatar and name both open the card, close button and Escape both close it, a Cc recipient opens *their* card, clicking a recent item fetches that message, and the copy buttons write `priya@fracktal.in` / `+91 98765 43210` / `Priya Sharma` to an actual clipboard
- `tsc` clean, production build clean, new files lint-clean, vitest `46 passed`

## Notes for the reviewer

- **`schema.generated.sql` is not regenerated.** It needs a live fully-migrated DB and this environment has no pgvector. It already lags (migration 118's table is missing too), so this matches current practice — but it is worth a regen on the VPS.
- **The message list is deliberately untouched.** Its rows have no avatar and the sender name sits inside the row `<button>` carrying selection, long-press and context-menu handlers; nesting a trigger there risked breaking list selection for little gain. Outlook's list doesn't open a card from the sender name either.
- **`ai-company-brain/specs/email_app_master_plan.md` §3.14** documents what the table already gives a future Contacts view and what still needs building. Two things want an owner call before that view ships: how two addresses for the same human merge (retrofitting identity onto a flat address table later is the expensive version), and photos (Gmail People / Graph need OAuth scope the app doesn't request).

title: BO-7 cheap wins: real call context in decide(), destructive flag, mutation hardening
body:
## Summary

First slice of BO-7 (`specs/competitive_hardening_2026-07.md`'s CH-1 item — sandbox hardening for agent code execution). Scoped via deep research into the current `permission_policy.py`/executor tool-dispatch/mutation-container code first (see conversation) — the backlog's "`decide()` is a no-op" framing turned out stale (it's real and tested), but three narrower, genuinely open gaps were confirmed and fixed here. The bigger half of BO-7 — a container boundary for the *normal* agent load path (`loader.py`'s `exec_module` of arbitrary git-pulled agent code) — is architecturally bigger (real RAM cost on the 4GB VPS, no natural process seam for MAF-native agents' in-process tool calls) and intentionally out of scope for this PR.

1. **Full call context reaches `decide()` for our own tools.** Every gate call site for platform tools passed `{"tool_name": tool_name}` only — no args/path/command — so `run_script` (which builds and executes a literal shell command from its own arguments) was approved purely on its "reversible" annotation, never checked against what it was actually about to run. `decide()`'s shell-denylist/workspace-containment checks now run as hard vetoes *before* the tool-annotation short-circuit; a new `build_tool_call_context()` maps `run_script`'s `path`+`args` onto `decide()`'s fields (deliberately not `code_task`/`install_dependency` — see code comments for why not). Traced every existing test in `test_permission_policy.py` against the reorder before touching it.
2. **`install_dependency` flagged destructive** in `tool_annotations.py` (shared-venv mutation, affects every agent in the process). Deliberately did *not* flag `run_script`/`code_task` — both are documented elsewhere as fast, non-interactive re-runs, and no tool yet wires a real `request_confirmation` call, so the addendum text agents see was reworded to not overclaim a confirmation card exists.
3. **Mutation-runner's `docker run` hardened** — it was the concrete "existing container pattern" the backlog wants generalized, but shipped with zero resource/capability flags. Added `--cap-drop ALL` (+ `--cap-add DAC_OVERRIDE`, required since the container's root user needs it to write the `acb`-owned bind mount) + `--security-opt no-new-privileges` + configurable `--memory`/`--cpus`/`--pids-limit`.

## Test plan

- [x] Traced all 39 existing `test_permission_policy.py`/golden-trajectory tests against the `decide()` reorder by hand before editing — all pass unchanged
- [x] 11 new tests: `decide()`'s new vetoes-before-annotation ordering, `build_tool_call_context()` mapping + fallback, `_gate_injected_tool` end-to-end blocking `run_script` on dangerous args
- [x] 2 new tests locking the hardening flags reach the real `docker_cmd` (fakes the subprocess call — full flow needs Docker)
- [x] `pytest tests/unit/` — 2283 passed (2272 baseline + 11 new), 0 failures
- [x] Trajectory suites referencing `install_dependency`'s annotation (`test_tool_scope_trajectory.py`, `test_tool_addendum_drift_trajectory.py`, `test_gtd_quality_trajectory.py`) — 33 passed

title: Live transcription: stable speakers, live bus, and the copilot console
body:
Makes on-page **live transcription** usable end to end, and lays the spine the meeting copilot will build on.

## What you can do after this deploys

Start a recording at `/notes` → live captions now also flow to the server, so a **"● Live now"** pill appears across the app and `/notes/live/<meeting-id>` shows the transcript **attributed by speaker**, with names picked up from self-introductions ("I'm Priya").

Requires `DEEPGRAM_API_KEY` (with key-management scope) — same key live captions already use. Without it, recording still works, just no live transcript.

## The design change

Live transcription used to be framed as a *disposable draft* thrown away when the batch pass ran. That traded accuracy for latency unnecessarily. Instead:

- **Chunk on pauses, not the clock.** Fixed windows cut mid-word, which is exactly where ASR loses context and diarization gets confused. VAD endpointing closes a chunk when a speaker actually pauses, so each chunk is a complete utterance.
- **A running voiceprint gallery** matches each utterance's speaker embedding against those seen so far, giving **stable speaker ids across chunks** incrementally — no end-of-file wait.
- **The batch pass becomes a refinement, not a redo.** It still owns the authoritative transcript, but now reconciles its own labels against the live ones by max time overlap (greedy one-to-one) and carries live-learned names across.

## Contents

| Area | Change |
|---|---|
| `live_speakers.py` | Voiceprint gallery, live name binding, roster, batch reconciliation |
| `live_transcript.py` | Stable ids on ingest; user-authed browser route beside the bot's machine-authed one |
| `live_session.py` + migration `119` | Presence registry, copilot opt-in (off by default) |
| Frontend | `LiveDock` presence pill, `/notes/live/[id]` console, caption relay |
| `meeting_bot/` | Pause endpointer, per-utterance embeddings, `CHROME_EXECUTABLE` |

## Verification

Ran the meeting-bot worker against a real PulseAudio/Xvfb/Chromium stack rather than reasoning about it, which caught two defects:

1. **Live segments almost never carried an embedding** (1 of 15 measured). An utterance's embedding only exists once it *closes*, but the ASR streams segments *during* it — so the voiceprint was silently never attached and the gateway fell back to label passthrough, defeating the gallery. Segments are now briefly held and released once their window lands, or untagged after a bounded wait. Same audio after the fix: **42 of 46**.
2. **Chromium launch had no executable override**, so any host whose browser build wasn't installed by that exact Playwright version died outright.

Also verified on real audio: the record path recovers a 440 Hz tone through null-sink → monitor → ffmpeg → Opus; the virtual-mic speak path carries audio; the energy-VAD default cleanly separates speech (RMS ~1700) from silence (0.0).

**Still unverified:** the Google Meet *join selectors* — that needs a real meeting, and is called out in the worker README. Doesn't affect on-page live transcription.

2275 unit tests pass; `tsc`, eslint and `next build` clean. All changes are additive and gated; migration `119` is idempotent.

title: AssemblyAI speech-to-text on both the batch and live paths
body:
Makes AssemblyAI the default speech-to-text, configurable in Settings → Models, with Deepgram kept as a working alternative and local sherpa diarization demoted to a true fallback.

Chosen for cost — roughly **$0.17/hr batch and $0.21/hr streaming with diarization, about half Deepgram** — and for explicit Hindi/English code-switching support, which Deepgram has [open quality issues](https://github.com/orgs/deepgram/discussions/1208) with.

## Batch — a native provider, not LiteLLM

AssemblyAI's API is **submit → poll**, which LiteLLM's one-shot `atranscription` cannot express (it only carries AssemblyAI as an opaque pass-through). So `assemblyai_provider.py` speaks v2 REST directly, behind the **existing `SttProvider` interface** — the notes pipeline is unchanged.

- Requests `speaker_labels` for diarization, and `language_detection` rather than a pinned language so mixed Hindi/English meetings aren't forced to one.
- The org glossary maps onto `word_boost`, with prose fragments filtered out (it wants vocabulary, not sentences).
- AssemblyAI's `A`/`B` speaker letters are normalised onto the shared `S1`/`S2` space, so `speaker_names`, the rename UI and live reconciliation stay provider-agnostic. Offsets convert ms → s.
- The registry resolves the tier first, then picks the provider by prefix — so AssemblyAI works set directly *or* behind `tier-stt`.

## Live — one setting, not two

`/notes/stt/live-token` now follows the configured STT tier when that provider can stream, so **choosing AssemblyAI for batch gets AssemblyAI live with no second setting**; otherwise it prefers whichever key exists. Deepgram's ephemeral-key minting is unchanged.

`LiveTranscription` (was `DeepgramLive`) speaks either the AssemblyAI v3 `Turn` protocol or Deepgram's, behind one `LiveCaption` shape.

## Fitting the rest of the app

- **Local diarization becomes a true fallback for free** — `maybe_diarize` already no-ops on an already-diarized result, so sherpa now only runs when the ASR returned no speakers.
- **Fixed a bug this would have introduced:** the "speakers aren't separated" hint hardcoded `deepgram/`, so it would have fired misleadingly on every AssemblyAI transcript. It now recognises AssemblyAI and a completed local sherpa pass.
- `ASSEMBLYAI_API_KEY` registered across settings, key store, env seeding and the Models UI (label, colour, icon, setup guide, "names speakers" badge).

## Verification

16 backend tests (routing, option mapping, ms→s, speaker-letter mapping, provider selection) and 8 vitest pinning **both wire protocols** — that's where a silent "live stopped working" regression would hide. Suite 2358; `tsc`, eslint and `next build` clean.

**Not yet exercised against AssemblyAI's servers** (no key available here). The batch v2 API is stable and I'm confident in it. Two things to watch on first use: the exact `speech_model` id (anything after `assemblyai/` passes through as `speech_model`, so a different id needs no code change), and **streaming diarization**, a paid add-on whose v3 query parameter I couldn't confirm from the docs. Live captions will work either way; per-speaker labels on the *live* path may need one parameter once the account docs are visible. Batch diarizes regardless, and batch is authoritative.

title: Deploy the self-hosted meeting bot with the stack
body:
The meeting-bot worker existed but nothing put it on the VPS — join-by-link needed a manual `docker compose up` there. It now deploys with everything else.

## What changed

- **`infra/docker-compose.yml`** — a `meeting-bot` service under the **`meetingbot` profile**, deliberately *not* `core`: each in-call bot is a real Chrome (~1–3 GB RAM + up to 2 CPU), so it must never start just because someone brought the stack up. `shm_size: 1gb` (Docker's default 64 MB `/dev/shm` crashes Chrome on real pages), a named volume so recordings survive a restart, and host-gateway resolution so the worker can call back with live segments.
- **`deploy.yml`** — builds and starts it, generates `MEETING_BOT_TOKEN` once, points the gateway at it (`MEETING_BOT_URL`, `NOTES_BOT_PROVIDER=selfhosted`, `NOTES_LIVE_CALLBACK_BASE`) *before* the gateway restart, then health-checks. Opt out with `MEETING_BOT_ENABLED=0`. Modelled on the existing WhatsApp-bridge block.

## Two things that would only have failed on the box

1. **Port collision.** The worker publishes on host **8095**, not 8080 — the gateway owns 8080 on the VPS (`deploy/hostinger/acb-gateway.service`). The obvious choice would have taken down the whole app rather than just the bot. Bound to loopback only, so nothing off-box can dispatch a bot.
2. **Compose env resolution.** The compose command passes `--env-file "$ENV_FILE"` explicitly, because a bare `.env` resolves against the *project directory* (`infra/`), not the app root — the substitutions would have come out silently empty.

A build or start hiccup skips the bot and never fails the deploy.

## Verification

9 guards pinning the port/profile/shm/volume/callback contract and the deploy wiring — none of which any other test would catch, since this code only ever executes on the VPS. Suite 2387.

**Still unverified:** the Google Meet *join selectors*, which need a real meeting. Everything else about the worker (recording path, virtual mic, VAD, HTTP contract, Chromium launch) was verified against a real PulseAudio/Xvfb/Chromium stack earlier and is documented in the worker README.

title: Live Meeting Copilot Phase B — the orchestrator
body:
An opt-in agent that listens to a live meeting and surfaces a talking point when a moment warrants it. **Off by default**; turning it off cancels the task, which unsubscribes it from the transcript bus — so spend stops immediately rather than the toggle being a lie.

## The cascade is the point

Running a model on every sentence would be expensive *and* noisy. Each stage is cheaper than the next and filters for it:

| Stage | What | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| **0** Windowing | closes on speaker turn, ~40 words, or ~15 s | free |
| **1** Trigger gate | questions, objections/risk, decisions, numbers + debounce + per-meeting cap | **free — most speech ends here** |
| **2** Decide | `tier-fast`, tiny context, strict JSON, confidence floor | cheap |
| **3** Craft | `tier-balanced`, only for what survives | rare |

Stages 0–1 live in `copilot_policy.py` and are **completely pure** — no LLM, no I/O. "Does this deserve a model?" should be inspectable and unit-tested, not emergent from prompt behaviour.

Two details that matter:
- **The cap and debounce are checked *before* the trigger patterns**, so a lively meeting can't run up cost through pattern matches.
- **A bounded rolling state** means the prompt never grows with meeting length — that's what keeps cost flat on a 3-hour call — plus a token-overlap dedup so the copilot can't re-raise a point it already made (the fastest way to become annoying).

## Auditable, and isolated

Output goes to a **separate event bus** from the transcript, so agent chatter never pollutes the record. Events persist to `copilot_event` (migration 121) with **per-event token cost**, making the budget guardrail inspectable rather than a black box. Budget exhaustion pauses and says so in the console.

Every failure mode — LLM error, bad JSON, slow model, budget exhaustion — degrades to *"no suggestion"*. The copilot consumes the transcript; it is never in the capture path.

## Console

Suggestions render on their own channel, each showing **what triggered it** so a tip is inspectable rather than an oracle. Only subscribed while the copilot is actually on.

## Verification

25 tests — the gate's triggers *and* that debounce/cap beat them, windowing, bounded state, dedup, and that `stop()` genuinely cancels the task. Suite 2419; `tsc`, eslint and `next build` clean.

**Not yet exercised against a live meeting** — the LLM stages need a real transcript flowing. The policy layer that decides *whether* to spend is fully tested; the prompt quality of what it says will need tuning against real calls.

title: Correct AssemblyAI model ids and add model discovery
body:
Chasing "why don't I see the latest AssemblyAI model?" surfaced a worse problem than the missing query.

## 1. The catalogued model ids were wrong (would have broken every transcription)

I shipped `assemblyai/universal` and `assemblyai/nano`. AssemblyAI's own docs enumerate **`universal-3-pro`** and **`universal-2`**. Since whatever follows `assemblyai/` is passed straight through as the model, every transcription would have failed with a confusing provider error on first use.

Catalogue now carries the real ids — Universal-3 Pro as the accurate one, Universal-2 as the broader-language/cheaper option.

## 2. The model field name is uncertain, so it's now self-correcting

The current pre-recorded API appears to take **`speech_models` (a required list)**; older accounts take `speech_model` (a string). Guessing wrong fails *every* request, and AssemblyAI's docs 403 automated fetches so I could not confirm it from here.

`transcribe()` now sends the documented plural form and **retries once with the singular** if the API rejects the field — self-correcting rather than a hardcoded bet on a detail I can't verify.

## 3. Model discovery — the original question

`_fetch_live_models` had no `assemblyai` branch, so it fell through to `return []` and only the static list showed. That's exactly what you noticed.

The honest constraint: **AssemblyAI publishes no model-list endpoint**, unlike the OpenAI-compatible providers we enumerate. So "Refresh" genuinely cannot discover models. It now does the useful thing instead — probes a cheap authenticated endpoint to prove the **key** works:

| Result | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| 200 | return the curated list |
| 401/403 | return nothing, so a bad key can't look fine |
| 429/5xx | still show the models — a rate limit shouldn't blank the picker |
| network error | return nothing |

Deepgram has the same no-endpoint situation; noted in the fallback comment.

## Verification

9 more tests — the ids are current and flagged as transcription models, both model-field forms build correctly, and all four probe paths. Suite 2428.

Still not exercised against AssemblyAI's servers (no key here), but the plural/singular fallback means the field-name uncertainty can't break your first run.

title: Live Meeting Copilot Phase C — meeting context
body:
A copilot watching only the transcript can tell *that* an objection was raised, but not who raised it or which deal it concerns — so its suggestions stay generic. This gives it the background that makes them specific.

## Three independent layers

| | Source | Needs |
|---|---|---|
| **1 BRIEF** | `meeting.copilot_brief` — a user-written briefing | nothing |
| **2 HISTORY** | past meetings sharing an attendee email, their summaries + still-open action items | nothing — it's our own database |
| **3 SYSTEMS** | `call_agent("agent-sales-assistant" \| "task-manager", …)`, fanned out in parallel | the agents registered |

Layer 1 is the highest-value source and deliberately first: no connector, no inference, and usually the only thing that knows what the meeting is *for*.

## Two load-bearing rules

**Assembled once, before the conversation.** An agent call takes seconds; a meeting moves faster. The pack is built at session start and cached, then rides along as compact `BACKGROUND` in both the decide and craft prompts — so context isn't re-paid per suggestion.

**Every layer degrades on its own.** No brief, no history, an unregistered agent, a timeout, Zoho not connected — each just omits its section. No combination breaks the copilot; it simply knows less. The console says so plainly when the pack is empty, rather than quietly being useless.

## Cost control

Layer 3 is **opt-in per session** (`live_session.deep_context`) because the fan-out spends tokens before a word is spoken — worth it for a customer call, not for a standup. Everything is capped on every axis, because the pack rides in *every* prompt and an uncapped history would quietly raise the price of every suggestion. Agents are instructed to answer `NONE` rather than narrate an empty result, so "I couldn't find anything" can't eat prompt budget every meeting.

## UI

A briefing box plus a **"what the copilot knows"** panel — so both *"why did it say that?"* and *"why is it being generic?"* are answerable.

## Verification

18 tests: layer ordering (human first), independent degradation, malformed attendees, the caps, and that a failing / chatty / empty agent can't hurt the pack. Migration 122. Suite 2456; `tsc`, eslint and `next build` clean.

Layer 3's usefulness depends on your Zoho/ClickUp data being populated and those agents registered — that part I can't verify from here, but it fails safe if either is missing.

title: Fix SQLAlchemy bind-param bug breaking App Workshop create/fork/publish/storage writes
body:
## Summary
- Root-caused the reported "Create failed (HTTP 500)" on `POST /apps`: a `:name::jsonb` bind param (a colon-param immediately followed by Postgres's `::` cast, no space) is silently mis-parsed by SQLAlchemy's `text()` bind-param scanner — it drops the last character of the param name and leaves the literal cast text unbound, which asyncpg then rejects with `syntax error at or near ':'`.
- This exact pattern was present at **6 sites** in the Custom Apps write path, all broken since Phase 0 because nothing before now exercised these statements end-to-end against a real Postgres: `create_app`, `fork_app`, `publish_app`, the `app_audit` logger (`record_app_audit` — its own try/except silently swallowed every failure, so `app_audit` has never actually recorded a row, meaning **usage stats on gallery cards have always shown zero**), and both `cc.storage` write paths (`actions.py`'s action-dispatch write, `runtime.py`'s `PUT` endpoint).
- Fix: add a single space before the cast (`:name ::jsonb`) — confirmed via direct SQLAlchemy bind-param compilation and end-to-end execution against a live local Postgres (create → fork → storage write → audit log all verified to persist correctly).
- Found and fixed the identical pattern in one unrelated feature during the sweep: `tasks/settings.py`'s GTD settings `PATCH` endpoint (`workflow_stages`, `status_stage_map`, `energy_windows`, `day_templates`).
- Added `tests/unit/test_sql_bindparam_jsonb_cast.py`, a regression guard that scans the gateway source for the broken shape so it can't silently return.

## Test plan
- [x] Reproduced the exact production failure by spinning up a local Postgres, applying the relevant migrations, and calling `create_app` directly — confirmed the `asyncpg.exceptions.PostgresSyntaxError` before the fix.
- [x] After the fix: `create_app`, `fork_app`, `_run_storage_set` (actions.py), and `record_app_audit` all verified to execute and persist correctly against the live test DB.
- [x] `uv run pytest tests/unit/ -q` — 2473 passed, 8 skipped

title: Side panel: visible close buttons + drag-to-resize, and artifact surface routing
body:
Two reported side-panel bugs, plus the routing rule that decides when an agent should render an artifact and where it should go.

## 1. Side panel fixes (`00f2fe5`)

**Close button was invisible.** Each tab's × was `opacity-0` until you hovered that exact tab — unreachable on touch, and undiscoverable on a pointer device unless you already knew it was there. Now always rendered: dimmed at rest, full strength on hover/focus, with an `aria-label` and a visible focus ring.

**Panel had a fixed width.** It was hard-coded `w-[30rem]`, so a wide table or dashboard had nowhere to go. The right edge is now a drag handle:

- drag to resize, **double-click to reset**
- **arrow keys** (Shift = coarse step) for keyboard users
- `role="separator"` with `aria-valuenow/min/max`
- clamped 320–1100px, persisted per browser
- a 7px hit area straddling the edge, since a 1px border is impossible to grab

Content reflows on its own — the panel was already flex throughout.

### Why pointer capture, not the existing window-listener pattern

`TimeGrid` does drags with `window` listeners, and I deliberately didn't copy it. **This panel renders artifacts inside an iframe**, and a window listener stops receiving `pointermove` the moment the cursor crosses it — the drag dies mid-gesture, which is exactly the path a user takes when narrowing the panel.

Measured both approaches on the same 200px leftward drag across an iframe:

| Approach | Samples received | Panel width |
|---|---|---|
| Pointer capture (shipped) | 9 | 480px → **280px** ✅ |
| Window listeners | 1 | 480px → **480px** ❌ |

The conventional pattern would have been visibly broken here.

### A latent bug this surfaced

`openDoc` built its next state without spreading the previous one:

```ts
_emit({ open: true, docs, activePath: doc.path });   // width dropped
```

Adding `width` to the store would have silently reset a user's resized panel every time a document opened. Fixed, and pinned by a test. TypeScript caught it, but only because the field was required.

Also: width is **not** seeded from `localStorage` at module load — that module is evaluated during SSR too and would desync hydration. `hydratePanelWidth()` applies it after mount, invisible in practice since the panel starts closed.

## 2. Artifact surface routing (`161eb9f`)

The kit shipped, but nothing told an agent *when* to reach for it. The guidance said "reach for UI eagerly" with no threshold and said nothing about inline vs panel — so the default stayed a markdown table in chat no matter how much data there was.

Added a rule keyed on **volume**, with numbers rather than judgement calls, because vague advice doesn't change model behaviour:

| The answer is… | Surface |
|---|---|
| A one-line fact, or narrative | Prose |
| ≤8 rows · ≤4 metrics · one chart | Inline card |
| >12 rows · several sections · scrolled/sorted/kept | Side panel |
| A deliverable they'll keep | Saved `outputs/*.jsx` |
| Something they must *act* on | React + `@cc/ui` |
| Genuinely could be either | **Ask** (`optionPicker` + `hitl`) |

Two tests that settle most cases: *would this need its own scrollbar inside a chat bubble?* (→ panel), and *am I about to type a markdown table?* (→ render it).

The rule goes in the always-injected addendum (~7 lines) because it has to fire unprompted; the fuller table lives in `design.md`, which loads on demand. `load_artifact_kit`'s docstring now says outright to reach for it without being asked whenever real data is about to be presented.

## Verification

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| Python unit tests | 2472 passed, 8 skipped |
| vitest | 63 passed (9 new for panel width) |
| `tsc --noEmit` | clean |
| eslint | clean |
| `next build` | passes |
| Browser drag-across-iframe | pass (table above) |

New tests cover clamping, non-finite input, snapshot stability (React #185), no-emit when pinned at a bound during a drag, width surviving open/close, storage round-trip, out-of-bounds stored values, and unreadable storage.

## Note

The drag was verified as an isolated browser repro of the exact handler pattern, not by driving the real panel — that needs an authenticated session with open documents. The store logic underneath it is unit-tested directly.

title: Copilot agenda + standing instructions (Phase D)
body:
Answers "how does the copilot know what this meeting is *for*" with three things that build on each other.

## 1. Standing instructions — a system prompt for every run

`copilot_config`, per user, prepended to the system prompt of **every** copilot run:

> *I run a 3D-printing company selling to manufacturing teams. Prefer commercial framing. Never suggest a discount — steer to value.*

The per-meeting brief changes every time; **how you want the copilot to behave doesn't**. Retyping that each meeting is how a feature stops being used. Set once from `/notes` (✨ button).

## 2. Conversational agenda building

Describe the meeting in plain language — *"30-min call with Acme to close the annual renewal"* — and the copilot drafts a structured agenda. Keep talking to refine it (*"drop the demo, add pricing"*); it returns the **full updated agenda**, never a diff.

## 3. Agenda-aware live feedback

The agenda is a structured list rather than more prose **precisely so it can be measured**. The copilot sees which items are still outstanding and nudges accordingly — *"you haven't touched pricing"* — which is impossible against a paragraph.

Coverage is a **pure token-overlap check, not a model call**, because it runs on every window and must cost nothing. A single passing mention deliberately does *not* count as covered — otherwise every item goes green the moment one common word is said and the nudging stops being useful.

## Fail-safe

A model failure, a non-JSON reply, or an empty agenda from the model all leave the user's agenda **untouched**. An empty agenda is treated as a bad response rather than a genuine "clear it", since that's far likelier.

Both cascade stages inherit the standing instructions, and the background is rebuilt per suggestion so coverage stays current — the context pack itself stays cached, only the cheap marks recompute.

## Verification

17 tests: shape coercion (models return messy lists — bullets, numbering, bare strings), coverage including the passing-mention case, rendering, and that no model failure mode can destroy the agenda. Migration 125. Suite 2490; `tsc` and `next build` clean.

Rebased onto latest main; migration-prefix guard passes.

**Phase E** (speaking into the call via the bot) and spoken answers back to the agent remain future work.

title: Note Taker settings + per-meeting-type copilot instructions
body:
Three things, following the shape the task manager and email apps already use.

## 1. Per-meeting-type copilot guidance

What deserves an interruption differs completely by meeting type. In a customer call a dropped objection matters; in a **1:1 an unspoken concern** does — and a sales nudge there would be *actively wrong*. All six templates now ship guidance suited to them, plus an agenda hint that seeds the drafter so "draft an agenda" produces something shaped like that meeting type.

| Type | Copilot lens |
|---|---|
| 1:1 | Trust conversation, not a status report — concerns raised obliquely, growth topics skipped again |
| Customer call | Commercial — unanswered objections, buying signals, loose commitments |
| Interview | Competencies not yet probed; never anything about a protected characteristic |
| Retro | Problems with no owner, blame aimed at people rather than systems |
| Standup | Blockers nobody offered help on; interrupt rarely |

**The layering is the interesting part.** Standing instructions ("who I am, how I work") and type guidance ("what matters in *this* kind of meeting") answer different questions, so they **compose** rather than replace. A user override displaces only the shipped default *for that one type* — every other type keeps tracking the defaults, so improving them still reaches anyone who hasn't customised.

## 2. A settings system

One row per user, one endpoint, read and written whole (`GET/PUT /notes/settings`): copilot behaviour, per-type overrides, defaults for new meetings, and the name the bot joins under (consent-relevant — people should be able to tell who is recording them).

**Sensitivity is three named levels rather than raw knobs.** The underlying controls are a minimum gap and a per-meeting cap; exposing those as numbers invites nonsense pairs. `gate()` now takes both as parameters so the levels map onto sane combinations — with a test that higher sensitivity really does mean *both* a shorter wait *and* a higher ceiling, or the label lies about what it does.

## 3. UI

`NotesSettingsModal` replaces the one-off copilot-instructions modal, showing each meeting type's shipped guidance **inline** so you can see what it *would* do before deciding to override it.

## Verification

12 tests: the composition and override precedence, that guidance genuinely differs by type, sensitivity ordering, and that the gate honours configured thresholds. Migration 126. Suite 2501 (stable across three consecutive runs); `tsc` and `next build` clean.

title: Make a failed Google Meet join explain itself
body:
Sending a notetaker to a Google Meet failed with nothing to go on. The worker was running fine on the box (deploy 867: `meeting bot UP on 127.0.0.1:8095`), so this was never a config gap — the bot was dispatched and couldn't get into the call, silently.

## Why nothing was visible

**The failure erased itself.** `/notes/bots/active` filters to running statuses, so a bot that fails leaves the set instantly and the "Notetakers in meetings" strip just empties — "it didn't work" became indistinguishable from "nothing happened". Recent failures (30 min) now stay in the query.

**The error was fetched and discarded.** `ActiveBots.tsx` received `b.error` from the API and rendered only the status label. It now renders the explanation.

## Two real defects in the join path

- **`_click_first` passed its timeout to the visibility wait but not to `click()`.** Meet keeps "Ask to join" *disabled* until a guest types a name, so a visible-but-disabled button burned Playwright's 30s default per selector — five selectors could exceed the whole 150s join budget before reaching the last one.
- **Nothing dismissed Meet's device dialogs.** The container has a virtual mic but no camera, so Meet puts a modal over the green room. The join button sits behind it, which presents *exactly* as "no join button found".

Either alone reproduces the reported symptom.

## Timeout and refusal were the same status

`_await_admission` returned `not_admitted` both when Meet said "you can't join this call" and when it merely ran out the clock in the waiting room. Those need opposite responses from a human — click Admit, versus the link will never work for a signed-out guest. Now split into `refused` / `timeout` / `in_call`, each with an error that names the fix.

`classify_body()` is pure so the phrase lists are tested directly. The costly confusion — treating "asking to be let in" as terminal — is locked by a test.

## A missed selector now says what it saw

Meet's DOM is not a public API, so selectors drift; the useful question is what the page actually rendered. Failures capture url/title/body **plus the label of every visible button**, exposed at:

- `GET /bots/{id}/diagnostics` and `/bots/{id}/screenshot` (worker)
- `GET /notes/meetings/{id}/bot/diagnostics` (gateway)

Also: waits for a real control rather than a fixed 3s sleep (Meet hydrates well after `load`, slower on 2 vCPU), and retries the green room once after a settle.

## Testing

- 2510 unit tests pass (12 new, covering refusal-vs-waiting classification, error diagnostics, and failure visibility)
- `tsc --noEmit` and `next build` clean
- Not verifiable here: the join against a real Meet call — that needs the deployed box, which is the point of merging

## Known gap, not addressed here

`LIVE_ASR_URL` is unset on the VPS, so a bot that joins successfully still produces **no live captions** — only the post-meeting transcript. Wiring the worker to AssemblyAI's streaming endpoint is follow-up work.

title: Give the meeting bot live captions
body:
Follow-up to #274. A bot that joins successfully still produces **no live transcript** — the live console stays empty for the whole call and text only appears once the meeting ends. That failure looks like success right up until the meeting is over, which is the worst shape for it to have.

## Cause

The worker's only ASR path was `LIVE_ASR_URL`, a self-hosted WhisperLive-style socket, and nothing sets it on the VPS. Meanwhile the gateway already knows how to stream — it mints AssemblyAI tokens for the browser recorder from the key in Settings → Models. The worker couldn't reach any of that, running in its own container.

## Approach

The worker asks for credentials rather than holding them:

- **Gateway** — `POST /notes/stt/bot-live-token`, authenticated with the shared bot token rather than a user session, returning the same `LiveToken` the browser gets. Provider choice stays in one place, so a bot and a browser can't end up transcribing through different providers.
- **Worker** — `_resolve_asr()` prefers a self-hosted `LIVE_ASR_URL` when set (it costs nothing per minute), otherwise fetches a token and connects to AssemblyAI streaming v3.
- **Deploy** — wires `NOTES_LIVE_TOKEN_URL` by default. Left opt-in, the silent failure above is what you'd get.

Shipping `ASSEMBLYAI_API_KEY` into the container would have been fewer moving parts, but it duplicates the source of truth and widens the blast radius. A re-fetchable endpoint also matters for a reason a join-time handover can't cover: these tokens live about a minute and meetings run hours, so a worker that loses its socket mid-call needs to be able to ask again.

## Protocol details worth flagging

- **Only completed turns are forwarded.** AssemblyAI streams a growing partial for every turn; the live bus appends rather than replaces, so forwarding partials would stutter the same sentence down the console one word at a time. This matches what the browser recorder already relays.
- **Word timings are milliseconds, the bus works in seconds.** The conversion matters beyond display — those spans drive speaker reconciliation against the voiceprint gallery.
- **Deepgram streaming from the worker isn't wired.** It logs that plainly rather than opening a socket that will never produce a transcript.

## Testing

- 2525 unit tests pass (25 new): AssemblyAI turn parsing, partial-dropping, ms→s conversion, protocol routing, self-hosted precedence, bot-token auth on the new endpoint, and a deploy-wiring guard so the token URL can't silently go missing
- `ruff` clean on changed files
- Not verifiable here: the actual AssemblyAI socket, which needs the deployed box and a real call

title: App Workshop: per-app npm dependencies for T2 (unblocks Three.js/3D)
body:
## Summary
- Unblocks building anything the vendored `react`/`react-dom`/`@cc/ui` set can't cover on its own — concretely, a 3D viewer needing `three.js`/`@react-three/fiber`, which previously hard-failed at the build step's import allowlist.
- New `apps/agents/agent-app-builder/build/install_t2_deps.mjs` (platform-owned, not editable by the builder agent) — the only sanctioned way a T2 app adds a package:
  - `npm install --ignore-scripts` — blocks the standard npm supply-chain RCE vector (a malicious package's postinstall script running arbitrary code before any of it ships anywhere), same rationale as `acb_skills/loader.py`'s wheel-only installs for the gateway's own Python deps.
  - Package-spec allowlist regex — plain name, optionally `@version` or `@scope/name@version`, no flags, no URLs (so a spec can't smuggle in something like `--registry=...`).
  - 300MiB `node_modules` size cap, removing `node_modules` and failing loudly if exceeded.
  - Scaffolds `package.json` if the app doesn't have one yet.
- `build_t2.mjs` now auto-detects an app-local `node_modules` and switches from the shared vendor cache + import allowlist to standard npm resolution rooted at the workspace — no allowlist in that mode, since the app can only import what it explicitly installed. Most T2 apps never opt in and keep paying zero extra build/disk cost.

title: Let a meeting be prepared before it starts
body:
Item 01 of the UX redesign plan, and the structural half of it.

A meeting moves through three phases — before, during, after — and the app had surfaces for the last two. Agenda, briefing and copilot context lived only in `/notes/live/[id]`, which doesn't exist until a session is already running. So the only moment you could tell the copilot what the meeting was about was *while it was happening* — exactly when you can't type. In practice the copilot walked in cold every time.

## What's new

The meeting page renders a prep view when a meeting has no recording and no segments: title, when, attendees, meeting type, agenda, briefing, copilot toggle, and the three ways to start. Almost everything it needs already shipped as an API (`/agenda/chat`, `/brief`, `/context/deep`, `/settings`) — what was missing was somewhere to use it beforehand.

`New meeting` on the library opens prep; `Record` still starts capture immediately.

## Three decisions worth flagging

**`meeting.copilot_enabled` is nullable, not `NOT NULL DEFAULT FALSE`.** Three states are needed, not two: on, off, and "not decided — follow the account default". With only two, turning the copilot off for one sensitive meeting would be silently undone by the global setting, which is the opposite of what "off" means. `copilot_should_run()` is pure so the precedence is testable without a session.

**`scheduled_at` is separate from the existing `start_at`.** `start_at` is when capture actually began, and the pipeline and library sort on it. Overloading it would make an unstarted meeting look like one that ran the instant it was created.

**`bot-join` now accepts an existing `meeting_id`.** Without this the bot creates a fresh meeting and the agenda, briefing, attendees and copilot decision you just set up are stranded on a different row — which would have made prep pointless for the bot path entirely. This was the non-obvious gap.

## The seam that makes prep worth doing

`live_session.begin()` honours the prepared decision and starts the orchestrator, so the copilot is listening from the first word rather than needing you to find the console mid-conversation. Fail-safe: a copilot that can't start must not take the recording with it.

## Two smaller ideas

- **Context meter** — three layers (briefing / history / agents), so "why is the copilot being generic?" is answerable *before* the meeting rather than after.
- **The meeting-type card shows its lens** — the copilot guidance that type applies is visible during prep, so "why did it say that?" is answerable in advance, and it links to the override in Settings.

## Testing

- 2536 unit tests pass (11 new): copilot precedence in all three states, partial-patch semantics, the `False` vs `None` distinction, migration nullability/idempotency, and the bot-join attach path
- `tsc --noEmit` and `next build` clean
- `ruff` clean on changed files

## Still to come from the plan

Two-column live console, library banded by state, header consolidation, outcome strip, visual pass.

title: Note Taker UX redesign: console, library, outcomes, visual pass
body:
Items 02–06 of the UX plan. #278 added the missing phase (prep); this reshapes the other two so the work already running is actually visible.

## Agenda coverage escapes the copilot

`coverage()` always knew which agenda items had been discussed — but it ran inside the copilot's loop, so it fed a prompt, showed nowhere, and vanished entirely when the copilot was off. It now lives on the transcript bus (`agenda_progress.py`), so *"you're 40 minutes in and haven't reached pricing"* works either way, and it still costs nothing (token overlap, no model call).

Two properties make it trustworthy, both tested:

- **Coverage latches.** An item discussed at minute five is still covered at minute fifty. Recomputing from a rolling window alone would let items blink back to uncovered as the window moved past them — worse than not showing coverage at all.
- **Bounded text, unbounded conclusions.** The word buffer is capped; the latch is O(agenda). A four-hour meeting doesn't accumulate a four-hour transcript in RAM.

## Live console: two columns

The transcript is what your eye rests on, so it gets the width. The copilot gets a rail — its output arrives in bursts and needs somewhere to arrive *to*. Setup panels are gone; they belong in prep, and six equal-weight cards above the transcript is what made this screen unreadable.

## Library: banded by what you'd do about it

Live / Coming up / Needs you / Earlier, replacing one reverse-chronological run. Rows report outcomes (*"2 actions waiting for approval"*) rather than mechanics (*"318 segments"*) — nobody scans for segment counts.

Banding is pure (`lib/bands.ts`) so the priority rules are testable; notably **live beats needs-you**, so an in-progress call can't be filed under triage. The list SQL computes the band signals in one query rather than N+1-ing the detail endpoint per row.

## Header: one primary action

It had grown to six peers, three of them the same intent, plus a template dropdown that asked you to classify a meeting before you'd said what it was. Template moved to prep in #278; the rest are behind **New meeting**.

## Outcome strip

A finished meeting leads with its yield — actions, notes, follow-up — instead of hiding actions in tab three. The agenda recap is free (coverage was computed during the call) and turns "what did we not get to" into the start of the next meeting.

## Visual pass: one speaker, one colour

Speaker colour was defined twice with different fallbacks, and not at all in the roster, avatars or list rows. `lib/speakers.ts` is now the single source, carried through transcript edge, name, avatar and chip — so a wall of text becomes scannable. Hues come from existing semantic tokens, so there's no second colour system to keep legible in both themes.

Fixed while unifying: an unnumbered key (a *named* speaker rather than `S1`) fell through to hue 0, so every named person looked like the same person.

## Testing

- 2545 backend tests, 90 frontend tests (25 new across coverage latching, band priority, and speaker hue)
- `tsc --noEmit`, `next build`, `ruff` all clean

One test I wrote was wrong and I corrected the test, not the code: it asserted two specific names get different hues, which five buckets can't guarantee. The property worth holding is that hashing *spreads* and is stable per key.

## Not included

- **Calendar integration.** "Coming up" only holds meetings you created by hand. Worth wiring Google Calendar so it populates itself — flagged as an open question in the original mockups and still open.
- Per-suggestion copilot feedback, and series grouping.

title: Artifact system: token audit — tier design.md, cap compile diagnostics
body:
A measurement pass over the whole artifact path, looking for tokens spent without buying anything. Two real problems, both fixed; the rest measured and left alone.

## 1. `design.md` was all-or-nothing — 5,413 tokens per call

`load_artifact_kit` was built with tiered loading. `load_design_system` never was, so every caller got the entire document. ~60% of it is three reference blocks — the report kit, the data-viz blocks, the React section — and an artifact needs **at most one**. An agent that wanted the colour palette also paid for the timeline-chart markup.

This compounds: the surface-routing rule merged in #271 deliberately makes agents render more often, so the load happens more.

| Call | Tokens | |
|---|---|---|
| `load_design_system()` | **3,345** | core — was 5,413 → **−39%** |
| `load_design_system("blocks")` | 350 | `cc-report` document kit |
| `load_design_system("charts")` | 1,176 | KPI/chart/table/timeline blocks |
| `load_design_system("react")` | 670 | React artifacts |
| `load_design_system("all")` | 5,413 | unchanged escape hatch |

The core keeps what's needed on *every* artifact — palette, typography, spacing, motion, do's/don'ts + anti-slop, the lint contract, and the surface-routing rule — and names what else is available.

Chunks are cut out of the real file at load time, so there's no second copy to drift. If someone renames a heading, the markers stop matching and it **falls back to the full document** — serving too much beats silently serving an empty reference. There's a test for that.

## 2. Compile diagnostics were unbounded — up to ~3,385 tokens

`artifact_lint` caps findings at 14. `formatErrors` joined *every* esbuild error. A file with 60 bad imports returned 60 copies of the same sentence — and error text is paid for twice, once when the agent reads it and again when it re-emits the whole artifact to fix it.

| | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| 60 bad imports | 13,540 chars / **~3,385 tok** | 1,061 chars / **~265 tok** (−92%) |
| Lines | 60 | 9 |

Three changes: de-duplicate identical messages with a `×N` count, cap at 8 distinct errors plus a remainder line, and shorten the per-occurrence allowlist message from four lines to one (the long "why" belongs in the docs, not stapled to every diagnostic). Still names the first offender, so it stays actionable.

## What I measured and deliberately left alone

- **Always-injected addendum: 5,642 tokens**, 43% artifact-related. Already scope-gated and working — a sub-agent gets **1,571**, and a scope without `emit_generative_ui` drops the UI guidance entirely. It's stable per scope, so prompt caching covers the per-turn cost.
- **No duplication** between the short per-scope blurb and the long-form guidance — they're mutually exclusive (verified, not assumed).
- **`load_artifact_kit` is already right**: 507-token index, ~60 tokens per component. It's the model the design-system tool now follows.
- **`@cc/ui` bundle cost** is unchanged and already small: an 8-component artifact is 21 KB vs 19.6 KB for bare React, i.e. the kit is ~1.5 KB after tree-shaking.

The addendum grew **+5 tokens** for the pointer that makes the cheap path discoverable — it buys back 2,068 tokens on every `design.md` load.

## Net effect

A typical artifact turn that loads guidance drops from ~11,055 tokens of input (addendum + full design.md) to ~8,992, and a turn that hits a broken compile saves a further ~3,100.

## Verification

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| Python unit tests | 2545 passed, 8 skipped |
| vitest | 65 passed (11 new) |
| `tsc --noEmit` | clean |
| eslint | clean |
| `next build` | passes |
| ruff (blocking gate) | clean |

New tests cover: core materially cheaper than full, core retains palette/anti-slop/surface-routing/lint, core omits the heavy blocks, sections are disjoint, aliases and case-insensitivity, `"all"` still complete, **nothing unreachable across the tiers**, unknown section lists what's available, marker-drift falls back to the full doc, diagnostics capped and de-duplicated, and repeat-count collapsing.

title: Calendar: plan on tap (not on open), per-run note in both modes, and note overrides the standing prompt
body:
## What & why

Addresses two issues with the AI planner: it auto-planned before you could add a prompt, and it wasn't obvious the per-run prompt actually reached (and could override) the LLM.

### 1. Plan on tap, not on open
The panel used to fire a plan the instant it opened, so a note typed afterwards was ignored. Now the panel opens on a **pre-run state** that invites an optional note + a plan-through horizon, and only plans when you press **Plan** / **Fit**. Changing the horizon **live-replans only once a proposal is already on screen** (before that it just updates the pending setting), so planning stays an explicit act.

### 2. Per-run note in **both** Plan and Fit
The note was already threaded to the LLM ranker for replan server-side, but the UI hid the box (with a stale "replan ignores free text" comment). **Fit** now accepts a per-run note too, and the "AI-ranked / fell back to priority" banner shows in both modes.

### 3. The per-run note **overrides** the standing prompt on conflict
Verified the LLM context is organized correctly and made the override explicit:
- **Standing planning philosophy** → *system* message.
- **Per-run note** → *user* message.
- Added a **PRECEDENCE** rule to the system prompt (and relabelled the note in the user message) so e.g. `"calls only, low energy"` wins over a standing `"front-load deep work"` for that run — while **never** overriding the ★ One Thing rule or the capacity limit.

End-to-end path confirmed: `note → run() → energy_note → /calendar/{plan,replan} → _replan_core → _llm_rank_day` (ordering) **and** `_horizon_from_note` (window). Both `apiPlanDay` and `apiReplan` already serialize `energy_note`, so no API change was needed.

## Files
- `calendar/PlanDayPanel.tsx` — remove auto-run; pre-run empty state; note box + AI banner in both modes; gate live-replan to post-first-run; pure horizon helpers (captured `openedAtMs` for labels, fresh `Date.now()` in `run`).
- `routes/tasks/calendar.py` — PRECEDENCE rule in the ranker system prompt + note relabel in the user message.

title: Actually ask AssemblyAI for speakers on live streaming
body:
Live transcription arrived with no speaker separation. It looked like a model problem; it wasn't. **We never requested diarization at all.**

## The bug

AssemblyAI streaming does not diarize by default — it's opt-in per connection via `speaker_labels=true` on the WebSocket URL, exactly like Deepgram's `diarize`.

The Deepgram path has always sent `diarize: "true"`. The AssemblyAI path sent `sample_rate`, `encoding`, `format_turns` and the token — and nothing about speakers. Both producers had the same omission: the browser recorder (`lib/live.ts`) and the meeting-bot worker (`app/live.py`).

## Also fixed

Both parsers now read the speaker from **either the turn or its words**. Which field carries the label varies by streaming model, and reading only one presents as "diarization is broken" when the data is sitting right there. The worker maps AssemblyAI's `A`/`B` onto our `S1`/`S2` space so live labels agree with the batch path, the rename UI, and batch reconciliation against the voiceprint gallery.

## Two things that aren't bugs but will bite

- **Streaming diarization needs Universal-3 Pro Streaming** or a multilingual streaming model. **Universal-2 has no streaming diarization** — and it fails by returning captions without speakers, not by erroring, which is indistinguishable from the bug above.
- **The streaming model is chosen independently of the `tier-stt` batch model.** Picking universal-2 in Settings → Models does *not* make streaming use universal-2. `ASSEMBLYAI_LIVE_MODEL` governs that, and it's unset, so AssemblyAI's streaming default applies.

Batch diarization is unaffected and has always worked — `build_request` sets `speaker_labels: True`, including on universal-2. So post-meeting transcripts had speakers while live didn't, which is the confusing pattern that was reported.

## Docstring correction

`assemblyai_provider.py` claimed AssemblyAI "diarizes on both batch and streaming" — true only if you ask, and only on a model that can. That sentence is a large part of why this looked like plumbing rather than a missing parameter. Corrected with the precise rules and the model caveat.

## Testing

- 2549 backend tests, 94 frontend (9 new): that the socket URL carries `speaker_labels=true`, turn-level and word-level speaker extraction, A/B → S1/S2 mapping, and that an undiarized turn reports *no* speaker rather than a wrong one
- `tsc`, `next build`, blocking `ruff` all clean

Not verifiable from here: the actual streaming response shape against a live key — which is why both parsers accept either field position rather than betting on one.

title: Org access control: members, roles, and per-user feature/agent access
body:
Phase 1 of [`specs/org_access_control.md`](ai-company-brain/specs/org_access_control.md) — the buildable subset of the existing `multi_user_organization_research.md` proposal.

## Why this slice

The research doc scopes 22–32 weeks across identity, memory, credentials, the entity graph, and the Action Broker. None of it is enforceable until there is **a principal with a resolvable permission set** — modules, memory scoping and credential scoping are all *consumers* of that one check. Building them first means building three private half-implementations of it. This PR is that check, plus the admin surface to drive it.

The starting state was thinner than the research doc implies: roles were an env var (`EXECUTIVE_EMAILS`) parsed in ~50 copy-pasted proxy files, two roles total, and **zero** feature or agent gating — every signed-in user saw every pane and could run every agent.

## What an admin can now do

Invite someone, give them a role, then add or remove individual pieces on top of it — without SQL and without cloning a role per person:

```
priya@fracktal.in   roles: [member]
  features : chat, email, memory, tasks, notes, dashboard, artifacts   ← no whatsapp, no build.apps
  agents   : email-assistant, task-manager                             ← not whatsapp-assistant, not app-builder
```

`GET /admin/members/{email}/access` returns each decision **with its provenance** ("denied for this person, overriding role `member`"), and the UI renders that verbatim. An admin who has to replay the resolution algorithm in their head to answer "why can Priya still see WhatsApp?" stops trusting the model.

## The model

- **One organization**; `organization_id` is carried everywhere so a second org is a data change, not a migration.
- **Five seeded system roles** (`owner`/`admin`/`manager`/`member`/`guest`) plus a non-assignable `agent_service`. `member` deliberately omits WhatsApp, Approvals, Integrations, Models and both Build panes — access is added, not taken away.
- **Per-user allow/deny overrides** layered on top, each recording its `reason`.

### Resolution is two layers, not flat deny-wins

This is the one design call worth reviewing. I first implemented the AWS IAM rule the research doc recommends — explicit deny always wins — and a test caught that it **cannot express the requirement**:

```
role:     agents:run:*                        baseline: every agent
override: agents:run:*                 deny   take the blanket away
override: agents:run:email-assistant   allow  hand two back
```

Under flat deny-wins that resolves to *no agents* — the wildcard deny swallows the specific allow, so an admin would have to clone a role per person, the exact failure roles exist to prevent. So overrides compete by **specificity** (exact beats wildcard; ties go to deny).

Role grants stay out of that comparison on purpose: an override of `feature:*` = deny must switch *everything* off, and it wouldn't if a role's exact `feature:chat` could out-specify it.

## Enforcement, in order of authority

| Seam | Where | Status |
|---|---|---|
| `require_permission()` | gateway route dependencies | **boundary of record** |
| `assert_can_run_agent()` | both `/agent/run*` endpoints | enforced |
| `GET /agent` registry filter | picker never offers a 403 | enforced |
| `AccessGate` + nav filtering | control plane | presentation only |

Agent-context intersection (an agent run can never exceed its caller) is implemented in `EffectiveAccess.intersect` and unit-tested; its full form — per-user credential and memory scoping — is research-doc §7–§8 and stays queued.

## Why this is safe to deploy

- `app_user.role` is **retained and dual-written**; `require_role()` is unchanged, so no existing route changes behaviour.
- The migration backfills `executive`→`admin`, `employee`→`member`, and bootstraps an owner — nobody is locked out on deploy.
- `get_current_user` upgrades the coarse role from the DB but **never downgrades** it, so an `EXECUTIVE_EMAILS` admin who has never signed in keeps working.
- Invariants enforced server-side: the org always keeps an owner; nobody assigns a role above their own rank; system roles are immutable; you cannot revoke your own access-management permission.
- Permissions are deliberately **not** in the NextAuth JWT — a JWT outlives an access change, and "I revoked WhatsApp an hour ago and they still have it" is what makes people distrust the whole model. Identity in the session, access resolved per request behind a 60s cache that every admin write invalidates.

⚠️ **One fail-open to note:** if the access tables are absent (migration not yet applied), the resolver degrades to the legacy `executive`/`employee` mapping rather than bricking sign-in. It does *not* apply to a member whose row exists — an unknown user gets nothing. This mirrors the contract `deps.py` already documents and should be removed when **BO-2** lands; flagged in spec §7.

## Verification

- Migration applied **twice** against a real Postgres 16 — idempotent; backfill and owner bootstrap confirmed correct.
- Resolver checked end-to-end against that database for owner / restricted member / unrestricted member / suspended / unknown.
- 2584 unit tests pass (48 new covering matching, validation, both resolution layers, agent inheritance, and the guards).
- Control plane builds and typechecks clean; new files lint clean. (The `Sidebar.tsx` `static-components` lint errors are pre-existing on `main` — verified against the baseline.)

## Deliberately not in this PR

Modules/teams, memory scoping, per-user credential scoping, entity-graph visibility + RLS, and everything SaaS — all still tracked in the research doc and phased in spec §8. Also: ~50 proxy routes still carry their own `EXECUTIVE_EMAILS` copy. `lib/gateway.ts` is the single replacement and new routes use it, but the sweep is cosmetic now (permissions resolve server-side from the email regardless), so it is left as follow-up.

title: Show the copilot on the recording screen
body:
Recording a meeting in-app and running the copilot both worked — but you couldn't tell.

The copilot's output lives in the console at `/notes/live/[id]`. The recording screen said nothing about it at all, not even whether one was running, and its copy still promised the copilot *"will appear"* — written before it existed.

That split is deliberate and stays: the console is the considered view, and recording survives navigation via the RecordingDock. What was missing is that the screen you actually sit on during your own meeting had no state and no control.

## What's added

`LiveCopilotStrip` on the recording screen: on/off with a toggle, a running suggestion count, and **the latest suggestion inline** with its grounding. Inline because during your own meeting you won't go looking for it — and a suggestion you never see is the same as no copilot. Depth stays in the console, and the link now says recording keeps running if you follow it.

Only subscribes to the copilot stream while it's on, so an off copilot costs nothing.

## Verified while tracing this path

The backend for in-app-recording + copilot was already complete, and I confirmed each link rather than assuming:

- `live_session.begin()` fires on the first recorded chunk, and auto-starts the copilot when the meeting was prepared with it on

title: Pin the streaming model that can actually diarize
body:
Asking for `speaker_labels` (#284) was necessary but not sufficient. Live diarization also needs a streaming model that supports it — and we were letting AssemblyAI pick.

## The model family confusion

AssemblyAI's **streaming models are a separate family from the batch ones**. Valid streaming ids are `universal-streaming-english`, `universal-streaming-multilingual`, and `u3-rt-pro` (Universal-3 Pro Streaming).

**`universal-2` is not a streaming model at all.** That's why selecting it in Settings → Models never affected live transcription — that setting only ever drove the batch pipeline. So the reported symptom had nothing to do with the model that was picked.

Of the streaming models, diarization needs **`u3-rt-pro`** or the multilingual one. That's now the default instead of whatever AssemblyAI would choose, overridable via `ASSEMBLYAI_LIVE_MODEL` if the cost tradeoff isn't worth it — captions still work on the others, just with every voice merged into one speaker.

## Second bug found while wiring this

The meeting-bot worker built its WebSocket URL **without `speech_model` at all**, so it silently discarded whatever model the gateway had chosen. A deployment could be correctly configured for `u3-rt-pro` and the bot would still connect on the default and return no speakers.

## Why both were expensive to find

They share a failure shape: a wrong streaming model returns a **working transcript with every voice merged into one**, not an error. That reads as "diarization is broken" rather than "misconfigured", which is what sent this hunting through the plumbing.

## Testing

- 2569 backend tests pass (5 new: default pinning, override, batch-tier isolation, and that the worker forwards the gateway's model)
- `ruff` clean

Updated one existing test that pinned the old "let the provider default" behaviour — that assertion described what we did, not what we wanted.
