title: Enforce feature access at the gateway, not just in the UI
body:
Stacked on #286 — review that first. Base is `claude/multi-tenant-user-management-1cb3ub`, so this diff shows only the enforcement work.

## The gap this closes

#286 shipped the permission mechanism but only applied it to `/admin` and the agent-run path. **Feature access was UI-deep.** Denying someone `feature:whatsapp` hid the nav item and blocked the route — while `GET /whatsapp/chats` still returned their data.

```
before →  whatsapp / email / tasks / notes / memory / apps: require_permission occurrences = 0
```

## Approach: gate at the router

Wherever a prefix has one audience, the gate goes on the `APIRouter` rather than each endpoint. The failure mode of per-route gating is the route someone forgets; router-level gating means an endpoint added next year is covered by default.

Router-gated: `whatsapp`, `email`, `tasks`, `notes`, `chat`, `actions`, `integrations`. `/memory` already required the internal token and is left alone.

## Mixed-audience surfaces, gated per route

A blanket gate would have broken each of these:

| Surface | Treatment | Why not blanket |
|---|---|---|
| `/settings` | writes need `feature:models`; reads stay open | The reads feed the chat model picker — gating them would break model selection for every ordinary member |
| `/integrations/oauth` | `authorize` + `refresh` gated, `callback` not | The callback is the provider's browser redirect |
| `/agent` | registry writes on `agents:manage`; runs stay per-agent; `/webhook/{source}` untouched | That webhook is deliberately unauthenticated for external callers |
| `/apps` | `require_app_author` (`feature:build.apps`) vs `require_app_viewer` (`apps:use:*`) | One prefix, two audiences: building an app ≠ using one the team shared |

Enforcing `apps:use:*` matters on its own — the permission was already offered in the admin UI and did nothing. A toggle that silently has no effect is worse than not offering it.

**Also fixes `/agent/run/async`**, which had no run gate at all. I missed it in #286 when gating the other two run endpoints.

## The exemptions are the load-bearing part

Six routes carry their own authentication and arrive with **no session and no internal token**:

| Exempt route | Its own auth |
|---|---|
| `/whatsapp/webhook` | Meta verify-token (GET), signature (POST) |
| `/whatsapp/bridge/{ingest,reclassify,labels,paired}` | `X-Bridge-Secret`, constant-time compare |
| `/email/oauth/{provider}/callback` | HMAC-signed `state` |
| `/email/webhook/microsoft` | `validationToken` echo + `clientState` |
| `/notes/meetings/{id}/live/segment` | `MEETING_BOT_TOKEN` |
| `/notes/stt/bot-live-token` | `MEETING_BOT_TOKEN` |

Gating any of these would not restrict access — it would **stop ingestion, silently**, until someone noticed missing data. The existing notes tests caught the meeting-bot case on the first run; a signature sweep across all gated routers found the other five before they shipped.

Exempting removes the *feature* check only. Each endpoint's own scheme still runs.

### Two properties keep the list honest

Both enforced by `tests/unit/test_org_access_enforcement.py`:

1. **Matching is on the route template, never the concrete URL** — so `/thing/items/webhook` cannot reach a gated route by spelling an exempt path in a parameter. There is a test for exactly that.
2. **Any route in a gated router taking no `UserContext` must be exempt or a declared UI read.** A new machine entrypoint added later fails the test instead of breaking production. The gateway DOX now carries this as an explicit warning for anyone adding a webhook.

## Audit trail

Admin writes now emit `acb_audit.record()` alongside their structlog line, per the gateway convention I skipped in #286. "Who could see what, and who changed it" is the first question after an incident and the first thing an access review needs. The override record captures the actual permissions and reasons, not just a count.

## Test change

`tests/unit/test_notes_live_http.py` stubbed `get_current_user` with a duck-typed object lacking `has_permission`. Replaced with a real `UserContext` carrying a resolvable permission set — more faithful to what the dependency actually returns.

## Verification

- 2612 unit tests pass (28 new: the gate's behaviour, exemption coverage, template-vs-URL matching, and a wiring check that fails if a router loses its dependency).
- Gateway boots with all 451 routes.
- Every exemption verified to match a real route template — a typo'd exemption is dead text that silently gates a machine callback, so that is asserted too.

## Deliberately unchanged

`/observability` and `/debug` keep their existing `EXECUTIVE` gate. Moving them to `feature:observability` would *widen* access to the `manager` role, and a PR that tightens access shouldn't quietly loosen one.

title: Scope integration credentials and org memory to the acting member
body:
Third in the series. Stacked on #290 (which is stacked on #286) — review those first; this diff shows only the credential and memory work.

## The gap

Until now an agent run received **every configured credential regardless of who invoked it**. An agent's `config.json` was effectively an entitlement: picking an agent that declares Zoho was enough to reach Zoho, whatever the caller's access said.

## Two new permission families

Both usable immediately from the existing member access editor, with the same Inherit / Allow / Deny control and provenance as features and agents:

| Permission | Means |
|---|---|
| `integrations:use:<service>` | Which third-party services an agent may use **on this member's behalf**. Distinct from `integrations:manage`, which is the right to add and rotate the credentials themselves. |
| `memory:write_org` | Writing organisation-wide memory. |

Personal and agent-scoped memory stay **ungated** — they are already keyed to the acting user and the running agent, so there is nothing to authorise. Org memory is the shared one, which is why writing to it is the act that needs a permission. Reads stay open to `member`: a recall that silently returns nothing is worse than one that works.

*(Correcting something I said earlier in this series: memory scoping was not missing. Personal / agent / org scopes already existed via contextvars. What was missing was the permission on the shared scope.)*

## How it works

`build_integrations()` takes an optional authorization predicate; the executor supplies it from the member's resolved access, reusing the same lookup that arms the memory gate so there is exactly one access resolution per run.

Two properties worth checking in review:

- **An agent cannot widen its own access.** Declaring more integrations produces more entries in `unavailable`, not more credentials. There's a test named for exactly this.
- **Filtering runs before the env injection.** At the streaming call site credentials are injected into the run's environment (B6 Tier 0, restored by token afterwards). Filtering first means an unauthorized credential never enters that environment — not merely absent from `state["integrations"]`.

Unauthorized services are reported through the existing `unavailable` map rather than raising, so a member missing one integration still gets a working agent that can explain what it cannot do.

## Two deliberate asymmetries

**Background runs are unfiltered.** The predicate is `None` unless the run is attributable to an *active* member — so cron, the reconciler, webhook-triggered runs, and any address without an `app_user` row behave exactly as before. This is the important one: starving those runs would fail *silently*, with no 403 and no error, just work that quietly stops happening. Who may start a run at all is already enforced upstream by `assert_can_run_agent`, so an unidentifiable address here means "platform-initiated", not "attacker".

**Migration 129 grants `integrations:use:*` to every seeded role except `guest`**, so nobody loses access on deploy — that preserves precisely the behaviour already in effect. The restriction only takes hold once an admin sets a per-user deny.

## What this is *not*

**Authorization, not isolation** — and the spec now says so out loud (§8a). During a run, resolved credentials still live in the process environment; an agent reading `os.environ` directly rather than `state["integrations"]` can still see what's there. Per-run scoping narrows the window, but the boundary is cooperative.

Real isolation needs the sandbox work (**BO-7**). The honest claim today is: *the platform will not hand a member credentials they are not authorized for* — **not** *a hostile agent cannot obtain them*. Those are different sentences and only the first is true.

## Verification

- Migration 129 applied **twice** against a real Postgres 16 — idempotent, grants correct (`member` gets `integrations:use:*` and `memory:read_org` but not `memory:write_org`; `guest` gets neither).
- End-to-end against that database: owner unfiltered, a member with a `zoho-crm` deny blocked on exactly that service, another member on the same role unaffected, background run with the filter off entirely.
- 2633 unit tests pass (21 new), covering the filter, the executor's authorizer across all four "no acting member" paths, the org-memory gate, and that a *broken* permission predicate fails closed rather than open.
- Control plane builds, typechecks and lints clean.

title: Two bugs a first test would have hit
body:
Pre-test review of the paths that actually get exercised. Both of these are in code I shipped this session, and both would have shown up on the first real meeting.

## 1. The agenda recap reported every meeting as a failure

Live coverage is held in memory and deliberately dropped when a meeting ends (`pipeline` calls `agenda_progress.reset`). The post-meeting recap then read that empty state back and rendered **every agenda item as "never reached"** — on every completed meeting, including ones where everything was covered.

Exactly inverted, on the feature I'd described as *"free, because coverage was computed during the call"*.

Fixed by reading the right source for the phase: the live buffer while the meeting runs, the stored transcript once it's over. The stored path needs no latch — a finished transcript already contains the whole conversation, so there's nothing to remember across calls.

## 2. The prep screen showed the wrong time outside UTC

It fed a `datetime-local` input a sliced ISO string, which is a UTC wall clock. A meeting set for **10:00 IST reopened showing 04:30** — and blurring the field then saved that wrong time back.

Now converted to the viewer's timezone properly. Worth noting this class of bug is invisible in a UTC-based test run, which is how it survived to here.

## Checked and found sound

- `attendees` / `agenda` JSONB columns both default to arrays, so `jsonb_array_length` in the new list query can't error on a NULL or an object
- Copilot auto-start is idempotent across reconnects (`copilot.start` guards on `is_running`)
- Band assignment puts a live meeting above "needs you", so an in-progress call can't be filed under triage

## Noted, not changed

`/notes` endpoints don't filter by `owner_email` — `_load_meeting` selects on id alone. This is a pre-existing pattern across the whole notes app, not something these changes introduced, and not a one-line fix to make safely in a pre-test pass. Flagging it rather than half-doing it.

## Testing

2572 backend tests, 96 frontend tests, `tsc`, `next build`, `ruff` all clean. 5 new tests, including one that reproduces the coverage-after-reset failure directly.

title: Separate the service identity token from the LLM key; sign the agent webhook
body:
BO‑2 residuals **#3** and **#4**. Fourth in the series, stacked on #291 → #290 → #286.

Both of these let a caller act as the platform, and both sit directly under the access-control work: the model in #286–#291 assumes a caller's identity means something. These two made that assumption false.

---

## 1. The LLM key *was* the identity token

`_get_internal_token()` fell back to `LITELLM_MASTER_KEY`, and the orchestrator handed agents whichever value it resolved to — **preferring `gateway_internal_token` when set**. So every agent held a credential granting `SERVICE_ACCESS`. An agent could `PUT /admin/members/{itself}/overrides` and grant itself anything, defeating the entire model the previous three PRs built.

Now two secrets with different jobs:

| Secret | Role | Checked by | Handed to agents |
|---|---|---|---|
| `GATEWAY_INTERNAL_TOKEN` | service identity → `SERVICE_ACCESS` | `require_internal_auth`, `get_current_user`'s Bearer branch | **never** |
| `LITELLM_MASTER_KEY` | the `/v1` API key | `require_llm_api_auth` (new) | yes — that is its purpose |

`/v1` accepts either, because the Next.js server and internal jobs route completions too. Everything else accepts identity only.

Every `/v1` client now reads `settings.llm_api_key`: `agents.py`, `_model_resolution.py`, `code_session.py`, `mutation.py` — which ships the value into a container as an env var, the worst possible place for a full-authority credential — and the executor's BYOK provider config. **A test asserts none of them resolves `gateway_internal_token`**, so the escalation can't come back by accident.

Callers that hit gateway *business* APIs (`skill-task-gtd`, the email/whatsapp agent repos, workspace upload) still use the identity token and are unchanged. Moving those to on-behalf-of auth is separate work.

**Upgrade path:** with `GATEWAY_INTERNAL_TOKEN` unset, identity still falls back to the LLM key so nothing 401s on deploy — but it warns on every resolution, because a silent fallback here is the vulnerability wearing a fix's clothes.

### What this does *not* fix

Agents run in-process (BO‑7), so one that reads `get_settings()` can still obtain the identity token. What's closed is the **shared-secret** exposure: the value most likely to leak outside the process — an API key, by design present in BYOK configs, provider settings and logs — is no longer an identity credential. The in-process path needs the sandbox.

---

## 2. `/agent/webhook/{source}` was unauthenticated

It dispatches an agent run with no auth and no `assert_can_run_agent` — a **fourth run path**, internet-reachable through Caddy, bypassing every gate added in #290.

Now HMAC‑SHA256 over the raw body in `X-CC-Signature`, with per-source secrets (`AGENT_WEBHOOK_SECRET_<SOURCE>`) overriding a global one, so one leaked integration can't trigger every agent. A valid signature *is* the authorization: it proves the platform's own secret produced the request, the same trust level as the internal token. There's no member to resolve — which is exactly why the signature is mandatory.

**It fails closed when unconfigured** (503, naming the variable to set), unlike the bridge and bot-token checks elsewhere that allow when unset. Those receive data; this one starts an agent run.

Safe to make strict: the audit report records that **nothing calls this path** — the provider receivers live in `ingestion/sources/*/webhook.py` and dispatch no agents — so there's no working sender to break.

---

## Also

Switched the identity comparisons to `secrets.compare_digest`, now that one of the two secrets is the high-value one.

## Verification

- 2652 unit tests pass (19 new): token resolution across provisioned/unprovisioned/absent, that the LLM key is refused on identity routes while `/v1` still accepts it, signature accept/reject/tamper/missing, per-source override precedence, source-name normalisation (`zoho-crm` → `..._ZOHO_CRM`), and the regression guard on `/v1` clients.
- Gateway boots with all 451 routes.
- `.env.example` documents both secrets and how to generate them.
- `FOUNDATION_BUILDOUT_CHECKLIST.md` BO‑2 updated: residuals #2/#3/#4 now ✅, **#1 (default-deny authentication posture) still open** — that's the remaining BO‑2 work, and it's authentication, not the permission model.

title: WhatsApp: sync profile pictures from the number, render them in the inbox
body:
## What

Chats in the WhatsApp app rendered as colored initials — no profile picture (DP) was ever synced for anyone. This pulls each contact/group's real WhatsApp profile picture across and renders it in the inbox, falling back to the existing colored-initials look wherever there isn't one yet.

## Why

WhatsApp doesn't push profile pictures proactively over the wire, but whatsmeow (the personal-number bridge) can ask for one per chat. Nothing did that yet.

## How

**Bridge (Go)**
- New `avatars.go`: a fixed-size worker pool (3) drains a bounded queue of "check this chat's picture" jobs, so a history-sync backfill (hundreds of chats surfacing at once) doesn't fire hundreds of concurrent WhatsApp API calls.
- A per-(account, chat) **TTL cache** (24h, in the bridge's own sqlite meta store) means a chat is asked about at most once a day, no matter how many messages it sends. The cached hash doubles as whatsmeow's `ExistingID` param, so an unchanged picture costs a cheap "not modified" round-trip instead of a full re-fetch + re-report.
- Wired from `onMessage` (live traffic — every inbound/outbound message) and `onHistorySync` (one check per conversation) — the history-sync path is what backfills every existing chat's avatar right after pairing.
- "No picture" / "hidden from you" answers are cached too, so they aren't hammered on every message either.

**Gateway**
- Migration `128`: `wa_chat_avatars`, keyed by JID (not the `wa_chats` UUID) — same reasoning as `wa_chat_labels`: an avatar can arrive before the chat's first message has synced.
- `POST /whatsapp/bridge/avatars` upserts; `/whatsapp/chats` `LEFT JOIN`s the avatar URL onto each chat row (1:1, unlike labels' many-to-many).
- The stored value is WhatsApp's own CDN URL — the gateway keeps the pointer, not the image bytes, the same "read-only mirror" posture as the labels sync (#243).

**Frontend**
- `ChatAvatar` renders the real photo once synced, falling back to the existing colored-initials look while missing or if the CDN URL 404s (WhatsApp's picture URLs do rotate). Used in the chat list and the conversation header.

## Testing

- Go bridge: `go build` + `go vet` clean.
- Gateway: 37 unit tests pass (7 new: avatar payload parser + ingest route — persist / unknown-account / bad-secret).
- Frontend: `tsc --noEmit` clean, vitest green (96 tests), production `next build` succeeds.
- Migration-prefix uniqueness test passes (`128` — this branch's earlier PR collided at `113`/`117`; synced onto latest `main` before adding this one).
- The live WhatsApp→bridge fetch couldn't be exercised in the sandbox (no paired number); built against whatsmeow's documented `GetProfilePictureInfo` contract, including its documented "unchanged" (`nil, nil`) response shape.

body:
## Summary
Grounded in research (Apple's Human Interface Guidelines design principles, and Anthropic's own published research on agent harnesses for app-building), plus a real, concrete bug found while investigating.

**The bug**: `ccIcon()`/`data-cc-icon` — the icon bridge injected into every app's sandboxed frame, already documented in `design.md` (shared with the chat-artifacts system) — was never actually wired up for Custom Apps. `SandboxedHtml`'s `icons` prop needs to be pre-resolved and passed in; the Workshop preview and the published run page never did that, so every Custom App calling `ccIcon('Name')` silently got nothing back.

**Fixed and extended**:
- New `extractCcIconNames(html)` in `ccBridge.ts` (regex, pure function, unit tested) — scans an app's HTML for `ccIcon('Name')` calls and `data-cc-icon="Name"` attributes. Wired into both the Workshop's preview (`edit/page.tsx`, both desktop and the phone-frame view) and the published run page (`[slug]/page.tsx`) via `buildIconMap` — the same resolver the chat-artifacts renderer already uses.
- `lucide-react` joins the T2 default vendor cache (pinned to the exact version `workbench/control_plane` itself uses — zero runtime deps of its own) and `build_t2.mjs`'s default-mode import allowlist, so T2 apps get real icon components for free, no install step. Verified end-to-end against a live build.
- `instructions.md`: a new "Icons" bullet (T1 → `ccIcon`/`data-cc-icon`, T2 → `lucide-react` directly, never emoji as UI iconography) and a new "Quality bar" section:
  - Anthropic's harness-design research found a generator asked to grade its own UI "confidently praises the work — even when... obviously mediocre." The actionable takeaway: actually look at the rendered preview before calling a round done, not just read back the code — ties directly to the desktop/phone preview toggle shipped earlier. Four judging criteria from that research: coherent, original (avoid "purple gradients over white cards" — the canonical AI-output cliché named in that research), craft, functional.
  - Apple's HIG principles (clarity, deference, hierarchy, consistency) translated into concrete rules already load-bearing elsewhere in the file: one primary action per view, hierarchy from size/weight/contrast not color alone, chrome defers to content, generous spacing, motion only with purpose.

## Test plan
- [x] `tsc`/`eslint` clean
- [x] `next build` clean
- [x] Full `vitest` suite green (101 tests, +5 new for `extractCcIconNames`)
- [x] `uv run pytest tests/unit/ -q` — 2565 passed (no backend files touched)
- [x] End-to-end verified a test T2 app importing `Save`/`Trash2` from `lucide-react` builds successfully via the default vendor-cache path

title: Default-deny authentication (closes BO-2) + hand off to multiplayer collaboration
body:
Final PR in the multi-tenant user management series (#286 → #290 → #291 → #293 → this). **Closes BO‑2**, and hands the remaining scope to the multiplayer agent collaboration workstream.

Two parts: the default-deny authentication work, and the handoff documentation.

---

# Part 1 — Default-deny authentication (BO‑2 residual #1)

## The problem

`get_current_user` never rejects — it **labels**. So every route was open unless it remembered to add a guard, and the failure mode of opt-in security is the route nobody opted in.

Two were found exactly that way:

| Route | What it did, anonymously |
|---|---|
| `GET /agent/workspace/{session_id}/history` | read an agent's **full file version history** |
| `POST /agent/workspace/{session_id}/promote` | **wrote** to the workspace |

Neither took a caller identity at all — the same IDOR family as the memory API that BO‑2's first pass closed. A scan of the assembled app found them; they weren't in anyone's list.

## The fix

`require_authenticated(public=...)` is attached **once** at `FastAPI(dependencies=[...])`, so a route added tomorrow is covered without anyone remembering anything.

It asks only *"who are you"*. `require_permission` and the feature gates still answer *"may you"* — a member with an empty permission set passes authentication and then fails authorization, which is the correct sequence and is tested as such.

`gateway.main.PUBLIC_ROUTES` is the complete anonymous-reachable set: `/health`, the three provider webhook receivers, the signed agent webhook (#293), both OAuth callbacks, the Graph notification, the Meta webhook, the four WhatsApp bridge endpoints, and the two meeting-bot callbacks. Each authenticates itself by another means or is a liveness probe. Matching is on the route **template**, so a path parameter can't spell a public path.

**Two tests keep the list honest:** a `PUBLIC_ROUTES` entry matching no live route fails (a typo is dead text; a stale entry is a hole held open), and a coverage test asserts every route in the assembled app carries the guard — 447 of 447 in prod.

**One structural exception:** Swagger/ReDoc/`openapi.json` cannot carry the guard (FastAPI mounts them with no dependency chain) and publish the entire API surface, so they're now dev-only.

## The resolver now fails closed

Its legacy `executive`/`employee` fallback existed because, before authentication was enforced, refusing everyone when the tables were missing would have been an outage with no way back in. That reason is gone — quietly granting an *approximation* of access is the access model silently not being the access model. `ACCESS_LEGACY_FALLBACK=1` is the recovery hatch. Safe because `deploy.yml` runs `apply_migrations.sh` **before** restarting the gateway.

This is the fail-open flagged in #286 and promised for removal once BO‑2 landed.

---

# Part 2 — Handoff to multiplayer agent collaboration

Multi-tenant user management is complete as Phase 1 and is **not being extended on its own track**. The remaining scope — modules/teams, session sharing, memory and transcript exposure — is the same set of primitives the multiplayer workstream needs, seen from the other direction. Building them twice would produce two group models to reconcile later.

**§10 of `org_access_control.md` is the integration contract.** It documents:

- **What is built and can be relied on**, with the file and function for each seam, so the other session doesn't re-derive it.
- **The four collisions**, each with where it bites in code:
  1. **modules/teams is unbuilt** and both workstreams need it — build once;
  2. **`chat_session.user_id` is single-owner** with no participants table (the comment still says *"future multi-tenant"*);
  3. **whose authority runs the agent** in a shared session — Phase 1 answered this implicitly for one user, and the default ("whoever typed") leaks. `EffectiveAccess.intersect()` already exists and is tested for exactly this shape;
  4. **the transcript is a second exposure boundary** — personal memory and tool output re-exposed to everyone in the room. Every Phase 1 seam assumes one viewer per run, so this is genuinely new surface.
- **What is deliberately absent**, with reasons, so absence isn't read as an oversight — including that credential scoping is *authorization, not isolation*, until BO‑7.
- **Where the design rationale lives in code**, since the docstrings carry the "why" that a spec summary flattens.

The planning index and the parent research doc now point at the handoff, so anyone arriving from either finds it rather than starting from a document whose §4 is now implemented.

---

## Verification

- 2668 unit tests pass (16 new).
- Gateway boots: 451 routes in dev, 447 guarded in prod.
- `.env.example` documents `ACCESS_LEGACY_FALLBACK` as a recovery hatch only.

## BO-2 is closed

All four residuals done across #290, #293 and this PR. What remains is **authorization depth** (now owned by multiplayer) and **true agent isolation**, which is BO‑7 and a different kind of project.

title: fix(chat): mobile UI — reachable delete button, collapse composer after send, compact bottom nav
body:
## Why

Three mobile chat UI fixes (from screenshots), all touch-affordance / layout issues.

### 1. Conversation delete button unreachable on touch
The per-conversation Trash button was `opacity-0 group-hover:opacity-100` — a pure hover-reveal, so on a touch device (no hover event) it never appeared. That's why the trash icon was nowhere to be found in the conversations drawer. Added `[@media(hover:none)]:opacity-100` so it's **always visible on touch** while staying hover-revealed on pointer devices. Since the control is now one tap away and deletion is irreversible (it wipes the thread's history), guarded `handleDeleteSession` with a confirm.

### 2. Composer grows tall and stays tall
The chat textarea auto-grows by setting `height` **imperatively** in `onInput`. Sending clears the text via React state (`setInput("")`), which doesn't fire `onInput`, so the inline height from the just-sent multi-line message is never reset — leaving a giant blank box while the agent processes. Added an effect that resets height to `"auto"` whenever `input === ""`.

### 3. Bottom nav taller than needed
The shared `MobileBottomNav` had doubled vertical padding (`<nav>` `py-1.5` + each tab `py-1.5`) and 21–22px icons. Trimmed to `py-1` and a uniform 20px icon (accent tabs keep emphasis via color + stroke weight). Reclaims ~10px app-wide.

## Verification
- `tsc --noEmit`: zero errors in the three changed files (`chat/page.tsx`, `AppShell.tsx`, `AgentChat.tsx`); the repo's other pre-existing TS errors are untouched.
- No new eslint findings.
- Presentational + a height-reset effect + a delete confirm; no API changes.

title: Artifacts: open rendered by default — side panel on desktop, sheet on mobile
body:
Opening an HTML or React artifact showed its source instead of the rendered thing. Four separate causes.

## Why it was broken

**1. The modal had a stale copy of the classifier.** `ArtifactViewerModal` is the *only* artifact viewer on mobile — the side panel is gated behind `!isMobile` — and it kept its own `classify()` in which `html`/`jsx`/`tsx` fall through to `CODE_EXTS`, so it handed them to the syntax highlighter. `DocumentPane` had learned to render those kinds; the modal never did, because the logic existed twice and drifted.

**2. The card's primary action was dead on mobile.** `ArtifactCard`'s "Open" button routes to the side panel, which doesn't exist there.

**3. React artifacts got no Open button at all.** The card's `DOC_EXTS` was `md/mdx/html/htm`, so `outputs/*.jsx` didn't qualify — which is why a `workload_dashboard.jsx` card shows only an expand icon and a download icon.

**4. The card itself wasn't clickable.** Opening an artifact meant hitting one of two 14px icons in the corner. The card — the large target with the filename on it — did nothing. The rendered view was reachable but not *discoverable*, which reads as "I open it and only see the source".

## The fix

**One classifier.** `lib/artifactKind.ts` is the single source, used by `DocumentPane`, the modal, and the card. `html`/`react` are tested **before** the code-extension set — that ordering *is* the fix, and reversing it turns every artifact back into a wall of source. Removing the duplication is the point: the drift between two copies caused this.

**The card is now the primary target.** Clicking it opens the artifact **rendered**, on the right surface:

| | Surface | Default view |
|---|---|---|
| Desktop | Side panel (resizable, beside the chat) | Rendered |
| Mobile | Full-bleed sheet | Rendered |

The user never has to know which they got. Only artifacts with a rendered view become clickable — a `.py` or `.zip` keeps icon-only actions rather than gaining a click that would just show source. Keyboard reachable: `role="button"`, `tabIndex`, Enter/Space, focus ring. Buttons inside `stopPropagation`, so Download still downloads.

**Both surfaces render first and switch to editing.** The side panel has Edit ⇄ Preview; the modal opens rendered with a **Preview / Code** toggle (source is otherwise unreachable with no side panel) plus **Edit** with a live preview, returning to rendered on save.

## A deliberate non-simplification

`DocumentPane` has no PDF or DOCX renderer. Rather than have the shared classifier lie about the file type to suit one viewer, it reports `pdf`/`docx` honestly and the pane collapses those into its existing "download it" state. A viewer may decline to handle a kind; what a file *is* shouldn't depend on which viewer opened it.

## Verification

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| Python unit tests | 2578 passed, 8 skipped |
| vitest | 110 passed (9 new) |
| `tsc --noEmit` | clean |
| eslint | clean (2 pre-existing warnings unchanged) |
| `next build` | passes |

Tests pin the exact regression: `.html` → `html` not `code`, `outputs/*.jsx` → `react`, and the counterpart that `src/components/Foo.tsx` stays `code`, so an agent reading its own source never has the viewer build and run it. Plus pdf/docx precedence, case-insensitivity, and `outputs/` matching.

## Note

Verified by types, tests and build — not on a real device, which needs an authenticated session with an artifact in it. The classification and routing logic is unit-tested; what remains unverified is layout only (the full-bleed container giving the iframe its height on a small viewport). Worth a look on a phone.

title: Resolve post-merge collisions with concurrent WhatsApp avatar work
body:
Follow-up to the access-control series (#286, #290, #291, #293, #296). Merging it onto `main` surfaced two collisions with WhatsApp avatar work that landed independently. **Both were caught by tests, not by review.**

## 1. Migration number collision

`128_whatsapp_avatars.sql` reached `main` while `128_org_access_control.sql` was in flight. `test_migration_prefixes` asserts numeric prefixes are unique, and failed.

Renumbered **the access-control pair**, not the avatars migration, since that one reached `main` first: `128 → 130`, `129 → 131`.

**Both had to move**, not just the colliding one. `131` seeds roles that `130` creates, and `apply_migrations.sh` applies in lexical order — leaving the second at `129` would have run it *before* its dependency, silently seeding nothing.

Every reference updated: the SQL headers, the `migration:128` `assigned_by` marker, four Python modules, two frontend modules, four `AGENTS.md` files.

## 2. `/whatsapp/bridge/avatars` would have broken

The new bridge endpoint carries no `UserContext` — correctly, since the Go bridge authenticates with `X-Bridge-Secret` via `bridge_secret_ok`. But both the feature gate (#290) and the app-wide default-deny guard (#296) would have **401'd it**.

That wouldn't have restricted access. It would have **silently stopped avatar sync**, with no error attached to it — exactly the machine-entrypoint failure mode the enforcement test was written for. It fired on the first real collision.

Added to the whatsapp router's exempt list, to `gateway.main.PUBLIC_ROUTES`, and to the enforcement test's expected set.

## Verification

- 2710 unit tests pass.
- The renumbered migrations applied in lexical order against a fresh Postgres 16 — `130 → 131` dependency satisfied, role backfill correct (`admin,owner` and `member` as expected).

title: End a live meeting from the console
body:
Reported: no way to stop a notetaker mid-meeting from the app. Confirmed, and it's specific.

## The gap

The only stop control for a bot was a small square icon inside the "notetakers in meetings" strip on the library page — not somewhere anyone looks mid-call. The **live console**, which is where you actually are while a meeting runs, had none at all.

In-app recording was already fine: `RecordingDock` is mounted globally in `AppShell` and carries stop/pause everywhere. This gap was specific to bot sessions.

## The fix

The console header now ends the session, branching on source because the two stop differently:

- **Bot** → `stopBot()`, which has the provider leave the call
- **Browser** → the recording is owned by the tab that started it. Same tab: stop it directly. A different tab or device: say so plainly rather than pretending the button worked

Confirmed before acting, because it isn't undoable — the bot leaves the call and can't be sent back into the same session. The confirm also states that audio captured so far still gets transcribed, so "stop" doesn't read as "throw away".

## Testing

2572 backend tests, 96 frontend tests, `tsc` and `next build` clean.

title: Fix icons, logos and images in full-page artifacts
body:
Logos and icons silently vanished from full-page artifacts. Four separate causes, all fixed here.

### 1. Full-page frames received no icon map at all

Inline generative-UI cards declare their icons via `props.icons`, but a full-page artifact is just a file with nowhere to declare anything — so `DocumentPane` and `ArtifactViewerModal` passed no `icons` prop. `ccIcon()` returned an empty string and every `[data-cc-icon]` placeholder stayed empty.

Both viewers now derive the map from the source itself via `iconsUsedIn()`, which recognises all three spellings — the `Icon` component's `name` prop, a raw `data-cc-icon` attribute, and a `ccIcon()` call in script. Only referenced icons are injected, so the `srcDoc` stays small.

### 2. The kit had no `Icon` component

A React artifact had no supported way to ask for an icon. Added an `Icon` component (`name`, `size`) to `@cc/ui`.

### 3. Remote image URLs fail silently and nothing said so

The sandbox CSP is `img-src data:`, so every CDN logo, favicon service and remote image tag is blocked with no visible error. The linter only ran on `.html`, so a React artifact with a remote logo got no warning whatsoever.

Added `lint_artifact_source()` for `.jsx`/`.tsx`, plus a `design.md` section spelling out what actually works: the `Icon` component, `data:` URIs, and the kit's own blocks.

### 4. Two render defects from the same reports

- `cc-badge` was scoped to `.cc-phase`. Used anywhere else it either came out unstyled or, as a bare grid child, stretched to full row height — a solid block of primary colour instead of a chip. It is now a standalone chip that holds its size in any grid or flex parent.
- A callout's `cc-tag` stretched the same way.
- A stat's unit jammed against the number with no gap, and inherited `line-height: 1` so a wordy unit ("risk-adjusted", "near-close") collided with the digits above.

### Note on module layout

`iconsUsedIn` lives in its own `iconRefs` module: it is pure string scanning, and keeping it free of the `react-dom/server` import lets it be tested under the node-environment vitest config.

### Known limitation

`iconsUsedIn` only matches literal names — resolution happens on the parent before the frame runs, so an icon name computed at runtime still renders empty. Documented in the module and covered by a test.

### Verification

Rebased onto latest `main` and re-run:

- vitest: **115 passed** (11 files)
- `tsc --noEmit`: clean
- `next build`: compiled successfully
- ruff blocking gate (`F821,F601,F602,F502,F7,B006`): clean
- pytest: **2760 passed, 8 skipped**

Two failures I did **not** fix, both confirmed pre-existing and unrelated: one eslint `set-state-in-effect` error in `ArtifactViewerModal` (present verbatim at the base commit), and an integration test that fails with `httpx.ConnectError` because no backend is running in this environment.

title: feat(email): recipient autocomplete — contact suggestions in To/Cc/Bcc
body:
## Summary

Typing an address in any composer now offers autofill from the people the mailbox already knows.

### Backend — `GET /email/contacts/suggest`
- Candidates union'd from three sources, strongest first: addresses the user has **sent** mail to (To+Cc of the Sent folder), the learned `email_contacts` directory (names parsed from signatures), and the `email_senders` rollup (everyone who has mailed the user).
- Matched case-insensitively on address OR display name; prefix hits rank above substring hits, then by occurrence count and recency. Dedup'd by address; the user's own connected addresses are excluded.
- Scoped to the caller's accounts (optionally one). Best-effort: `[]` on any failure (e.g. the contacts migration not applied) — a typeahead must never error the composer.

### Frontend — `RecipientInput`
Drop-in replacement for the plain comma-separated inputs (same `value`/`onChange` contract):
- Suggests for the **token at the caret**, so editing mid-list completes that address only; already-entered addresses are never re-offered.
- Debounced (200ms, min 2 chars), stale responses discarded; dropdown shows name + address; ↑/↓ + Enter/Tab/Esc keyboard support; mousedown selection so blur can't eat the click. Picking inserts the bare address plus a trailing `, ` ready for the next recipient.
- Wired into all eight recipient fields: inline reply To/Cc/Bcc (EmailDetail), Drafts editor To/Cc/Bcc (ConversationView), pop-out composer To/Cc (ComposePanel).

## Testing

- Backend: **925 email tests passed**, incl. new tests for the suggest endpoint's sources/ranking/self-exclusion and its best-effort failure mode.
- Frontend: `tsc --noEmit` clean, `next build` clean, vitest **115/115**, zero new eslint issues (RecipientInput lints clean).

title: Workflows app — visual automation builder over the agent fleet
body:
Adds **Workflows** — a visual builder that runs deterministic automations over the existing agent fleet, integrations, and code modules. Spec: `ai-company-brain/specs/workflows_app.md` · RFC: `docs/workflow-editor/README.md`.

Ten commits of Workflows work (82 files) on top of earlier already-reviewed branch history; `main` is an ancestor, so this fast-forwards cleanly.

## What it is

A workflow is **data, not code** — a React-Flow graph persisted verbatim, compiled at publish time into an immutable version that runs on **MAF `WorkflowBuilder`**. There is no second runtime: constraint #6 is strengthened, not weakened. Editing never breaks a live automation, because runs execute versions, never the draft.

Every node type resolves through the platform's own registries at run time, so the builder can never offer a capability the platform doesn't actually have, and node config never holds a secret:

| Need | The node | Resolved by |
|---|---|---|
| Call an LLM | agent | live agent registry → `orchestrator.executor.run_agent` (MAF batch path) |
| Touch an external system | tool | `acb_skills` integration registry; write-class dispatches through the Action Broker |
| Custom logic | module | Module Studio — AST-validated, import-free pure transforms |
| Branch / gate / delay | condition, set, approval, wait | engine |

## Shipped features

- **F1/F2** gallery + three-pane editor (palette · canvas · inspector) with run console; duplicate, search, delete
- **F3/F4** served node catalog (never hard-coded) and `{{…}}` references with design-time validation
- **F5/F9** Test runs with live per-node status over SSE; run history, and clicking a past run replays its recorded results onto the canvas
- **F6** publish → immutable versions; rollback republishes an old version as a new one, never mutating history
- **F7 Module Studio** — describe a transform in plain English, get a validated typed Python module, test it against sample data, save it to the org library
- **F8/F10** all five trigger kinds: manual, api, webhook (per-workflow tokened URL + optional HMAC), schedule (cron scanner with CAS claims), event (platform event bindings)
- **F11** approval node — pauses the run into the **existing** `/approvals` inbox via the Action Broker; resume replays completed nodes from stored outputs, so no side effect fires twice
- **F13** workflows callable by any agent as tools
- **F14 Workflow Copilot** — describe a change in the editor, get the updated graph; modules it needs that don't exist are generated, validated, and saved automatically
- **F15** keyword capability search powering both the palette and the copilot (semantic ranking is deliberately deferred to BO‑22, platform-wide)
- **wait node** — ≤60s sleeps inline; longer pauses durably with a deadline and the scheduler resumes it, so "wait 2 days, then follow up" survives a restart

## Safety

- **Publish authority** (`workflows:publish`, migration 133) on publish/rollback/disable/enable — the acts that arm triggers to run unattended. Drafting and Test runs stay open to any member with the feature.
- **Publish gate** blocks unresolved `{{refs}}`, secret-shaped strings, and write-class nodes with no approval ancestor.
- **Auto-disable** after 5 consecutive failed runs from unattended triggers, with the reason recorded and a one-click re-enable (spec R2).
- Startup sweep marks runs orphaned by a restart as failed rather than leaving them "running" forever.

## Testing

`uv run pytest tests/unit evals/trajectories` → **2,985 passed**, no Docker required. Engine semantics are pinned by a CI-blocking golden trajectory eval (`evals/trajectories/test_workflow_engine_trajectory.py`), and `skill-eval.yml` re-runs it on any `routes/workflows/**` change. Frontend typecheck and lint clean.

## Before this runs

Apply migrations **132** (tables + feature slug), **133** (publish capability), **134** (automation health), then regenerate `infra/postgres/schema.generated.sql` — none could be applied from the build container.

Known limits, all documented in the spec rather than hidden: runs are supervised asyncio tasks in the gateway process (durable queueing is BO‑20), the module runtime is restricted-execution and **not** a sandbox for untrusted code (BO‑7), and loops / parallel fan-out are Slice 3.

title: Stream ASR only while something is reading it
body:
Streaming speech-to-text is billed per minute and ran for the whole meeting regardless of whether anything consumed it. With the copilot off, nothing did — the archival recording still goes through the batch pipeline afterwards and produces the same transcript at batch prices. So a copilot-less meeting was paying a live rate for a feature nobody was reading.

## Three modes, not a boolean

"Follow the copilot" is the right default but not the only sensible answer:

| Mode | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| `auto` *(default)* | Stream only while the copilot is on — the saving |
| `always` | Stream regardless, for live captions without an agent |
| `never` | Never stream; record and transcribe afterwards only |

## How it's enforced

The gateway owns the decision (`live_wanted`), and both producers ask it rather than each deciding for itself:

- **Browser recorder** passes its meeting to the token endpoint and gets a `409` when nothing is listening. The existing `onUnavailable` path already degrades to record-only, so this needed no new failure handling.
- **Meeting-bot worker** polls a cheap `/live/wanted`, derived from the per-meeting callback URL it already receives — so no new field in the join contract.

## Both edges, not just the start

Turning the copilot **on** mid-meeting begins streaming within the re-check interval; turning it **off** closes the socket and stops the meter. A start-only check would leave a four-hour call streaming for an agent that was switched off in minute three — which is most of the cost this is meant to avoid.

## Failure directions, chosen deliberately

- **Unreachable gateway → keep streaming.** Losing captions on a real meeting is worse than one meeting's spend, and both sides fail open consistently.
- **Unrecognised mode → fall back to `auto`, not `always`.** Of the two ways to be wrong, silently spending money is the worse one.

## The tradeoff, stated rather than buried

In `auto`, a copilot-less meeting gets no live captions **and no live agenda coverage** — both are fed by the transcript bus. That's a direct consequence and it's in the settings copy, not just the commit message. `always` buys them back.

## Testing

title: Workflow triggers that actually fire — schedule bootstrap, timezones, honest ticks, real webhook URLs
body:
An audit of "do schedules survive a restart?" found something worse than a durability gap: **the schedule trigger did not work at all.** This fixes that and three related defects, all on the path a first real automation takes.

## The bootstrap trap (the big one)

`compute_due_fire()` only looks forward. With `last_fired_at IS NULL` it asked *"is the NEXT tick already in the past?"* — false at every instant except an exact tick boundary. So a new schedule produced no tick, never got a `last_fired_at`, and therefore produced no tick. Forever.

Simulated over a week of 30-second scans:

```
before:  new daily 09:00 schedule -> 0 runs in 7 days
after:   same schedule            -> 7 runs   (weekdays-only correctly gives 5)
```

The scanner now **arms** an unseen trigger (`_claim_baseline`, guarded on `last_fired_at IS NULL`) instead of firing it — a cron says *when*, not *how far back to catch up*.

Second half of the same bug: `update_workflow` rewrites trigger rows wholesale, so **every canvas save reset `last_fired_at` to NULL**, dropping the already-fired-this-tick guarantee and parking the schedule back in the dead state. Fire state now carries across for unchanged schedules (`_trigger_identity` = kind + cron@timezone); editing the cron or zone deliberately re-arms, so moving a 9am job to 10am can't fire a surprise catch-up.

## Timezones

Cron was UTC-only, so "weekdays 9am" meant 9am in London and 2:30pm in Bangalore — and drifted an hour twice a year anywhere with DST. Schedules now carry an IANA zone (`config.timezone`, default UTC) validated at save time alongside the expression: an unknown zone is a 422 the maker can act on, not a schedule that silently never runs. The zone is a wall clock, so 9am stays 9am across a DST change.

## No silently dropped ticks

The CAS claim commits *before* `start_run`, so a tick refused afterwards — concurrency cap reached, published version missing — was consumed with only a log line, leaving an unexplained gap in run history. Every path out of a claimed tick now writes a terminal run row with the reason. Recorded as `cancelled`, not `failed`: the workflow didn't break, the platform declined to start it, and being busy must never feed the auto-disable policy.

## Webhook URLs that the sender can actually call

The editor built the URL from `window.location` — the control plane, whose `/api` proxy does `JSON.stringify(await req.json())`. That changes the bytes, so an HMAC the sender computed **can never verify**, and non-JSON bodies (plenty of providers post form-encoded) arrived as `{}`. The UI was offering a secret field that was guaranteed to 401.

The gateway now names its own public URL (`PUBLIC_API_BASE_URL` → `hook_url`/`hook_path`), and shows the path with an explanation when that origin is unset rather than inventing one that 404s in production. A raw-passthrough Next route is the safety net for a control-plane URL someone already copied: byte-exact body, caller's headers, no internal bearer attached — the token in the path is the whole credential.

## Durability, now documented

Spec §3.3a is a full matrix of what survives what (restart while idle / mid-run / mid-wait / mid-approval, multi-worker CAS, downtime catch-up, clock skew). Short version: **the schedule is a database fact and the scanner is a stateless reader of it** — there is no OS cron and no scheduler daemon; APScheduler is a parser only.

## Testing

23 new tests: cron maths pinned across timezones and a DST boundary, arming and firing as separate tests, both dropped-tick paths asserting the recorded reason, the CAS pinned so a losing worker starts nothing, and save-preservation pinned in both directions. Full suite **3,062 passed**; frontend typecheck and lint clean.

## Deploy note

Set `PUBLIC_API_BASE_URL` on the gateway (e.g. `https://api.commandcenter.fracktal.in`) or the editor will show the hook path without an origin. Migrations 132–134 still need applying.

title: Typed tool arguments + a golden workflow fixture corpus
body:
Spends two references we had already imported but never used, and adds the test layer that keeps them honest.

## The gap

The tool registry declared `args_schema` per action. The catalog served it. The inspector rendered a raw JSON textarea and nothing validated the contents — so a ClickUp node with no `list_id` published happily and failed only when a real run reached the API.

## `args_schema` is now load-bearing

One parser (`engine/tool_args.py` — a `type[?][|description]` mini-language over a closed type set), three consumers:

- **Editor** — a typed field per argument with help text and required markers, plus a JSON escape hatch for what a form can't express. The gateway serves the **parsed** form, so the browser never re-implements the grammar and the two can't disagree about what's required.
- **Publish** — refuses a tool node with a missing, unknown, or mistyped argument (`tool_args`), reporting *every* problem at once so one attempt yields the whole fix list.
- **Runtime** — `execute_tool` re-checks before dispatch, because a draft Test run, a copilot-authored graph, and a version published before an argument existed can all reach a handler publish never saw. For a broker-gated write, that check is what stops a proposal being filed for a write that cannot succeed.

`{{refs}}` satisfy required checks and skip type checks on both sides — they resolve at run time, and demanding literals would make the state bus useless for the fields that need it most. Type checking only reports container-vs-scalar category errors: crying wolf about a number in a string field trains makers to ignore the messages that matter. An unknown type name degrades to `string` rather than raising — one typo must not take the palette down for every other tool.

## Two test layers, both mutation-verified

**Contract test (35).** Holds each declaration to its handler by AST-scanning for `args.get("x")` / `args["x"]`. The drift it hunts is specific: a handler grows an input the schema never declares, so the editor never offers the field and publish never demands it. The detector is itself tested against a known-drifting handler, and `_broker_write`'s dynamic `target_field` gets an explicit test since static scanning can't see it.

**Fixture corpus (n8n's pattern).** Whole workflows as JSON paired with an expected outcome, one generic runner — adding coverage is adding a file. Seeded with the spec's reference workflow through both condition branches, plus three gate fixtures that must *fail* to publish.

Fixtures assert **which seams were crossed**, not just the status — a workflow reporting "succeeded" while silently never calling the integration is exactly what a shallower assertion misses. Tool schemas and destructive actions come from the **real** registry, so fixtures break when the shipped catalog changes.

Proven able to fail before being trusted:

| Mutation | Result |
|---|---|
| State bus stops resolving `{{vars.list_id}}` | `lead_triage_high_priority` fails |
| Approval no longer gates the run | `lead_triage_high_priority` fails |
| Publish argument check deleted | `gate_missing_tool_argument` fails |

The pre-existing golden trajectory now compiles against the real schemas too — its ClickUp node had been missing `list_id`, which is precisely the drift this catches.

## Testing

**3,103 passed** (unit + trajectories), frontend typecheck and lint clean.

## Docs

n8n added to the RFC reference list with what was taken from it (typed node parameters; golden workflow fixtures), spec F3a, `evals/README.md`, gateway `AGENTS.md`.

title: Multiplayer rooms, memory compartments, and the BFF identity boundary
body:
Multi-person chat rooms, per-room memory clearance, and a fix for a privilege-escalation pattern that had been fixed twice locally and kept coming back.

Specs: `docs/multiplayer/README.md`, `docs/multiplayer/memory-clearance.md`, `docs/multiplayer/bff-identity.md`, `ai-company-brain/specs/groups_sessions_authority.md`

## What's in it

**Rooms.** A room is a `chat_session` row plus participants — no new object, because every transport primitive is already thread-keyed. Membership replaces ownership everywhere (`gateway/rooms.py`, `SESSION_VISIBLE_SQL`, `resolve_room_access`), which is the same answer when a session has one participant. Messages carry authorship set-once, so three racing writers cannot rename an author and a human turn is always attributed to the authenticated caller. A shared run acts at the **intersection** of every participant's access, viewers included, and the room header reports the resulting capability cap — what the room cannot reach and who is the reason — because the intersection rule's failure mode is mystery.

**Memory compartments.** A run reads at the clearance of its least-cleared viewer. In a room, nobody's private compartment loads — not the owner's, not the typer's — while `prefs:` travels so the agent still writes the way you like. The boundary is that excluded scope keys are never passed to `search()`, so there is no retrieval to leak, rather than a retrieval we hope the model ignores. The session-memory cache key carries a clearance fingerprint; without it a thread cached while solo would keep serving the owner's private block for the rest of the TTL after someone was invited in.

**The identity boundary.** `acb_auth/deps.py` §1b reads a bearer-matched call with no identity headers as the platform acting as itself and grants `SERVICE_ACCESS` — `*`. The BFF holds that token, and ~70 route files each carried a copy of `if (session?.user?.email) h["X-User-Email"] = …; return h` — so no session did not degrade to anonymous, it escalated past every `require_permission`. 74 of 88 gateway-forwarding routes could do it; 38 sat under a `proxy.ts` public prefix and needed no session at all, including agent registration, code-mutation approval and the integration key inventory.

`lib/gateway.ts` is now the only module that reads `GATEWAY_INTERNAL_TOKEN`. `gatewayHeaders()` throws without a member; `serviceHeaders(reason)` is the only bearer-only path and takes a written reason. All 86 route files migrated — roughly 960 net lines of duplicated identity logic removed. The same omission existed in three Python agent tool clients and is fixed there too.

## Behaviour changes to know about

- **Routes now run as the actual member**, so gates that were being satisfied by `SERVICE_ACCESS` start enforcing. Writes to `/settings/llm/*` need `feature:models`; agent registration needs `agents:manage`. Migration 130 backfills `executive` → `admin`, whose bundle holds both, so admins are unaffected; the model picker's reads are ungated so members keep a working picker.
- **`proxy.ts`** no longer pretends to be the authorization boundary. Signed-out page navigations redirect; signed-out API calls get a 401 instead of a redirect to an HTML sign-in page.
- **Agent tool clients raise** when no acting user can be resolved, rather than calling the gateway as the platform. Every surface they reach is per-person, so a run with nobody attributed has nothing to do rather than everything — but a scheduled sweep that ran without `ACB_AGENT_USER_EMAIL` will now fail instead of silently working.
- **Migrations 136–139** are new and need applying on deploy.

## Verification

Backend 3214 passing, frontend 132, 0 type errors, per-file ruff parity against main. The one backend failure is the pre-existing `test_runs_degrades_to_empty_without_db`, which asserts no database and so fails whenever Postgres is up.

Honest gaps, stated because they matter for a change this size:

- **`next build` has never run.** `@tiptap/*` and `@xyflow/react` are declared in `package.json` but absent from the sandbox's `node_modules`, both pre-existing. `tsc` and `eslint` are clean, but CI is the first real compile.
- **Verification of the identity hole was per-link, not end-to-end.** The proxy list, the missing `auth()` calls, and the gateway's response to a bearer-only request were each confirmed directly; no full Next-plus-gateway exploit was run.
- **The access tables are now load-bearing in a way they weren't.** `resolve_access` fails closed when they're absent. Previously that barely mattered for these routes because they forwarded as the service principal; now, if the production database lacks the org role rows migration 130 seeds, members resolve to no access. Worth confirming against the live database before or right after deploy.

Two adjacent findings recorded in `bff-identity.md` §6 rather than fixed here: `scripts/setup_secrets.sh` seeds `GATEWAY_INTERNAL_TOKEN=${LITELLM_KEY}`, so the two secrets `deps.py` calls deliberately distinct start life as one value; and `require_internal_auth` fails open when no token is configured, which means this invariant rests on the token actually being set.

title: Fix the deploy build: gateway headers must be per-request, not per-process
body:
Fixes the deploy failure:

```
Error [NoIdentityError]: No signed-in member to act as
Error: Failed to collect page data for /api/settings/llm/enabled-models
```

## Cause

Two routes had this at **module scope**:

```ts
const HEADERS = await gatewayHeaders({ "Content-Type": "application/json" });
```

The originals were a static object literal in that position. The migration in #309 rewrote the literal in place, which turned a constant into a top-level `await`.

**Failing the build was the lucky outcome.** Module scope runs once per *process*, at import. Had a session been resolvable there, `HEADERS` would have named whichever member imported first, and every later request would have been served as them — a cross-user identity leak from a line that reads like a constant. The headers are now built inside each handler, where the acting member actually is.

## Also

Eight routes marked `force-dynamic`. A handler that resolves the signed-in member can never be statically evaluated; without the directive, page-data collection runs it with no request and no session. Six were gateway-forwarding; `chat/suggestions` and `sessions/compact` call LiteLLM rather than the gateway but still resolve an identity, so they qualify for the same reason.

## Two new invariants

The existing sweep had already seen this and could not say so — it printed `?()` for these two files, unable to name the enclosing function because there wasn't one. That was the signal, unread. Now it fails explicitly on:

- a module-scope `await gatewayHeaders(…)` / `headersActingAs(…)`
- a route that resolves an identity without being `force-dynamic`

Verified by reintroducing the pattern and watching the test fire, rather than trusting that it would.

## Verification

`next build` now runs locally: `npm ci` installs `@tiptap/*` and `@xyflow/react`, which were declared in `package.json` but absent from the sandbox — that gap is what let both this and the previous failure through. Compiled successfully (exit 0), 0 type errors, 0 lint errors, frontend 134 passing.

title: fix(email): Email Cleaner bulk archive/delete — correctness, provider verification, and archived mail leaving the list
body:
## Summary

Reported: archiving a set of senders in the Email Cleaner left the rows sitting there, so the action looked like it had done nothing. Investigating turned up two genuine defects plus the scope question.

### 1. Archive was un-deleting trashed mail (bug)
A sender-wide "Archive all" carries no folder filter, so the set-based UPDATE swept that sender's **trashed and junked** mail back out into the archive — silently un-deleting mail the user had already thrown away. Archiving is now scoped to non-disposed mail; trashing keeps its full reach (archived mail is still live mail you may want to bin).

### 2. `affected` over-reported (bug)
Rows already in the target state were matched and returned, so "Archive all" on an already-archived sender claimed *"Archived 320 emails"* having moved none — and re-pushed 320 no-op calls at the provider. Every action now excludes rows it would not change; a 0 result says so plainly instead of reading as a broken button.

### 3. Archived mail now leaves the cleaner (scope change)
`/email/senders` excludes archived mail by default, alongside the trash/junk/drafts it already excluded — so archiving a sender clears its row off the list.

- `include_archived=true` restores the whole-mailbox view, surfaced as an **"Include archived"** toggle. It exists for the one case that needs it: the preset Marketing / Cold Email rules label AND archive in the same pass, so those chips only fill in with archived mail counted.
- Senders carrying a saved disposition (unsubscribed / auto-archived / approved) stay listed in either mode — their mail is archived by definition, and hiding them would empty the Unsubscribed and Auto-archive tabs, leaving the user unable to review or undo their own decisions.
- The optimistic update drops archived rows to match, and the notice reports what actually changed (including per-sender failures, which the bulk path used to swallow silently).

### 4. Provider-side archive verified and made reliable
Read both providers: **Gmail** archives by removing the `INBOX` label via `batchModify` (with a per-message fallback), **Outlook** moves to the well-known archive folder and re-keys the message id. Both are correct — the gap was purely in failure handling:

- `bulk_apply` (base + Gmail) takes an optional `failed_out` list. Failures were logged per message and otherwise discarded, so a run where every call 429'd looked identical to a clean one.
- The reconciler retries what failed (3 attempts, 2s/8s backoff) — this covers the dominant real cause, Gmail 429 / Graph 503 under a large sweep.
- What still will not apply has its **local folder reverted**. The mirror said `archive` while the provider had the mail in the inbox, and the next sync (provider is authoritative for `folder`) pulled it back minutes later — the "I archived it and it came back" symptom. The mirror now matches the mailbox.
- Outcomes are logged: `email.bulk_reconcile_ok` / `_incomplete` (with failed/total) / `_unauthed`, so a live failure is diagnosable.

## Testing

- Backend: **949 email tests passed** — new coverage for the bin guard, delete's reach, changed-rows-only counting, default scope excluding archived while keeping disposition-holders, `include_archived` restoring it, failed-id reporting, retry-then-revert, and a clean run leaving folders untouched.
- Frontend: `tsc --noEmit` clean, `next build` clean, vitest **134/134**, no new eslint issues.

title: docs: qm prior-art — steer before floor control, skills index, no ambient room credentials
body:
Reads [`yc-software/qm`](https://github.com/yc-software/qm) (a multiplayer agent harness, released 2026-07-29, MIT) at commit `7f2c916` and lands the findings in our corpus. **Docs only — no code, no schema, no behaviour change.**

## Why it's worth a doc

qm is the closest prior art to our multiplayer work that exists, and it independently reproduced our most contested design decision. `memory-clearance.md` §3.3 says *"a run reads at the clearance of its least-cleared viewer"*; `groups_sessions_authority.md` §3 says the permissions twin. qm reached the same rule with no contact with this design and applied it to **three** resources — transcript replay, shared file handles, and **network egress** (allowed hosts = intersection across the audience, denied = union), all failing closed on an empty audience.

That is worth recording for two reasons: the rule is not an over-engineering of ours, and egress is a third enforcement point we don't use.

## The three findings that change what our docs say

| | Finding | Lands on |
|---|---|---|
| **QM-1** | **Steer before floor control.** qm ships rooms with *no baton at all* — a second person's turn folds into the live run as a mid-turn steer, the second surface stands down so the reply isn't posted twice, and steer signals are durable. This inverts README §8's Phase 2 ordering. §5.2's supersede fix survives regardless. | WS-10 |
| **QM-2** | **Skills index, bodies on demand.** One line per skill in the prompt + lazy body materialization + connector gating + index inside the cache-stable prefix. `skills_scope_out.md` §5 already named "progressive disclosure" as the core-floor diet without a reference implementation; this is one. Attacks the ≈5.4k addendum half — the ≈10.3k schema half still needs its own answer. | WS-23 |
| **QM-3** | **No ambient credentials in a shared room.** Supersedes §6.4's single `acting_identity` *in direction*: nothing ambient, every credential needs a grant bound to that room, with a consent protocol whose load-bearing rule is *"only the owner's own reply is approval — a relayed 'they said it's fine' is not."* | WS-10 Ph3, WS-2, WS-1 |

Plus QM-5 (tenure windows should narrow the **model's** replay, not only a viewer's) and QM-7 (environment attachment as a second answer to `agent-kinds.md` §9 Q1).

## Where we're ahead, recorded so we don't regress

`subject:` compartments express a case qm structurally cannot — the CEO's restricted Falcon and collaborative Acme facts share one notebook, so its only protection is to forget both in a channel. That is exactly the `context_policy='room'` failure `memory-clearance.md` §1 rejects. Also ours: semantic partition inside the query (theirs is a 300-bullet flat file injected wholesale), the per-viewer private hint, the share-mid-conversation moment, several agents per room, and clearance-tagged replay — where their own `SECURITY.md` concedes the gap on the same mechanism.

## Checked, not assumed

qm refuses to label a compacted summary that spans two personal scopes, since a summarizer is otherwise a laundering path. **We don't have that exposure**: `acb_llm/context.py::fit_messages_to_context` truncates, it never summarizes. Noted in `memory-clearance.md` §7 as a guardrail for *if* WS-9 adds summarizing compaction — not as a live gap.

## Corpus discipline

Per WS-0, the new spec is registered in the single-owner registry as **reference-only — it owns no work item and no status**, so it can't become a competing source of truth. The specs it links stay authoritative. Age caveat is stated in the doc header: qm is three days old, and its own `SECURITY.md` says it is "not a hardened public or multi-tenant service boundary" — same posture as us. Nothing here reads as "they solved it in production."

Also carries a "what not to copy" section: their skill approval flow is nominal (every call site auto-reviews under a `system:*` pseudo-reviewer; only org promotion is a real gate), `trustTier` on skill packs is stored and never read, and their security postures are mutually exclusive by construction (`strict` turns screening *off*).

## Node cards

- **Summary** is derived from the node's own config — the agent's actual instruction, the tool's catalog description, the wait duration, the assignment count.
- **Detail chip** shows what the block is bound to: `zoho.create_lead`, `{{triage.intent}} equals lead`, `email-assistant`.
- **Badges** surface flags worth seeing unselected — a destructive tool reads `write`, an approval reads `pauses run`, a long wait reads `parks the run`.
- **Footer** carries live run state, the last run's duration, and the node id you write `{{refs}}` against.
- Unconfigured nodes say so ("no agent selected yet") rather than rendering blank — the same signal the validator gives at publish.

`describeNode()` replaces `summarize()`: every node type answers summary/detail/badges from its config plus the catalog.

## Edges

New custom `ccEdge`:

- A condition's branch is **labelled yes/no and coloured** (solid green / dashed muted) instead of inferred from geometry — the `sourceHandle` *is* the routing key.
- The wire a run is flowing through **lights up** during a Test run, so the path is followable without reading the console.
- **`+` on any wire** arms an inline insert: the next block picked is spliced between the two ends and rewired (RFC §5.3.1, previously unbuilt).

## Around them

- Topbar **trigger chip** now says what fires the workflow (`webhook · schedule · 0 9 * * 1-5`) instead of a bare count.
- **Palette** rows carry the same icon plates the canvas will, so a block is recognisable before and after it is dropped; group headers pick up their category hue.
- **Inspector** header mirrors the card it configures (same plate, same kind eyebrow), and the reference chips became an "Available data" section.
- A **describe-to-generate bar** sits on the canvas (RFC §5.4) and hands off to the Copilot pane, so graphs are still applied, undone and explained in one place.

The mockup's own slate/azure palette and light/dark tokens were deliberately **not** copied — the editor uses the CommandCenter design system, which was the mockup's stated goal ("reads like CommandCenter"). The category hues already matched.

title: feat(email): multi-account audit — the chat assistant is now configured per account, not just scoped to one
body:
## Audit result

Checked the multi-account plumbing end to end. **The data and automation layers were already correct**; there was one real gap, in the assistant.

### Verified per-account (no change needed)
- **Schema** — every email table is keyed by `account_id` and cascades from `email_accounts`: rules + actions, executed rules, assistant settings, knowledge, learned patterns, rule patterns, rule guidance, thread status, AI drafts, senders, newsletters, contacts, embeddings.
- **Rules engine** — rules are loaded `WHERE account_id = :aid` and evaluated per account, so each mailbox genuinely has its own rules engine. Same for the cleaner's label projection and the auto-categorize sweep.
- **Drafting** — already resolves About / signature / models (rule, draft, compose, chat) / voice profile / learned patterns / reply memories by `account_id`, with a per-account Mem0 scope (`email_memory_scope`).

### The gap
The **chat assistant knew *which* account to act on but nothing about *how* that mailbox should be handled.** The persona carried the account list, the active `account_id` and the open email — never the account's About, standing instructions, or writing style. So the same assistant conversed identically on a work mailbox and a personal one, and only its tool calls differed. Drafts were already per-account (the server loads settings by `account_id`), which made the inconsistency easy to miss.

- `buildEmailAssistantPersona` now takes the active account's settings and emits them as a scoped block, stating they apply to the **ACTIVE account only** so the model doesn't carry them across a switch. Standing instructions are marked binding; the auto-derived learned style is marked advisory — matching the precedence the drafter already uses.
- Both entry points feed it: the email app (which already fetched these settings for the chat model and discarded the rest) and the chat app, which now also passes the resolved account id.
- `/assistant/settings` returns `learned_writing_style` so the chat can match the voice the drafter already writes in.

### Left as-is deliberately
The chat agent's `remember()` namespace stays user-global. That ContextVar doubles as the agent's gateway-auth identity, so an account suffix would break every tool call — the per-account scope lives on the gateway side (`email_memory_scope`), where drafting uses it. Flagging it as a known, documented trade-off rather than changing it silently.

## Testing

- Backend: **952 email tests passed**.
- Frontend: new `emailAssistantPersona.test.ts` (7 cases) — the persona names the active account, carries its configuration, marks instructions binding and learned style advisory, swaps cleanly when the account changes, and degrades to account-awareness when settings haven't loaded or are blank. `tsc --noEmit` clean, `next build` clean, vitest **141/141**, no new eslint issues.

## Summary

A chat thread is keyed by *agent*, not by account, so one conversation can span mailboxes. The active account was inherited silently from whatever the inbox happened to be showing — switching it swapped the assistant's per-account instructions mid-thread with nothing in the transcript to say so. title: feat(whatsapp): place and answer WhatsApp calls from CommandCenter
body:
Adds a working dialer at **WhatsApp → Calls** so a QR-paired personal number can place and answer WhatsApp voice calls, and records each call's audio as the media seam the note taker needs.

Merging this deploys it — `deploy.yml` fires on push to `main`, rebuilds the bridge from source (`CGO_ENABLED=0`), and restarts the service.

## Why this shape

WhatsApp Desktop can call because it ships a full VoIP stack. `whatsmeow` carries call *signalling* only, so the bridge could see a call happening but never hear or place one. [`meowcaller`](https://github.com/purpshell/meowcaller) supplies the missing half in pure Go — MLow codec, SRTP, RTP, relay — on the session we already hold.

Meta's Cloud API calling product can't do this: it's 1:1-only, needs per-number enablement by Meta, and has no media leg here yet. The bridge transport is the only path that reaches group calls at all. Background and alternatives: `ai-company-brain/specs/whatsapp_calls_note_taker.md`.

## What's included

| Layer | Change |
|---|---|
| `whatsapp_bridge/calls.go` | New. Place 1:1 / group (by group id or ad-hoc), answer, reject, hangup, phase registry, per-call WAV recording, retention sweep. |
| `session.go` | `meowcaller.NewClient` attached in `newClient` — before `Connect`, which the library requires. |
| `main.go` | `POST /call`, `/call/{hangup,answer,reject}`, `GET /calls`. |
| `routes/whatsapp/transport/calls.py` | Authenticated proxy + the bridge event seam. Enforces account ownership, which the bridge cannot — it only knows a shared secret. |
| `core.py` | `provider` on the account model; `/bridge/call-event` added to feature-gate exemptions. |
| `whatsapp/calls/page.tsx` | The dialer. |
| Deploy | Seeds `WHATSAPP_BRIDGE_CALL_RECORD_DIR` and `..._RETENTION_DAYS` into `.env`. |

## Known limits — read before testing

- **Calls are listen-only.** There's no outbound microphone path, so the person you call hears silence while we record them. Fine for note-taking; it is not yet a usable phone call.
- **Transcription isn't wired.** The event endpoint logs the recording path; nothing feeds it to `acb_stt` yet.
- **Group audio is mixed**, so group calls need ordinary diarization rather than per-participant attribution.
- **Inbound calls are never auto-answered**, deliberately — a number that picks up strangers is both a consent problem and a ban signal.
- **This has never been run against live WhatsApp.** Builds, vets and tests pass; the wire protocol is unproven.

## Risk

Calling from an unofficial client is outside WhatsApp's Terms of Service and the number can be banned; `meowcaller`'s group support is marked experimental. Use a number you're willing to lose, never the main line. The dialer leads with this rather than burying it, and only offers bridge numbers.

Recording is on by default (it's the point) at ~115 MB per call-hour, swept after 7 days. `WHATSAPP_BRIDGE_CALL_RECORD_DIR=` disables it entirely.

## Verification

Go builds, vets and tests clean (`gofmt` clean); `next build` passes with `/whatsapp/calls` registered; `tsc` clean on `src`; 3285 Python tests pass, including 21 new ones covering ownership, bridge-down, error propagation and the secret gate.

Two bugs the tests caught and fixed: `/bridge/call-event` was missing its feature-gate exemption (there's a test that enforces exactly that), and `finish()` rewrote the call's end timestamp on its second invocation — which happens on most calls, since `OnEnd` races an explicit hangup — stretching the recorded duration.
