title: feat(whatsapp): a debug report you can paste when a call misbehaves
body:
Every round of debugging this feature has started from "it doesn't work" and spent a day narrowing down *where*. A failing call left almost no trace: the phase is one word, errors were gone by the time anyone looked, and the interesting part is always **where in the sequence it stopped**.

## Server timeline

The bridge now records, per call:

- dialling — **what was actually sent vs what was typed**
- every phase transition with elapsed time
- relay bound / media active
- browser audio attached and detached, with frame counts each way
- **first microphone frame up**, **first peer frame down** — the two events that separate "socket open" from "audio flowing"
- websocket close **status codes** when either leg dies

Served from `GET /calls/events`, proxied at `GET /whatsapp/calls/{id}/events`. Capped ring buffer, tail-preserving — the end of a failing call is the informative part.

## Browser timeline

Microphone acquisition (with the `DOMException` name on failure), AudioContext sample rate and state, worklet load, socket open, first frame each way, and on close: **`code`, `reason`, `wasClean`, frames sent, frames received**. Those numbers identify a WebSocket failure and were previously thrown away — `onerror` gives nothing, `onclose` gives everything.

## One button

A clipboard icon on any call assembles both timelines plus readiness into plain text, copies it, **and renders it** — the clipboard is blocked often enough that a report you can't get out of the browser is no report at all.

Deliberately excluded: peer phone numbers and the audio token. Neither helps diagnose a protocol bug; both are worth not pasting into a chat.

## Example

```
=== WhatsApp call debug report ===
call: 8F2C...  (outgoing direct)
phase: active  media_ready: true  audio: 12.4s
client audio state: live

--- server timeline ---
20:14:02.118  [signal] dialled "919876543210" (typed "+91 98765 43210"); offer on the wire in 412ms
20:14:03.402  [phase] calling → ringing (+1.28s)
20:14:09.771  [media] relay bound, media active (+7.65s)
20:14:09.902  [audio] browser attached (mic + speakers)
20:14:10.113  [audio] first microphone frame received from the browser
20:14:10.240  [audio] first peer frame sent to the browser

--- browser timeline ---
...  socket CLOSED code=1006 reason=(none) clean=false sent=214 received=0
```

That last line is the kind of thing that used to take a day.

## Verification

3317 Python tests (4 new on the timeline), Go race-detector clean, `tsc`/`eslint`/`next build` clean.

title: fix(access): three live defects — Notes was readable, deletable and sendable-as by any colleague
body:
## Three live access defects, fixed

Found by a forensic audit of the multi-tenancy substrate. All three are live **at one organisation** — independent of any tenancy question.

### 1. 🔴 Notes: readable, deletable, and sendable-as by any colleague

`_LIST_SQL` had **no owner filter**, and its `query` searches `m.transcript` — so the meeting library was a **full-text search over every recorded conversation in the company**. `_load_meeting` had no predicate either, so `GET`, `PATCH`, `PUT`-scratch, attendees, speakers and the **hard DELETE** all worked on any id you could name.

**And the first attempt at the fix didn't close the worst part.** It used a sentinel actor `"auto"` so background generation could dispatch without a human in the request. That sentinel was **request-triggerable**:

> Bob holds `feature:notes` and knows the id of Alice's meeting. He `POST`s `/summarize` or `/retranscribe`. Generation **deletes Alice's existing action items**, re-creates them, then calls `auto_dispatch` — which sails past the ownership check on the strength of the string `"auto"` — and **sends an LLM-drafted email from Alice's mailbox** to a real external recipient, audited under Alice's name.

Neither gate stops it: `MIN_AUTO_CONFIDENCE` is an LLM score, not authorization, and `auto_dispatch_emails` **defaults to True** when the owner has no config row.

**The sentinel is gone.** `triggered_by` is now a **required, no-default** parameter threaded from the endpoint through `auto_dispatch` → `generate_notes` → `enqueue_summary` → `run_transcription`. A dropped argument is a `TypeError`, not a silent return to acting as anybody.

**Seven request paths reach `_dispatch`** — the review found two, the repair found five more:

| # | Path | actor | Owner-scoped at the endpoint? |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `POST /notes/actions/{id}/dispatch` | `user.email` | yes (404) |
| 2 | `POST …/actions/approve-all` | `user.email` | seam only |
| 3 | `POST …/summarize` | `user.email` | **yes, new** |
| 4 | `POST …/upload` → pipeline | `user.email` | seam only |
| 5 | `POST …/recordings/{rid}/complete` | `user.email` | seam only |
| 6 | `POST …/retranscribe` | `user.email` | **yes, new** |
| 7 | `POST …/bot-join` → poller → ingest | `meeting_bot.requested_by` | seam only |

Path 7 carries **`requested_by`, not the meeting's owner** — using the owner would have laundered the requester's authority into the owner's and left the hole half-open.

`summarize` and `retranscribe` are *also* owner-scoped at the endpoint, independently of the seam, because `summaries.py:295` lets any member **destroy a colleague's action-item triage queue** whether or not anything is ever dispatched. That's data loss, not just send-as.

### 2. Identity trust — narrower than the audit claimed

**The gateway is not anonymously spoofable.** The original audit overstated this, and the correction matters: with either secret provisioned, a bare `X-User-Email` with no Bearer resolves to `NO_ACCESS`, and `require_authenticated` 401s on an empty email. There is exactly one place in the gateway or `packages/` that reads that header.

The real exposure is narrower: **`GATEWAY_INTERNAL_TOKEN` falls back to `LITELLM_MASTER_KEY`** — a key every agent holds — and that key can then assert any identity. Now refusable behind `GATEWAY_REFUSE_LLM_KEY_IDENTITY`, which **defaults to today's behaviour exactly** and is **inert** once a distinct token is provisioned (both pinned by tests that pass before *and* after).

`require_internal_auth` / `require_llm_api_auth` deliberately **still** accept the fallback. They fail open on an empty expected token, so wiring the flag through them would have turned a mis-provisioned box from *"the LLM key authenticates"* into *"everything authenticates"* — the opposite of the intent.

### 3. `resolve_room_access` failed open

One code path served both *"no session row yet"* and *"any DB error"*, returning **full owner access**. Only the error path flips. The genuinely-new-conversation case keeps its own named constructor and its own test, because every new chat passes through it. All 15 call sites were enumerated first — **none caches a denial or treats it as permanent**, and the frontend already falls back to a solo room on a failed fetch. The refusal names the outage rather than accusing the member.

### Also fixed, from review

- **The owner predicate was case-sensitive** while the dispatch check casefolded. An IdP that changes UPN casing between sessions (Entra does) would have **emptied a member's own library** and 404'd them out of their own meetings — the exact "locked out of my own work" shape this repo has been burned by. Now `lower(…) = lower(…)`, defined once in a shared predicate.
- **Four guard docstrings in `agent.py`** asserted the *opposite* of the shipped behaviour ("any DB error resolves to True", "allow on a DB hiccup so legitimate cancels never get stuck"). Those are what the next engineer reads when a ticket says "cancel 403'd during the outage" — they pointed at reverting the fix.
- **The token-fallback check re-implemented its own precedence ladder.** If the two drifted, the flag would start refusing a *legitimately provisioned* token — on a flagged box, a total member lockout. Now one resolver returning `(token, is_fallback)`.

### 🔴 Owner action — the edge protection does not exist yet

Everything here is defence in depth **behind a boundary that isn't applied**. Editing `deploy/` was correctly blocked as owner-gated. In the `api.commandcenter.fracktal.in` `reverse_proxy` block, after `header_up X-Real-IP`:

```
header_up -X-User-Email
header_up -X-User-Role
```

Strip **both** — a forged role alone still upgrades `_coerce_role`. **Apply to the API vhost only**; the UI vhost sets identity headers *after* the `extra` spread and never forwards inbound ones.

**Precondition, worth one grep before `systemctl reload caddy`:** every on-box caller must reach the gateway over loopback. Verified in-repo — `GATEWAY_URL` defaults to `127.0.0.1:8000`, browser traffic is same-origin and proxied server-side, and `GATEWAY_PUBLIC_URL` is used only for OAuth redirects and webhook URLs, never for an outbound call carrying identity headers. If one *were* pointed at the public URL, stripping would land it in `SERVICE_ACCESS` — a widening, not a lockout.

To flip `GATEWAY_REFUSE_LLM_KEY_IDENTITY` later: set `GATEWAY_INTERNAL_TOKEN` in **both** `/opt/acb/app/.env` and `workbench/control_plane/.env.local` first (the BFF mirrors the same fallback), deploy, confirm sign-in, *then* flip — at which point it is already inert, which is the proof it's safe.

### Lockout risk in these changes

- Auto-dispatch now refuses on an empty or non-owner `triggered_by` — **fails safe**: notes still generate, the item stays a draft with a retryable error.
- `summarize`/`retranscribe` now 404 for non-owners. Both are browser-only; no machine caller exists (verified).
- **Legacy `owner_email IS NULL` rows stay visible to everyone.** They predate the owner column, both insert paths sit behind `require_feature_router` so the set **cannot grow**, and excluding them would make members' own old meetings vanish.
- No new env var changes behaviour by default.

### Verification

```
uv run pytest tests/unit/test_notes_owner_scoping.py tests/unit/test_default_deny_auth.py \
  tests/unit/test_org_access_enforcement.py tests/unit/test_gateway_auth_gating.py \
  tests/unit/test_rooms.py -q                              -> 73 passed, 14 skipped
uv run ruff check . --select F821,F601,F602,F502,F7,B006   -> All checks passed!
all 20 notes suites                                        -> 242 passed
```

The 14 skips are `test_rooms.py` — no local Postgres with migrations 138+139. **The three new room tests do run**, because they monkeypatch `_load_room` rather than needing a DB.

The P0's red was proven by restoring only the *pre-fix authorization semantics* (keeping the new signature, so the failure is the security claim rather than an arity error):

```
E  AssertionError: a colleague's request made the owner's mailbox send
E  assert [('alice@frac....in', 'auto')] == []
[info] notes.auto_dispatched dispatched=1 triggered_by=bob@fracktal.in
```

Its paired test (owner triggers → still sends, actor is *Alice*) also goes red under the revert, so the pair pins both directions.

**No migration, no `.env` change, no `deploy/` change.**

### Not closed — named rather than left to be rediscovered

`AGENTS.md` now lists these, and counts **request paths, not call sites**, since that undercount is what produced the P0:

- Read paths in `recordings`, `live`, `qa`, `copilot`, `share`, `actions`
- `actions.py` single-item approve/reject — any member can flip a colleague's action item and copy its description into their own GTD list
- **`meeting_bot.bot_join`** lets a member flip a colleague's prepared meeting into `status='recording'`
- From the same audit, separate tickets: Workflows have no owner filter (any member reads/edits/deletes every workflow, including other people's `hook_token`), the `org` subject expands across orgs, the Centers feature-slug mismatch makes Centers unreachable by anyone including the owner, and `schema.generated.sql` is stale (predates migration 130)

title: feat(BO-23): a backup path that can restore one table, not just the whole VPS
body:
## BO-23 — a backup path that can restore one table, not just the whole VPS

### The recovery position this replaces — measured, not inherited

Queried against the live VPS on 2026-08-03:

| | |
|---|---|
| Application-level backup | **none** — no dump, no cron, no script, anywhere |
| Hostinger VM images | **2 retained**: `2026-07-22`, `2026-07-29` |
| Age of the newest one | **5 days** |
| Worst-case RPO | **~7 days of data loss** |
| Restore time | `restore_time: 3457` ≈ **58 minutes** |
| Granularity | the **whole machine** — code, `.env`, every volume |
| VPS snapshot | **none** (`id: 0`, `created_at == expires_at`) |

So *"recover one dropped table"* was not an operation this system could
perform — the only lever reverted the entire box to a point up to a week
earlier. Meanwhile **140+ migrations replay forward-only on every release**
under `ON_ERROR_STOP=1` with no down-migrations.

The databases are **193 MB** (`acb`) and **11 MB** (`litellm_proxy`) with
**67 GB free**. There was never a cost reason for the gap.

### What ships

**`scripts/backup_db.sh`**

- **Every non-template database, enumerated not hardcoded.** `litellm_proxy`
  holds API keys and spend records — an `acb`-only backup would have silently
  missed it, and so would any database added later.
- **Cluster globals dumped separately.** Roles and passwords live in the
  cluster, not in any database. A per-database dump restored into a fresh
  cluster comes up with **no roles and every `GRANT` failing** — a bare-metal
  rebuild would have been impossible from database dumps alone.
- **`-Fc`, not plain SQL**, so `pg_restore --table gtd_task` can pull one table
  out. A plain dump only replays whole, which is useless for the case that
  motivated the ticket.
- **Integrity-checked on every run** with `pg_restore --list`. A truncated or
  half-written dump fails *then*, not at 3am during an incident. This is the
  difference between having a backup and believing you have one.
- **`--verify-restore` proves a different claim**: it restores into a scratch
  database and compares `public` table counts against live. The cheap check
  proves *readable*; this proves *restorable*. ~20s on 193 MB.
- Manifest with sha256, the migration high-water mark, the app commit, and
  anchor row counts — so "what was true when this was taken" is answerable
  without restoring it.

**`scripts/restore_db.sh`** — the default is deliberately the safe one. With no
flags it builds `acb_restored_<ts>` and touches nothing live, which is what you
actually want mid-incident. Overwriting live requires `--target acb --force`,
takes an **unconditional pre-restore dump first**, and stops the gateway so
users are not served half-restored state while it runs.

**Pre-migration hook (done-when 4)** — the migration runner now takes a dump
before replaying the ladder and **fails closed** if it cannot. Placed in the
script rather than the pipeline YAML so it also covers anyone running it by
hand, which is when it is most likely to matter. `SKIP_PRE_MIGRATION_BACKUP=1`
overrides, on purpose and in writing.

### One repo-specific trap this is designed around

Backups land in `/opt/acb/backups`, **outside `/opt/acb/app`**. The release
pipeline runs `git reset --hard`, which has already destroyed tracked runtime
state in this repo's history. Anything under the app dir is one release away
from being gone.

### 🔴 Not done — and the box stays unticked because of it

- **Nothing schedules this.** The `acb-backup.service` / `.timer` units are
  written **verbatim in §5 of the spec** but could not be created: `plan-guard`
  blocks agent writes under `deploy/`. That refusal is correct — it just means
  an owner applies them. Until then backups happen only on a release or by hand.
- **No restore has been executed.** By BO-23's own rule — *a backup nobody has
  restored is not a backup* — tooling alone does not close this.
- **`BACKUP_REMOTE` is unset**, so these sit on the same disk as the database
  they protect. That covers bad migrations and dropped tables; it does not
  cover losing the disk, the box, or the provider account. The script warns
  loudly on every run rather than implying otherwise.
- **PITR deliberately not attempted.** It needs `archive_mode`, a WAL
  destination with real capacity, and a **production Postgres restart** — a
  poor trade before anything is even scheduled. Nightly verified dumps take the
  RPO from ~7 days to ≤24h; PITR is the *next* step, not the first one.

### A deviation worth flagging

Done-when 3 asked for the runbook at `deploy/hostinger/RESTORE.md`. It is at
**`ai-company-brain/specs/backup_and_restore.md`** instead, for the same
`plan-guard` reason. The clause's *intent* — that the runbook contain a
verification step and not just commands — is met (§6).

Done-when 5 (replacing the `deploy/hostinger/README.md:115` "add it later"
note) and the `deploy/AGENTS.md` half of done-when 6 are **still open** for the
same reason. `infra/AGENTS.md` is updated.

### Verification

```
bash -n scripts/backup_db.sh    -> syntax OK
bash -n scripts/restore_db.sh   -> syntax OK
bash -n scripts/apply_*.sh      -> syntax OK
```

**These scripts have not been executed.** They talk to a production database,
and both this repo's guard and the runtime classifier refused — correctly. The
verification that actually closes BO-23 is in §6 of the spec and is three
commands the owner runs once.

### An honest note on how this PR went

Two independent guards refused work during it: `plan-guard` blocked writes
under `deploy/`, and the runtime classifier separately blocked the live VPS
changes. The old §BO-23 predicted a gate collision here and was right, though
in the opposite direction from the one it anticipated — authoring
`scripts/*_db.sh` was permitted; the systemd units were not.

title: fix(WS-13): Centers were unreachable by everyone, owner included — FEATURES never listed them
body:
## WS-13 — Centers were unreachable by everyone, owner included

### The defect

`allowed_features()` (`packages/acb_auth/acb_auth/permissions.py:321-323` pre-fix) is
`tuple(f for f in FEATURES if self.can_use_feature(f))`. `FEATURES` was sixteen literal
slugs with **no `center.*` entry**, so:

- `GET /auth/me` (`routes/admin/me.py:84`) returned a `features` array containing no Center
  slug **for every principal**.
- `lib/nav.ts:229-232` filters items by `allowed.has(p.feature)`; `:233` then drops any
  section whose items emptied — removing the **section heading** too.
- `/centers/sales` hit `AccessGate`'s "You don't have access to this" — **for the owner**.

An owner holding `*` and an admin holding `feature:*` *do* match `feature:center.sales`
under `permissions.py:198-207`. But nothing ever asked, because the slug was never a
candidate. **`140_center_features.sql:5-7`'s own comment — "owners and admins see all
Centers via their `feature:*` baseline" — was false as written.**

`feature_catalog` is never read for nav or authorization. Its one runtime read
(`routes/admin/roles.py:345-356`) feeds the admin role editor only.

### The part that makes this worse than a missing entry

`validate_permission` is grammar-only (`permissions.py:167-193`) and **accepts**
`feature:center.sales`. So granting always worked — and
`routes/admin/groups.py:341-362` has been **writing `allow feature:center.<slug>`
overrides since 2026-08-01** whenever a member joins a Center group, pinned by
`tests/unit/test_admin_groups.py:338`.

**The system has been writing grants it could not display.**

⚠️ **Operational consequence of merging:** those existing override rows become effective
immediately. Centers will appear for those members with no admin action. Intended, but
this is not a "nobody gains until someone grants" change.

### The fix

Six slugs added to `FEATURES` in `140_center_features.sql:20-25` sort_order. Order is
load-bearing twice — `allowed_features()` emits in tuple order, and
`routes/admin/members.py:540-543` renders the member access editor in tuple order.

Plus two consistency edits the same defect had left behind: `types.ts:55`'s
`category` union was missing `"centers"` while the DB already emits it, and the roles
page rendered every chip under a hardcoded "Apps" heading.

### 🔴 The real fix is the invariant, and it took two rounds to get right

The root cause is not the tuple. **Three registries were kept in sync by comment only**
and drifted. The first attempt added an invariant test — and two reviewers, independently,
found it did not hold:

**Hole 1 — vacuous if its own source empties.** It derived the expected six from
`CENTER_GROUP_SLUGS` and then iterated *that*. The verifier emptied `CENTER_GROUP_SLUGS`
to `()` and re-ran: **`1 passed`**. It defended the regression that happened, not its
mirror image.

**Hole 2 — it pinned the wrong registry.** The UI reads `lib/centers.ts` (feeding
`nav.ts:113` and `access.ts:66`). The test pinned `groups.py`. Nothing connected them —
so following the documented recipe at `department_centers.md:178`, *"a `lib/centers.ts`
edit + one feature row"*, **reproduced this entire bug with a fully green suite**.

The documented recipe still produced the bug the branch exists to fix.

Both closed. `test_every_center_has_a_feature_slug` now asserts against a literal anchor
before iterating; `test_centers_registry_matches_the_feature_vocabulary` **parses
`centers.ts` from disk** and checks both directions — a Center whose feature is missing,
and a grantable `center.*` reaching nothing. A missing registry file **fails, it does not
skip** (a test that skips in CI protects nothing).

`department_centers.md` §2 now carries a five-place registration checklist naming what
each omission breaks and which test enforces which row.

### Corrections found along the way

- **The registration points are five, not four.** A new Center also needs an `org_group`
  seed row, or the group pairing the test asserts has nothing behind it.
- **`memory-clearance.md:601` had two stale citations, not one** — `CAPABILITIES` shifted
  by the same added lines as `FEATURES`.
- **`department_centers.md` Q3 repeated Q2's wrong one-edit promise** two lines below;
  fixing only `:178` would have left it.
- **`test_allowed_features_follows_catalog_order` (`:205-207`) was tautological** —
  `assert allowed_features() == FEATURES` self-compares and stayed green under a mutation
  that broke the exact behaviour its name claims to guard. Rewritten against literals.

### Verification

```
uv run pytest tests/unit/test_org_access_control.py tests/unit/test_default_deny_auth.py \
              tests/unit/test_admin_groups.py -q       -> 85 passed (baseline 84, +1)
uv run ruff check . --select F821,F601,F602,F502,F7,B006 -> All checks passed!
cd workbench/control_plane && npx tsc --noEmit           -> exit 0
npx vitest run                                           -> 163 passed
pytest tests/unit/ --collect-only                        -> 3553 collected, 0 errors
```

Mutation-proven, three ways, each restored byte-identical (sha256 before == after):

| Mutation | Before repair | After repair |
|---|---|---|
| remove a slug from `FEATURES` | 1 failed | **2 failed** |
| empty `CENTER_GROUP_SLUGS` | **1 passed** ← hole 1 | **2 failed** |
| add a 7th Center to `centers.ts` (the documented recipe) | **1 passed** ← hole 2 | **1 failed** |
| registry file absent | — | **fails, does not skip** |

I re-ran the `centers.ts` mutation myself rather than taking the report: red with
`AssertionError: Centers in centers.ts whose feature is absent from FEATURES:
['center.rnd']`, restored, sha256 identical, 50 passed.

### Reviewer verdicts

`ws-verifier` **PASS** · `diff-reviewer` **APPROVE** (one P2 = hole 2, repaired here).

The reviewer specifically attacked and **could not substantiate** the central risk —
that this over-grants. Only `owner` (`*`) and `admin` (`feature:*`) gain all six;
`manager`, `member`, `guest`, `agent_service` grant literal slugs with no wildcard and
gain nothing. Per-department scoping holds: `permission_matches` never lets
`feature:center.finance` cover `feature:center.sales`. A repo-wide grep finds **zero**
backend `require_permission("feature:center.*")`, so no authorization surface widened —
the Center page is a static scaffold whose sub-apps are each separately gated. Suspended
and degraded principals fail closed: `decide()` returns `inactive` *before* any wildcard
evaluation.

### Not fixed — named rather than left to be rediscovered

- **`workbench/control_plane/src/app/page.tsx:11-12`** renders `NAV_SECTIONS` with **no
  access filter at all**, so the home grid advertises every pane — Centers, Admin,
  everything — to every viewer **including signed-out ones**, while the sidebar hides
  them correctly. This is why the bug looked half-present. Recorded in
  `workbench/AGENTS.md` and the WS-13 row. Whoever fixes it inherits a real decision:
  `useAccess()` returns null on first paint and nav's convention for null is "show
  everything" so the sidebar doesn't visibly shrink — that default is wrong for a landing
  page, and no spec answers it.
- **`routes/admin/roles.py:357-363`** hardcodes `"category": "apps"` in the
  `feature_catalog` fallback, so on a pre-migration box Center chips render under "Apps".
  Cosmetic and self-disclosing (the fallback sets `label: f`, so the chip reads literally
  `center.sales`).
- The `feature_catalog` migration row is not machine-checked — that needs a SQL parser in
  a unit test. Recorded as checklist row 2 instead.

### Live-verify owed

Nobody has exercised `GET /auth/me` against a live DB to see `/centers/sales` render for a
real principal. It is a sound inference from two files read directly, not an observation.

**No migration** (`140:16-17` already widened the CHECK to include `'centers'`), no `.env`,
no `deploy/` change. WS-13 stays 🟡 — the People directory read view is still open, and
flipping it green would be a lie.

title: docs(WS-14): Centers C was pointing at three things that do not exist
body:
## WS-14 — Centers C was pointing at three things that do not exist

**⚠️ Stacked on #348.** Both touch `work_plan.md` and `department_centers.md:3`.
**Retarget this PR to `main` BEFORE merging #348** — this repo's own history records that
`gh pr merge --delete-branch` on a base auto-closes the stacked child, and you then cannot
reopen it while the base ref is missing.

WS-14 was audited and returned **NO-GO** on 7 of 7 contract points. This makes it
dispatchable. **Docs only** — plus one docstring, called out below.

### What an implementer dispatched on the old row would have built

**Three of the four bullets pointed at things that are not there.**

1. **Shared mailboxes.** `email_account_member`, cited as Phase-2 content by both
   `department_centers.md` and `org_access_control.md:311`, **exists nowhere** — 0 hits
   repo-wide across `*.sql` and `*.py`. And `work_plan.md` §4 assigns the work to
   `email_app_master_plan.md`, which contains **zero** occurrences of "shared mailbox".
   The named owner does not own the work in fact.
2. **Team-instanced agents.** The bullet sends the implementer to `agent-kinds.md` §6 for
   sales/billing/delivery agents. **None of the seven agents in that roster exist**;
   `apps/agents/` holds exactly six. Worse — the roster calls `task-manager`,
   `orchestrator` and `app-builder` *personal*, while all three shipped `config.json`
   files say `"instancing": "shared"`. **An implementer "aligning agents to the roster"
   would have silently re-partitioned three live agents' memory and blob store.**
3. **Per-Center approvals.** Not a filter — there is nothing to filter on.
   `66_pending_actions.sql:13-38` has no requesting member, no group, no Center.

Each is now rewritten against what is actually in the tree, with the traps recorded as
traps.

### 🔴 The P1 the reviewer caught — acceptance that passes without the feature

C1 (the tasks team slice) is the one AGENT-SAFE bullet and the whole near-term value of
WS-14. Its first draft of acceptance **could go green with no way for anyone to create a
grant**: add the table, widen the read path, and have the tests `INSERT` grant rows in a
fixture. Every clause passed — including the one that forced *a* validated write path but
never an endpoint, a caller, or a surface, so a repository helper reached only from tests
satisfied it verbatim. It would have merged with grants creatable only by hand-written SQL
against production.

Repaired: done-when 1 now names `POST /tasks/projects/{id}/grants` and
`DELETE …/grants/{subject}` on the shipped `/tasks` router, the exact permission
(`feature:tasks` + project ownership — **no new slug, no `admin:*`**), and the status codes
(404 unseeable / 403 seeable-but-not-owned) mirroring `routes/apps/_common.py:459-475`.
Done-when 2 requires the grant under test to be created **through that route**, explicitly
rejecting a fixture INSERT.

It also pins a trap worth more than the clause: the module must be added to
`routes/tasks/__init__.py:7-18`, because routers register by import side effect — **a
module left out mounts nothing while direct-call tests still pass green.**

**`role` was cut from the proposed schema, not hedged.** Every C1 clause is a read-path
clause, so the column would have shipped with exactly one legal value and no reader. The
way back is recorded (additive `ADD COLUMN` at the next free number, R1).

### This PR committed the exact sin it exists to fix

Its first draft asserted that `pending_actions.actor` is *"the proposing agent … not the
human behind it"* and that no group is derivable from any existing column. **Both
`routes/apps/tools.py:393` and `routes/apps/actions.py:345` write
`actor=f"app:{slug}:{email}"`** — the requesting human is in the row, and a group *is*
derivable. An absolute the tree falsifies, carried in four places.

Retracted and replaced with the measured table of all five proposer shapes. The C4 verdict
**survives on better reasoning**: a human appears in only two of six proposers, so a
Center-filtered inbox is silently empty for every workflow-, publish- and
provider-originated proposal. The column must be *written by every proposer*, not parsed
out of an ad-hoc string.

### TV-1 finally has a board row — and its done-when was unsatisfiable

`tenancy_and_visibility.md` §2 TV-1 passes all seven contract points and was **the single
most dispatch-ready ticket in the corpus** — but `work_plan.md` §2 had no row for it, and
the loop selects from §2. Minted as **WS-14a**.

Its own acceptance was broken: done-when 2 demanded a hermetic test *"verified red before
the fix"*, while §7 named `test_session_authority.py` and `test_rooms.py` as the home —
both `skipif` without a database. **The fixture would have skipped green.** Demonstrated,
not asserted: those two files plus `test_app_grants.py` give `34 passed, 21 skipped`.

Split into a hermetic string assertion with a named guard-free home
(`test_org_access_control.py`, verified to have no `skipif`) plus a DB-backed half that
must quote `passed`, not `skipped`.

### Other corrections

- **`_load_room_row` does not exist** — 0 code hits; the two hits repo-wide were the doc
  lines citing it. Real symbol is `_load_room` (`gateway/rooms.py:149`), and
  `_load_room_state` is a *different* function, so the wrong name was actively
  mis-suggestive. Ranges were right; only the symbol was wrong.
- **"the shared validator, not a copy of it" named no module, and no shared home existed.**
  Both subject validators are route-local and disjoint, so satisfying it meant importing a
  private symbol across route packages. Home now proposed and justified:
  `packages/acb_auth/acb_auth/permissions.py` — pure by contract, already owns the
  permission vocabulary, and all three consumers already import `acb_auth`, so **zero new
  import-graph edges**.
- **Six wrong anchors in `tenancy_and_visibility.md`** — under a header claiming *"every
  claim re-measured at `520476ab`"*. They were wrong **at that commit**. All corrected and
  re-verified.
- **R4:** PR #346 merged today; three statements still called it pending.
- **D13 registered** in `work_plan.md` §3, labelled `agent-proposed, owner may overrule` —
  distinct from D11/D12's `owner-answered`.

### The one `.py` change

`routes/rooms.py:101-106`, **docstring only**, `git diff --numstat` = `4 4`, no executable
line touched. The old text claimed `_valid_subject` is *"identical to
`grants.is_valid_subject` on purpose"* — **false**: that one is
`email | agent:<name> | agents:*` and rejects `org` at `grants.py:77`. Rooms alone honours
`group:`, which is the mechanism D12 depends on, so the docstring was actively misdirecting
implementers of this very ticket.

Deliberately rewritten **line-count-neutral**: `_valid_subject` still spans `:100-111` and
the correction still sits on `:103`, so eight anchors four documents publish stay valid.
Fixing one citation by invalidating eight would have been a net regression.

### Verification

```
uv run ruff check . --select F821,F601,F602,F502,F7,B006  -> All checks passed!
uv run pytest tests/unit/test_org_access_control.py tests/unit/test_admin_groups.py \
              tests/unit/test_default_deny_auth.py -q     -> 85 passed
git diff --name-status bebbd924..HEAD                     -> 6 .md M + 1 .py M, zero A
```

I re-derived the `actor` correction myself rather than accepting either agent's version:
`system:action_broker` appears only in `action_broker/broker.py` (audit events), so it is
**not** a `pending_actions.actor` — five proposer shapes, not six. That correction came
from the implementer, against the reviewer.

### Loop record

`spec-auditor` **NO-GO** (7/7 contract points) → `ws-implementer` → `diff-reviewer`
**REQUEST-CHANGES** (1×P1, 4×P2) → one repair round.

Corrections ran in every direction, including against me: my brief's leak-site range
`:385-392` clipped the wrapping group (correct: `:384-393`), and I passed through the
audit's "6 call sites" for `instance_key` without re-measuring — it is **4**; the extras
were docstring mentions. Both caught by the agents I was briefing.

### Still open — yours

- **Shared mailboxes is `OWNERLESS IN FACT`.** Either `email_app_master_plan.md` gains a
  shared-mailbox section, or §4's owner assignment changes. Reassigning ownership is not an
  agent's call, so it is recorded, not decided.
- **`org_access_control.md` §9 Q2** — per-Center approvals is OWNER-GATE by construction.
- **D13** (`gtd_project_grant` over a shared `object_grants`) is agent-proposed; the
  reasoning engages the alternatives, including why reusing `app_grants` is strictly worse
  (its `app_id UUID NOT NULL REFERENCES apps(id)` key). Overrule on the merits if you
  disagree.

title: feat(WS-24): the gate for letting colleagues onto the platform — and an org-wide HR exposure it found
body:
## WS-24 — the gate for letting colleagues onto the platform

**⚠️ Stacked: #348 ← #349 ← this.** Retarget **#349 and this PR to `main` before merging
#348** — merging a base with `--delete-branch` auto-closes its stacked children, and this
repo has been burned by that.

Exactly one person is signed in today. "Is it safe to invite colleagues?" kept being
re-derived in conversation and answered inconsistently — including by me. This makes it a
command you run and a document with `file:line` behind every claim.

### 🔴 The finding that justifies the whole ticket

**Any colleague on the default `member` role can read your entire HR directory, and write
to it.**

`routes/tasks/people.py:22` imports the **feature-gated** `/tasks` router
(`tasks/core.py:27-30`) and adds no scoping of its own:

| Route | Line | Scoping |
|---|---|---|
| `GET /people` | `:80-84` | takes `_user` and **never uses it**; `SELECT * FROM gtd_people` at `:98` |
| `POST /people` | `:190` | `user` only for `_uid()` attribution |
| `PATCH /people/{person_id}` | `:241` | same |
| `POST /people/{person_id}/resume` | `:303` | same |
| `POST /people/embed` | `capability.py:225` | same |

`member` holds `feature:tasks` (`130:235`). So every colleague could read every person's
name, email, title, department, manager, skills **including résumé-extracted ones**,
capacity and ClickUp id — and add a person, edit anybody's record, or upload a résumé onto
it.

This is HR data, and it is exactly the surface D12's department privacy exists to protect.
`tasks/accounts.py` **is** scoped (`_assert_account_owner` at `:190, 259, 285, 325, 406`),
so the gap is specific to the people layer, not a blanket one.

Filed as blocking item **N4**. **Not fixed here** — this ticket is the gate; N4 is work it
schedules.

It hid behind the same feature flag as the task list, which is why every prior summary of
"what can a member see" answered for `gtd_items` and stopped. Mine included.

### 🔴 The gate almost caused the outage it exists to prevent

G2's done-when claimed a `[PASS]` meant `GATEWAY_INTERNAL_TOKEN` was set in **both**
`/opt/acb/app/.env` and the workbench's `.env.local`. The check only ever read the first —
and its own remediation said *"restart the gateway and the workbench"*, not *"redeploy"*.

Follow that exactly: `.env` has the token, `.env.local` does not, the BFF keeps sending
`sk-local-dev-change-me` (`gateway.ts:58-61`), `bearer_ok` is false while `x_user_email` is
present and an internal token **is** configured → `deps.py:356-361` returns **`NO_ACCESS`
for every signed-in member**. The readiness check would have reported green while locking
the org out — the same shape as the July incident.

Now reads both files, SKIPs the workbench half off-box, and FAILs naming the lockout when
they disagree.

### What ships

**`scripts/onboarding_preflight.py`** — 7 checks, PASS/FAIL/SKIP with remediation attached,
non-zero exit on any FAIL, `--mode local` for agents. Never prints a secret; every DB
statement is a `SELECT`.

It refuses to answer what it cannot see. Check 7 (default-deny) **will not** PASS locally,
because `resolve_access` degrades to `is_active=False` on an unreachable DB too
(`access.py:159-167`) — so a local PASS would be indistinguishable from a broken DSN.
Checks 1 and 2 SKIP locally for the same reason after this round's repair.

Current local run: **exit 1**, `1 pass · 2 FAIL · 4 skip`.

**`ai-company-brain/specs/colleague_onboarding.md`** — the gate (G1–G4, AGENT-SAFE vs
OWNER-GATE, per-item done-whens), the runbook (invite → role → Center group → verify, with
an off-boarding step), and the **capability matrix**: 30+ cells, each carrying the
`file:line` that settles it, plus **5 admitted UNVERIFIED** rather than guessed.

### Three designs that change meaning with a second person

Confirmed directly, all deliberate, none a bug — but all consequential now:

1. **Any `member` can read *and write* every agent's memory compartment.**
   `routes/memory.py::_authorize_agent` (`:103-109`) gates on `can_run_agent`;
   `_authorize_scope` (`:128-167`) calls it without passing `write`; `member` holds
   `agents:run:*`. The docstring says shared-by-design — coherent for one user, a shared
   space for a team.
2. **4 of 6 first-party agents declare `instancing: "shared"`** (orchestrator, task-manager,
   app-builder, apis-config) → `instance_key()` returns `''` (`manifest.py:235-246`) → one
   common artifact workspace, not per-user.
3. **`data:org:read` has zero consumers.** Declared (`permissions.py:132`), granted
   (`130:205,221,258`), listed (`access.py:148`), read by nothing. **So my earlier warning
   that `manager` "sees org-wide data" was wrong.** Manager's real breadth is
   `admin:members:read` — the auth floor for the *entire* `/admin` package
   (`admin/_common.py:77-91`) — plus approvals, observability, WhatsApp and
   `memory:write_org`. Minted as **D14** (`agent-proposed, owner may overrule`).

### A correction affecting every role summary in the corpus

**Grants come from two migrations, not one.** `131_integration_memory_permissions.sql:70-78`
also gives `member` `integrations:use:*` **and `memory:read_org`**; `guest` gets nothing
(`131:80`). Every summary anywhere quotes `130` alone and is therefore incomplete.

Also corrected: `org_access_control.md`'s manager Grants cell read *"all `feature:*` except
`build.*`"* — wrong in **five** slugs, not one (`130:216-221` omits workflows, integrations,
models, agents and every `center.*`).

### Also repaired this round

- **Check 4 asserted a restore path it never looked for.** It tested a timer, a directory, a
  MANIFEST and an age — no dump format, no row count, no restore script — while its own
  docstring said it existed to prevent exactly that. A `pg_dump --schema-only` timer would
  have printed "Backups run, land, and are recent" with **zero rows** backed up. And it
  looked for artifacts BO-23 never specifies, so G3 could never have gone green. Now
  measured against BO-23's four done-whens verbatim.
- **Checks 1 and 2 could PASS vacuously** in local mode — deployment claims evaluated
  against a dev `.env`, with the banner only caveating SKIPs.

### Verification

```
uv run ruff check . --select F821,F601,F602,F502,F7,B006  -> All checks passed!
uv run pytest tests/unit/test_org_access_control.py tests/unit/test_admin_groups.py \
              tests/unit/test_default_deny_auth.py -q     -> 85 passed
python -m py_compile scripts/onboarding_preflight.py      -> ok
uv run python scripts/onboarding_preflight.py --mode local -> exit 1
```

Exit code verified without a pipe — a piped `$?` reports `tail`, not the script.
**Never pointed at production**; `--mode local` only, and `work_plan.md` §6 now registers
"never run the preflight against prod" as an owner gate.

### Loop record

`ws-implementer` → `diff-reviewer` **REQUEST-CHANGES** (2×P1, 2×P2) → repair round. The
repair agent hit a session limit mid-edit, leaving `org_access_control.md`'s callouts
ordered (a)(c)(b); I verified the rest was coherent and fixed the ordering by hand.

Corrections ran against me repeatedly: two premises in my repair brief were wrong (check 4
never referenced `scripts/backup_db.sh`; there were no R1-R4 items in this PR), and my
`manager` "org-wide data" claim was false.

### Still open — yours

- **G1 Caddy strip** — both `plan-guard` and the runtime classifier refused agents. The
  exact patch is in the preflight's remediation and spec §1 G1.
- **G3 backups** — needs #347, then the timer.
- **G4** — N1–N4. **N4 is the sharpest** and should probably be first after G1.
- **D14** — whether `manager` keeps `admin:members:read`. A write to the access model, which
  §6 reserves to you.

title: fix(N4): the HR directory stops being org-wide read and write
body:
## N4 — the HR directory stops being org-wide read *and write*

**⚠️ Stacked: #348 ← #349 ← #350 ← this.** Retarget each child to `main` before merging its
base, bottom-up — merging a base with `--delete-branch` auto-closes its children.

Found while building the WS-24 readiness gate (#350). **This is the sharpest item that gate
turned up, and the only blocking one that did not need the owner.**

### What was open

`routes/tasks/people.py:22` mounts on the **feature-gated** `/tasks` router
(`tasks/core.py:27-30`, whose only dependency is `require_feature_router("tasks")`) and added
no scope of its own. `member` — the default role for a new employee — holds `feature:tasks`
(`130:235`).

So every colleague could read the whole roster (name, email, title, department, manager,
skills **including résumé-extracted ones**, `resume_summary`, `years_experience`, capacity,
current load, ClickUp id) and **add a person, edit anybody's record, or upload a résumé onto
it**. `GET /people` took `_user` — the underscore is the code stating the identity is unused.

It hid behind the same feature flag as the task list, which is why every prior summary of
"what a member can see" answered for `gtd_items` and stopped there.

### The decision — owner-answered 2026-08-04

**Directory open, HR fields restricted.** The roster stays visible to anyone holding
`feature:tasks`; the HR half is admin-only; writes are admin-only. Both rejected alternatives
(fully org-wide read; Center-scoped read, which needs D13's unbuilt grant shape and breaks
cross-team delegation) are recorded in the spec's DECISION block.

| | Non-admin member | Admin / owner |
|---|---|---|
| name, email, role, title, department, team, `reports_to`, `clickup_user_id` | ✅ | ✅ |
| `skills`, `skills_source`, `resume_summary`, `years_experience`, capacity / load / available | ❌ nulled | ✅ |
| `POST /people`, `PATCH /people/{id}`, `POST /people/{id}/resume`, `POST /people/embed` | ❌ 403 | ✅ |

### 🔴 Two things the brief did not ask for, and the fix is wrong without them

**1. The search box was an oracle for the column being hidden.** `GET /people?q=` appends
`EXISTS (… unnest(skills) …)`. Strip `skills` from the response but leave that clause and the
protection is cosmetic — you can binary-search a colleague's résumé skills through a query
parameter. The clause is now dropped for non-admins, and that is mutation-verified.

**2. The read fix alone would have destroyed data.** A non-admin now loads `skills: []`, and
`PersonEditor` **round-trips `skills` on save**. Without the write gate landing in the same
change, a member opening and saving a person would have **wiped that person's skills**. The
two halves are not independently shippable, and the PR says so rather than leaving the next
person to discover it.

### Implementation choices, each reusing an existing mechanism

- **Writes: `admin:members:manage`** — an existing `CAPABILITIES` entry, already the
  permission governing member records, bound the same way as `admin/members.py:145-146`.
  **No new slug**: a new slug is nobody's grant until an admin creates it, which would have
  broken HR features for the owner too.
- **HR reads: `admin:members:read`** — reused, not reinvented. It is `admin/_common.py:77-91`'s
  package floor and exactly what `admin/me.py:96` returns as `is_admin`. The owner's `*`
  matches both, verified by `permission_matches` and by test.
- **Projection at the serialization layer, not SQL.** `_row_to_person(row, *, include_hr)` is
  keyword-only with **no default**, so a missed call site is a `TypeError`, not a silent leak —
  the same discipline as the `triggered_by` fix in #346. Fresh containers per call; a
  module-level `[]`/`{}` would alias into every response.
- A shared seam in `tasks/core.py` (`can_read_hr_fields`, `require_people_write`) so the rule
  has one home. `can_read_hr_fields` **fails closed** on a non-`UserContext`.

### `fetch_people_for_clarify` is untouched — deliberately

`people.py:107-135` takes `db` only and feeds AI delegation/clarify. It has its own query, so
a serialization-layer projection leaves it structurally unaffected. Pinned by a test that
asserts full data **and** its signature is `["db"]` — because had the projection gone in at the
SQL layer, agent delegation would have silently degraded with nothing failing.

### Verification

```
uv run pytest tests/unit/test_tasks_people_scoping.py -q                    -> 35 passed
uv run pytest tests/unit/test_org_access_control.py test_admin_groups.py \
              test_default_deny_auth.py -q                                  -> 85 passed
uv run pytest tests/unit/test_tasks_gtd.py test_tasks_archive_upstream.py \
              test_task_broker_handlers.py test_org_access_enforcement.py -q -> 174 passed
uv run ruff check . --select F821,F601,F602,F502,F7,B006                    -> All checks passed!
cd workbench/control_plane && npx tsc --noEmit                              -> exit 0
```

`test_org_access_enforcement.py` (the route-wiring audit) was run specifically because route
dependencies changed.

Mutation-proven, tree restored byte-identical each time:

| Mutation | Result |
|---|---|
| `include_hr` forced true | `1 failed` — `assert ['firmware','C++','RTOS'] == []` |
| drop `dependencies=` from `POST /people` | `4 failed` — wiring, both non-admin cases, and `DID NOT RAISE` for anonymous |
| leave the `unnest(skills)` search clause in | `1 failed` — `'unnest(skills)' is contained here` |

I re-ran the first mutation myself rather than taking the report: red on
`test_a_member_does_not_receive_the_hr_half`, restored, sha256 identical.

Writes are pinned **per route** — 4 routes × {member, manager} = 8 refusal cases, plus a wiring
test and a 401-not-403 anonymous test each. Counting routes rather than call sites is the
lesson from #346, where a review found two paths and the repair found seven.

### Frontend — verified, not assumed

Only `PeopleView.tsx` and `PersonEditor.tsx` read `OrgPerson`, and `mapOrgPerson`
(`tasks/lib/api.ts:301-327`) already coerces null → `undefined`, null skills → `[]`,
null `skills_source` → `{}` — exactly the shape nulling produces. `PersonRow` degrades into its
existing **"No capacity set"** branch and hides skill chips behind `p.skills.length > 0`.
PeopleView's search is **client-side**, so the `q` change affects only the `gtd_people` agent
tool, not the UI.

**A wart, reported rather than hidden:** the "Add person" button and row-click editor still
render for a non-admin; Save now surfaces the 403 inline. That matches this repo's stated
doctrine (`lib/access.ts:126-129` — hiding a control is a courtesy, not a boundary), but
gating those affordances on `is_admin` is worth a follow-up slice.

Agent path: `skill-task-gtd`'s `gtd_people` tool calls `GET /tasks/people` **as the acting
member**, so an agent run for a non-admin now sees the restricted directory. Correct under the
intersection rule, and recorded in the DECISION block.

### Not closed

- **`domain` and `status` are not restricted** — they fall outside both of the owner's
  enumerated lists. `domain` is résumé-fillable, so it is a partial leak of résumé depth.
  Recorded in the DECISION block with the one-line fix (`HR_FIELDS` + `_blank_hr()`) if you
  want it closed.
- **N1, N2, N3 remain open** — Notes read paths in `recordings`/`live`/`qa`/`copilot`/`share`/
  `actions`, single-item approve/reject, and the `meeting_bot.bot_join` recording hijack.
- **G1/G2/G3 are unchanged and owner-gated.** The WS-24 gate is **not** green: 1 of G4's 4
  tickets is closed. Both the spec header and the board row say so explicitly rather than
  implying progress means readiness.

**No migration**, no `.env`, no `deploy/` change.

title: fix(N1/N2/N3): Notes was private to its owner in the library only
body:
## N1/N2/N3 — Notes was private to its owner in the library only

**⚠️ Stacked: #348 ← #349 ← #350 ← #351 ← this.** Retarget each child to `main` before
merging its base, bottom-up.

PR #346 owner-scoped the Notes **library** — list, get, delete, dispatch — and named six
more surfaces it did not close. This closes them. **16 routes enumerated, 15 scoped, 1
deliberately left machine-authed.**

### 🔴 First: the scope I was given was incomplete, and the gate said otherwise

N1 was specified as five files. Enumerating `routes/notes/` exhaustively found **ten more
modules with routes and zero owner predicates** — and two of them are as sharp as anything
in N1:

- `GET /meetings/{id}/live` — the live caption stream of anyone's meeting
- **`POST /meetings/{id}/say` — makes the notetaker speak a line into somebody else's call**
- `GET` / `PUT /meetings/{id}/note` — read **and overwrite** anyone's generated notes
- `GET /meetings/{id}/actions` — anyone's action list

Filed as **N5**, with a done-when, and deliberately placed **outside G4** — G4's own
done-when is "each of §4's four tickets meets its own done-when", and all four now do.
Re-scoping an owner-facing gate mid-flight is the owner's call, not an agent's.

**🔴 OWNER DECISION: does N5 block colleague #1?** My previous answer — that N1–N3 was the
last of the blocking list — was wrong, because the enumeration behind it was not exhaustive.

### What shipped

| Route | Decision |
|---|---|
| `POST /meetings/{id}/upload` · `…/recordings/start` · `…/{rid}/chunk` · `…/{rid}/complete` · `GET …/audio` | **scoped** (chunk/complete via a `_recording_path` join binding the predicate) |
| `POST /meetings/{id}/retranscribe` | already guarded at `:337` — **not double-guarded** |
| `POST /meetings/{id}/ask` | **scoped**, and *before* the transcript read |
| `POST …/share/email/draft` | **scoped** |
| `GET …/copilot/stream` · `…/copilot/events` | **scoped**; stream checks *before* `StreamingResponse` opens |
| `POST /stt/live-token` | **scoped** when it names a meeting |
| `GET …/live/wanted` · `POST /stt/bot-live-token` | **left machine-authed** — reasoning below |
| `POST /actions/{aid}/approve` · `/reject` | **scoped** via `_load_action` (N2) |
| `POST /meetings/{id}/actions/approve-all` | was safe at the `_dispatch` seam but answered **200-empty**; aligned to 404 |
| `POST /meetings/bot-join` (attach branch) | **scoped** (N3) |

### Three judgement calls, made explicitly

**`live/wanted` stays machine-authed.** The caller is the bot worker in its own container
holding `MEETING_BOT_TOKEN` with no member identity. An owner predicate needs an owner, and
both ways to invent one — trusting a client-supplied email, or falling back to the meeting's
own `owner_email` — turn the bot token into a way to assert an identity. It discloses one
boolean and gives the same answer for a nonexistent id. Pinned by a test.

**`share.py` implements no sharing.** Read end to end: no grant, no token, no redemption
route. The draft returns to the caller's own compose window and the send is a separate
`/email/send`. So there is no redemption to leave open — the whole route is a read, and it is
scoped.

**N3's principal is the caller, not the meeting's owner.** Resolving against the row's own
`owner_email` would compare the meeting to itself and pass every time. The `requested_by`
asymmetry from #346 is preserved, and a test pins that the ingest side still reads it.

One stated departure: N3 binds the predicate **into** the `UPDATE` rather than doing a
preceding `load_owned_meeting`. Same predicate, same 404, and no TOCTOU window. Recorded in
the spec as a departure rather than smuggled.

### 🔴 A production defect found on the way, not fixed

`/notes/meetings/{meeting_id}/live/wanted` is in **neither** `main.PUBLIC_ROUTES`
(`main.py:489-490`) **nor** `core.router`'s exempt list, while both its siblings are in both.
So `require_authenticated` and then the feature gate 401 the worker before `_check_bot_auth`
runs — **the poll that decides whether to keep paying for streaming ASR is dead in
production.**

Not fixed here: the repair *opens* a route, which is the opposite of this change's direction,
and no acceptance criterion asks for it. Filed in the spec, `AGENTS.md`, and the test
docstring.

### Verification

```
uv run pytest tests/unit/test_notes_owner_scoping.py -q          -> 57 passed  (was 21)
uv run pytest test_tasks_people_scoping.py test_org_access_control.py \
              test_default_deny_auth.py -q                       -> 101 passed
uv run pytest tests/unit/test_org_access_enforcement.py -q       -> 31 passed
uv run ruff check . --select F821,F601,F602,F502,F7,B006         -> All checks passed!
full Notes suite, 20 files named individually                    -> 280 passed
8 × test_meeting_bot_*.py                                        -> 85 passed
```

**Red-first, the honest way:** a pre-fix tree was rebuilt with the guards removed **but the
parameter renames and imports kept**, so every failure is the security claim rather than an
arity error. **16 failed, 41 passed.** Fifteen read `DID NOT RAISE HTTPException`; the
sixteenth reads `assert 409 == 404 … 'no transcript yet'` — i.e. the oracle itself.

Four mutants, each restored byte-identical by sha256 (post-fix digest `993e9db4…`):

| Mutant | Result |
|---|---|
| drop `load_owned_meeting` from `get_audio` | 1 failed |
| drop the predicate **and** the `:owner` bind in `_load_action` | 3 failed |
| drop the predicate from `bot_join`'s UPDATE | 1 failed |
| compare against `nobody@x` in `get_audio` | 2 failed — the **owner-still-allowed** half |

I ran a fifth myself: rebinding `_load_action`'s `:owner` to a fixed address fails
`test_approving_your_own_action_item_still_creates_the_task`,
`test_rejecting_your_own_action_item_still_works` and the differently-cased-sign-in case —
so the owner half is pinned, not just the refusal half. Tree restored byte-identical.

**A stated limit of the fake:** it decides whether to scope by the *parameters* a query binds,
not the SQL text (that is #346's deliberate design — it survives the case-insensitivity fix).
A mutant deleting only the predicate text while keeping the `:owner` bind would **not** go
red. Mutants 2 and 3 remove both, which is the realistic regression.

### Preserved on purpose

Case-insensitive comparison (an IdP that changes UPN casing between sessions would otherwise
empty a member's own library), and the `owner_email IS NULL` arm for legacy rows — both
pinned by tests, both properties #346 established for good reasons.

### Board

**G4 is CLOSED — 4 of 4.** The gate is **not** green: G1, G2 and G3 are unchanged and two are
owner-gated. Both the spec header and the WS-24 row say so explicitly:

> *G4 closed the holes that survive a correct identity; G1/G2 are about the identity itself,
> and an owner predicate applied to a forged one is not a control.*

### Corrections to my brief

`recordings.py` had **one** `load_owned_meeting` call site before this change, not two. And
"leave `live/wanted` as is" preserves a route that **does not work**, rather than one that
works differently.

**No migration**, no `.env`, no `deploy/` change.

title: N6a — the sign-in queue: 53 knocks, and the system told nobody
body:
## N6a — the sign-in queue: 53 knocks, and the system told nobody

**WS-24 / N6a** · owning spec `ai-company-brain/specs/colleague_onboarding.md` §6 (new).

`/admin/members` was push-only: the only way an `app_user` row was ever created is
an admin typing an address into Invite (`members.py:168-183`). Somebody arriving at
the front door created nothing anyone could see. The refusal *was* logged
(`access.py` — `access_unprovisioned_signin`, with the email), but to journald,
where nothing reads it back and rotation eventually eats it.

**This is not hypothetical.** Measured on the box while writing the ticket:

    53 refusals   ishaanpilar@fracktal.in
    first  2026-08-03T16:21:15Z
    latest 2026-08-04T10:46:56Z   (still recurring)

One colleague spent eighteen hours telling the system he wanted in, fifty-three
times, and the owner had no way to find out except being told out of band.

### What shipped

| | |
|---|---|
| **migration 143** | `access_request` — unique on `lower(email)`, first/last seen, attempt count, `pending\|approved\|denied` + `CHECK`, `decided_by`/`decided_at`, partial index on pending |
| **the capture** | `resolve_access` persists the knock instead of only logging it |
| **the queue** | `GET /admin/members/requests`, `POST …/{email}/approve`, `POST …/{email}/deny` |
| **the UI** | a **Requests** tab with a count badge, Approve (role picker) + Deny, and an external-domain chip |
| **dw11** | the roster now labels `invited` as **"invited — never signed in"** |

**Approve provisions *and* activates in one action.** An approval already is the
decision to let somebody in, and they are demonstrably at the door — re-creating
the two-click trap inside a brand-new feature would have been perverse.

### 🔴 The write is on the auth path, and `resolve_access` is not sign-in-only

The single sharpest thing in this diff. `resolve_access` is called with **other
people's** emails — `routes/rooms.py:215` fans it out over room participants,
`access.py` folds it over session subjects, and there are two more callers. An
unconditional write in the `row is None` branch would have filled the queue with
people who never tried to sign in — precisely the harm the separate-table decision
exists to avoid.

Gated on a keyword-only `record_request: bool = False` with **exactly one** opt-in
call site (`deps.py`). A tree-scan test enforces that, so the safety property is
"the default is `False`", not "we enumerated the callers" — the enumeration was
wrong twice during review.

### 🔴 A P1 found in review, then two more instances of the same shape

Three rounds, and the third one is the interesting one because it explains the
other two.

**Round 1 — cross-gate escalation.** Approve is gated on `admin:members:invite`;
suspending and off-boarding are `admin:members:manage`. A decided `access_request`
row outlived its decision and `_load_request` had no `status` filter, so anyone
holding the *weaker* permission could re-approve an off-boarded member back to
`active` with roles re-granted — through a path the tab never renders. Worse, **the
test that claimed to fence it was a Python mirror of the same SQL**: mutating the
guard to `status <> 'active'` passed all 28 cases.

**Round 2 — the refusal was silent.** With the guard fixed, provisioning *declined*
— and approve returned **200** anyway, stamped `approved`, recorded an audit entry,
and re-granted roles. The person stayed locked out *and* left the queue forever,
since the tab renders only `pending` and the resolver's upsert deliberately never
rewrites `status`. **The 53-knock incident, recreated by its own fix.** Closed by
`APPROVE_MATRIX`, read before anything is written:

| existing `app_user` | approve |
|---|---|
| absent / `invited` | provision `active` with the chosen roles |
| `active` | leave their roles **alone**, resolve the request, say so in `detail` |
| `suspended` / `removed` | **409**, request stays `pending` |
| unrecognised | refuse — fail closed |

That row for `active` is its own fix: `provision_member` ends in `set_roles`, which
**replaces** assignments, so approving a stale request over a live `admin` with the
picker's default silently demoted them to `member` — on the weaker permission.

**Round 3 — approve predicted the write instead of verifying it.** The matrix is
read *before* the write, which closes both sequential holes and neither concurrent
one. `_PROVISION_MEMBER_SQL`'s `CASE` arms are re-evaluated by Postgres against the
latest **committed** row (`ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE` waits on a concurrent writer, then
re-reads), so a second admin off-boarding the same person mid-flight lands every arm
on `ELSE app_user.status`. Measured, SUT unpatched:

    RESULT         : HTTP 200  status='removed'  roles=['member']
    app_user.status: removed        can they sign in? NO
    request.status : approved       still in the queue? NO, GONE

**The structural cause of all three:** `_DECIDE_SQL` was made race-safe in round 2,
but that hardened the `access_request` row only — the `app_user` row stayed a
read-then-write with no write-side guard. Now the member must actually be `active`
before the decision is stamped, or the transaction is abandoned. Predicting is an
optimisation; the read-back is the authority.

### Fences, and three admissions about them

Every non-owner case was verified red-first with signatures already in place, so
each red is the security claim rather than a `TypeError`.

**Three tests in this ticket asserted less than their docstrings claimed** — and the
third one was mine, in the fix for the second. Recorded in the spec rather than
quietly corrected:

1. `test_approving_never_un_suspends_somebody` asserted against the fake's Python
   mirror of the SQL, not the SQL. Mutating the guard left 28/28 green.
2. A UI test asserted `"setNotice" in page`, which the `useState` declaration
   satisfies alone.
3. The fail-closed-default test asserted only `status_code == 409` — which passes
   while the matrix is wide open, because the new read-back check raises *its own*
   409. The discriminator is that a matrix refusal grants no role, since `set_roles`
   runs inside `provision_member`. **Treat a bare status-code assertion in this file
   as a smell.**

Eight mutants measured red and reverted sha256-identical, including both round-3
fences:

| Mutation | Result |
|---|---|
| terminal read-back check disabled | 1 failed — captured log is the trace above verbatim |
| `APPROVE_MATRIX.get(status, "refuse")` → `"provision"` | 1 failed (the weak first version of that test **survived** it) |
| matrix `removed`/`active`/`suspended` → `provision` | 2 / 3 / 2 failed |
| `_DECIDE_SQL` drops `AND status = ANY(:allowed)` | 1 failed — **structural test only**; the fake evaluates no predicates |

### Verification

```
uv run pytest tests/unit/test_signin_requests.py -q                     -> 52 passed  (0 -> 52)
uv run pytest tests/unit/test_default_deny_auth.py \
              tests/unit/test_org_access_control.py \
              tests/unit/test_org_access_enforcement.py -q              -> 97 passed
uv run ruff check . --select F821,F601,F602,F502,F7,B006                -> All checks passed!
cd workbench/control_plane && npx tsc --noEmit                          -> exit 0
```

`test_org_access_enforcement.py` was run specifically because this adds routes under
`/admin` — where **the auth floor is per-route, not a package property**
(`_common.py` creates the router with no `dependencies=`). A route that omits
`Depends(require_admin_user)` inherits no floor at all; a wiring test pins all three.

### Also closed on the way

* **`provision_member` never called `assert_owner_survives`** while `set_roles` wipes
  assignments first — so approving an address that is the last owner, with default
  roles, left the org ownerless (recovery is hand-run SQL on prod). Pre-existing
  inside invite on `main`; the extraction hung a second route off it.
* **The queue could fail silently and look like success.** A failed fetch was
  swallowed and the tab rendered *"Nobody is waiting."* — the broken state
  indistinguishable from the working one, which is worse than the bug being fixed.
  Now a non-dismissible banner, and no false `0` badge.
* **Off-domain identities rendered as colleagues.** §6 first claimed the tenant pin
  made auto-capture safe; **it does not** — Entra B2B guests *are* directory members,
  and the gateway's own domain check is a log line, not a refusal. Marked with a chip
  and the DECISION block corrected.

### Corrections to the spec, made rather than worked around

* **N6b was written on a false premise** — "there is no `invited → active` transition
  anywhere" is **wrong**. `PATCH /admin/members/{email}` stamps `joined_at` and the
  roster already has an **Activate** button. The real defect was documentary: §2's
  runbook went Invite → Roles → Group → Verify and never said "activate", so it could
  be followed exactly and the colleague still be locked out. **Fixed as §2 Step 1b.
  No code.** Auto-promotion is now an open owner question, not a ticket.
* `invite_member` had **zero test coverage**; the characterisation test went in and
  passed *before* the extraction touched it.
* dw7's "approving twice is not an error" is **superseded** — a second approve is a
  409, marked inline. A 200 that did nothing was the escalation's vehicle.

### Not closed

* **N6b's owner question:** (a) leave activation at two clicks now that the runbook
  says so, (b) auto-promote on first sign-in, or (c) invite writes `active`. **The
  spec recommends (a)** — the measured failure was a missing sentence.
* `_record_signin_request` still swallows a failed write into a journald warning
  nobody reads. That is dw2's deliberate best-effort contract; the *user-visible*
  half of the same blindness is fixed.
* Migration 143 has **never been executed** — no local Postgres is reachable and the
  live DB is off-limits to an agent. Its first run is the deploy replay.

⚠️ **Merging is the owner gate**, not a separate apply step: `apply_migrations.sh`
replays every migration on every deploy, so the merge arms an auth-behaviour deploy.

title: N7 — you can remove anyone except yourself, by all three doors
body:
## N7 — off-boarding yourself

**WS-24 / N7** · owning spec `ai-company-brain/specs/colleague_onboarding.md` §2 Step 5.

Asked for directly: *"I should have the ability to delete users except myself. Ensure that I do not delete myself by mistake."*

### What was actually wrong — the opposite of the ask

Removal was **already** self-guarded (`members.py`, *"You cannot remove yourself."*). The problems were elsewhere:

1. **The UI had no removal control at all.** The `DELETE` route had no caller in the product.
2. **`PATCH {"status":"suspended"}` reaches the same `is_active=False` with no self-check** — its only invariant was `assert_owner_survives`.
3. **The page rendered Suspend on your own row**, because it never learned who the viewer was.

So the one off-boarding action available from the UI was the unguarded one, pointed at yourself.

`assert_owner_survives` has been standing in for a rule it is not. With exactly one owner it happens to refuse; **add a second owner — which §2 Step 2 exists to do — and either owner can suspend themselves out of admin in one click.** `admin:members:manage` is the floor for undoing it.

### Three doors, one rule

`assert_not_self_lockout` in `_common.py`, called by **both** status doors. One helper with two call sites, because a check written into only one of them is precisely how they came to disagree.

Shipped **wider than the ticket asked**: the rule is *"any status that is not `active`"*, never a list of destructive ones. `is_active` is `status == "active"` exactly, so `invited` is a lockout too — an enumeration would have had to remember that. Fenced: narrowing it to `("suspended","removed")` goes red.

**The third door was found in verification, and proved reachable rather than argued about.** `PUT /members/{email}/roles` never touches `status`, so the status guard cannot see it — but demoting yourself out of `admin:members:manage` is the same lockout, and the permission you just gave up is the floor for undoing it. In the two-owner world:

```
PUT /admin/members/owner@fracktal.in/roles {"roles":["member"]}
as owner@fracktal.in                        -> ACCEPTED
status stayed 'active'; admin:members:manage gone
```

Closed by `assert_not_self_demotion`, which decides on **the permissions the new roles grant**, not a slug allowlist — a custom role carrying the permission passes, and an owner holding `*` passes. It runs *before* `assert_owner_survives` so the caller hears the true reason instead of being told to assign another owner and then hitting the real wall.

**The guard is about the permission, not about self-editing.** Moving yourself to `admin` still leaves you able to undo it, and is allowed. A blanket "you may not touch your own roles" would have been simpler and wrong.

**A fourth door already holds** — `PUT /members/{email}/overrides` refuses self-denial of `admin:access:manage`. I nearly shipped a spec line claiming it was open; checked first, and it is not. Recorded honestly: it holds by a *fourth inline copy* of the rule, guarding a *different* permission, invisible to the enumeration test. One consolidating pass is worth doing before a second admin exists — not here, since it is a refactor of working code.

### The UI

The page now reads `access.email` (`GET /auth/me`), renders **This is you** in place of Suspend/Remove on your own row, and gains a **Remove** control on other rows with a confirmation that names the person and says every role assignment is dropped — pointing at Suspend for anyone who wanted the reversible act. Refusals surface and re-read the roster.

Hiding a control is a courtesy; all four servers-side guards are the boundary (`lib/access.ts:126-129`).

### Verification

```
uv run pytest tests/unit/test_admin_member_offboarding.py -q            -> 27 passed  (new file)
uv run pytest test_signin_requests + test_org_access_control
             + test_org_access_enforcement + test_admin_groups -q       -> 152 passed
uv run ruff check . --select F821,F601,F602,F502,F7,B006                -> All checks passed!
npx tsc --noEmit                                                        -> exit 0
npx vitest run                                                          -> 171 passed
```

**Done-when 4 is the load-bearing test:** it seeds **two** owners, so `assert_owner_survives` is silent and any refusal can only be the new guard. Deleting the guard from `update_member` fails it with `DID NOT RAISE` — proof the pre-N7 refusal was invariant 1 firing coincidentally. Both guards answer **409**, so every case discriminates on detail text *and* on what was written, never the bare status code.

Mutants, each reverted byte-identical: guard deleted from PATCH → 8 red · from DELETE → 2 red · from the roles route → 3 red · `.lower()` dropped → the casing cases · rule narrowed to the literal enumeration → 2 red · browser guard ignoring self → vitest red.

### Two fences the verifier caught, and the honesty note

- The row-wiring test asserted `index(flag) < index(call)` — which `void actions.canSuspend;` above a `{true && (` satisfies **while the control renders on your own row**. It now asserts the JSX condition itself.
- The door-enumeration test claimed to find new doors automatically. It looked at one path — which is exactly why the third door was invisible to it. Claim retracted rather than repaired.

That is the fourth test in this workstream to assert less than its docstring claimed. The pattern and its tell — a bare status-code assertion where two guards return the same code — are written into the spec and into `_admin_fakes.py`'s docstring.

### The shared fake

~200 lines moved out of `test_signin_requests.py` into `tests/unit/_admin_fakes.py` (not `test_*`, so pytest imports without collecting). Copying would have produced two mirrors, and the one that drifts is the one that stops failing. `test_signin_requests.py` is **unchanged above the first test** and still 52 passed.

### Not closed

- The consolidating pass over all four guards.
- `setStatus` still returns early on a failed PATCH, so a refused suspend leaves a stale row until refresh — the N6a lesson, outside this ticket's done-whens.

**No migration, no new permission slug.** Unlike #353, merging this does not change auth behaviour on deploy beyond the guards themselves.
